---
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:20}
  In a general preorder, joins and meets don't always exist, but just as not all limits in a category need to exist so that we can talk about them, so too can we still use the notions of joins and
  meets in general preorders. So we don't assume they exist, but do assume that they fulfill their universal property if they do.
  
  Note how this is similar to several category-theoretic notions, e.g. separated presheaves. On a deeper level, the elements of a plain monoid are only connected through its monoid
  multiplication, so
  if we make this operation partial, we suffer a big loss.\footnote{Unless, of course, we add further structure, such as a source-target typing.} But the elements of a preorder have a categorical structure that partial operations can be described through using
  universal properties. This is why it is not particularly problematic to state our definitions without existence assumptions.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{defn_:29}
\index{downward-bounded preorder}
\index{upward-bounded preorder}
  A preorder \(P\) is \emph{upward-bounded} if it has a largest element \(\top\). \(P\) is \emph{downward-bounded} if it contains a smallest element \(\bot\). \(P\) is \emph{bounded} if it is
  upward- and downward-bounded.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{defn_:58}
\index{dense element}
\index{small element}
  Given an upward-bounded preorder \(P\), an element \(a ∈ P\) is \emph{small} if the only \(b\) such that \(a ∨ b = \top\) is \(\top\).
  Dually, an element \(d\) in a downward-bounded preorder \(P\) is \emph{dense} if the only \(c\) such that \(c ∧ d = \bot\) is \(\bot\).
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{xmp:55}
  In each bounded preorder, \(\top\) is dense and \(\bot\) is small.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- terminology-1: body_md -->
\label{trm:1}
  If \(a ∨ b = \top\) we say that ``\(a\) joins with \(b\)''. More generally, if \(a ∨ b = c\) we say that ``\(a\) joins with \(b\) to \(c\)''. Dually for meets.
<!-- end terminology-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prp:1}
\index{small element!ideal property}
  The small objects of an upward-bounded preorder are stable under downward closure and binary unions, i.e. an ideal in the lattice-theoretic sense.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
\label{prf:20}
  Given \(a \leq b\) with \(b\) small and \(c ∈ P\) such that \(a ∨ c = \top\), then by monotonicity of joins \(b ∨ c = \top\), so that \(c = \top\)  by smallness.

  Now let \(a, b\) be small, \(c\) such that \((a ∨ b) ∨ c = \top\) and \(d\) be some common upper bound of \(b\) and \(c\) (one exists because \(\top\) is one). Then each common bound
  \(e\) of \(a\) and \(d\) is \(\geq (a ∨ b) ∨ c = \top\) and thus equal to \(\top\), so that \(a ∨ d\) exists and is \(\top\). So by smallness of \(a\), \(d = \top\), so \(b ∨ c = \top\), so
  \(c = \top\) by smallness of \(b\).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{xmp:9}
\index{Boolean algebra!smallness}
  No non-trivial element \(a\) of any Boolean algebra is small or dense, since it has a negation \(¬a\) such that \(a ∨ ¬ a = \top\) and \(a ∧ ¬ a = \bot\). In particular, smallness and density
  in the subobject lattice of every set are trivial.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{defn_:61}\index{unreachable preorder}
  An upward-bounded preorder \(P\) is \emph{unreachable} if \(\top\) is the only element in \(P\) that is not small.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{xmp:75}
  Any total order with a top element is unreachable.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- observation-1: body_md -->
\label{obs_:1}
\index{globe category}
\index{cube category}
\index{simplex category}
  Let \(⬢\) be any of
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:22} the simplex category \(▲\), given by the order-preserving functions between finite ordinals,

  \item\label{item:35} the cube category \(■\), given by the free strict monoidal category generated by an object \(■^{1}\) with two maps \(ι_{0}, ι_{1}{:} ■^{0}  
  \mathrel{\vcenter{\offinterlineskip
    \ialign{##\cr
       \hfil$\hookrightarrow$\hfil\cr
       \noalign{\vskip -0.3ex}
       \hfil$ 
  \scalebox{1}[-1]{\(\hookrightarrow\)}
$\hfil\cr
    }}} 
 ■^{1}\) from the monoidal
    unit \(■^{0}\), (see e.g. \cite{grandisCubicalSetsTheir})

  \item\label{item:41} the globe category \(●\), given by objects \(●^{n}, n ∈ ℕ\) with maps generated by \(σ, τ{:} ●^{n} → ●^{n + 1}\) subject to the relations \(σ⨾ σ = σ⨾ τ\) and \(τ⨾ σ = τ⨾ τ\),

  \item\label{item:42} the category of finite abstract polytopes and lattice-preserving maps \(⬟\), i.e.:

    \begin{enumerate}
    \item \label{item:43} lattices \(L\) with a top \(\top\) and a bottom \(\bot\),

    \item\label{item:44} such that all total sub-orders between \(\top\) and \(\bot\) have the same length, meaning that there exists a unique ranking function \(\mathbf{rank}{:} L → N\),

    \item\label{item:46} \(L\) is \emph{strongly connected}: for any two elements \(a, b ∈ L\) it holds that in the full sub-lattice \([a, b]\) of elements in \(L\) between \(a\) and \(b\) there exists a
      sequence connecting any two proper faces.

    \item\label{item:45} satisfies the \emph{diamond law}: if \(\mathbf{rank}(a) = \mathbf{rank}(b) - 2\) and \(a \leq b\), then there exist precisely two elements between \(a\) and \(b\).
    \end{enumerate}
  \end{enumerate}

  Then each object of \(⬢\) has only finitely many subobjects.
<!-- end observation-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{defn_:25}
  An upward-bounded preorder \(P\) is \emph{atomic} if for each non-top element \(x\) there exists an atom \(α ∈ P\) such that \(α \leq x\).
  Dually \(P\) is \emph{coatomic} if for each non-bottom element \(x\) there exists a co-atom \(ω ∈ P\) such that \(x \leq ω\).
  \(P\) is \emph{atomistic} if each element of \(P\) is the join of the atoms below it and \emph{coatomistic} dually.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{xmp:11}
  Each finite preorder \(P\) is atomic and coatomic.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:8}
  \index{small element!co-atom characterization} Let \(P\) be a coatomic upward-bounded preorder. Then \(a ∈ P\) is small if and only if it is under all co-atoms in \(P\).
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Assume \(a\) is small and let \(ω\) be a co-atom. If \(a \nleq ω\), then \(ω ∨ a\) is larger than \(ω\) and thus \(\top\). By smallness, \(ω = \top\), contradicting \(ω < \top\). Hence \(a \leq ω\).

  Conversely, suppose \(a\) lies below every co-atom and let \(b\) be such that  \(a ∨ b = \top\). If \(b \neq \top\), there exists a co-atom \(ω\) with \(b \leq ω\); then \(a ∨ b \leq ω < \top\), a
  contradiction.
  Thus \(b = \top\) and \(a\) is small.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{coR_:2}
\index{unreachable preorder!criterion}
Let \(P\) be an upward-bounded preorder bounded by exactly one co-atom. Then \(P\) is unreachable.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
\label{prf_:16}
  Since \(P\) has a co-atom \(ω\), there exists an element \(a\) below \(\top\). for any such \(a\) let \(b\) be such that \(a ∨ b = \top\). If \(b < \top\) then \(a, b \leq ω\) so that
  \(a ∨ b \leq ω < \top\). Thus, \(b = \top\).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{coR_:3}
\index{dense element!atomistic}
  Let \(P\) be atomistic with an atom. Then no non-trivial element of \(P\) is dense.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
\label{prf_:4}
  This follows immediately from the dual of \cref{■pn_:8} and \(a = ∨_{α \leq a} α\) with each \(α\) being an atom.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\index{topological density}\index{nowhere dense subset}
  \label{xmp:7}
  A closed subset \(A\) is small in the lattice (more precisely co-frame) of closeds \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) of a topological space \(X\) if and only if the only closed subset \(B\) such that
  \(A \cup B = X\) is \(X\), so if the closure of its set-theoretic complement is \(X\) itself, and hence if it is
  nowhere dense. Dually, an open subset is dense in our sense if and only if it is dense as a topological subset.

  We can also ask for dense elements of \(\mathbf{C}(X)\). If \(X\) is Hausdorff, this can only happen in trivial cases, but it is common in algebraic geometry. For
  instance, in the spectrum \(X\) of a local ring \(R\) with a maximal ideal \(m\), the closed subscheme corresponding to \(R/m\) is contained in every other closed subscheme and
  thus ``closed-dense''.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:40}
  So \cref{defn_:58} generalizes the topological notion of density. But the reason we use the name ``density'' instead of the formal dual, ``largeness'', is a categorical one: if a subobject
  \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) in a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\), then per definition \(ι ∧ κ\) is non-empty for each non-initial \(κ{:} B \hookrightarrow X\), which implies that the
  pullback \(κ^{*}(ι)\) of \(ι\) along \(κ\) exists and is non-initial. So a dense subobject is one which is non-empty in every other subobject. We will investigate such categorical
  phenomena in \cref{sec:inter-categ-size}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{xmp:63}
  \index{manifold boundary!smallness in disk category} \index{small disk} Let us study smallness in the category \(\mathbf{TDisk}\) whose objects are \(n\)-dimensional (closed)
  disks \(●^{n}\) and whose morphisms are closed continuous functions. The join \(ι ∨ ι'{:} ●^{n'} \hookrightarrow ●^{n}\) of two closed embeddings
  \(ι{:} ●^{m} \hookrightarrow ●^{n}, ι'{:} ●^{m'} \hookrightarrow ●^{n}\) is the smallest \(n'\)-dimensional disk in \(●^{n}\) containing both \(ι\) and \(ι'\), if it exists. It follows from \cref{le↘_:1}
  below that the image \(\mathbf{Im}(∂ ●^{n'})\) of the manifold-boundary of \(●^{n'}\) is contained in the set-theoretic union of \(ι\) and \(ι'\). So in particular, if
  \(ι ∨ ι' = \top_{●^{n}}\) then \(∂ ●^{n} \subseteq ι \cup ι'\), and conversely, \(\top_{●^{n}}\) is the only disk in \(●^{n}\) containing \(∂ ●^{n}\). Thus,
  \(ι ∨ ι' = \top_{●^{n}}\) if and only if \(ι \cup ι'\) contains \(∂ ●^{n}\).

  Given now \(ι{:} ●^{m} \hookrightarrow ●^{n}\), if \(ι \cap ∂ ●^{n}\) is nowhere dense in \(∂ ●^{n}\), then every closed subset \(ι'\) of \(●^{n}\) such that
  \(ι \cup ι' = ∂ ●^{n}\) has to contain \(∂ ●^{n}\), so that it has to be \(\top_{●^{n}}\). Conversely, if \(ι \cap ∂ ●^{n}\) is not nowhere dense in \(∂ ●^{n}\), then it contains an
  \((n-1)\)-dimensional disk \(κ\). Then the closure \(\overline{∂ ●^{n} ∖ κ}\) of the complement of \(κ\) in \(∂ ●^{n}\) is an \((n - 1)\)-dimensional disk \(ι'\) such that
  \(ι ∨ ι' = \top_{●^{n}}\).

                                                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                             

  So since everything is a disk the size measure becomes one on the boundary.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{le↘_:1}
  \index{manifold boundary} Let \(●^{n} \subseteq ℝ^{n}\) be the closed \(n\)-disk, and let \(ι{:} ●^{m} \hookrightarrow ●^{n}\), \(ι'{:} ●^{m'} \hookrightarrow ●^{n}\) be closed embeddings whose join
  \(ι ∨ ι'{:} ●^{n'} \hookrightarrow ●^{n}\) exists in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathbf{TDisk}}(●^{n})\). Then the image of the manifold boundary \(\partial ●^{n'} \subseteq ●^{n'}\) under
  \(ι ∨ ι'\) is contained in the set-theoretic union of the images of \(ι\) and \(ι'\).
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Write \(D := (ι ∨ ι')(●^{n'})\) for the image of the join and \(S := ι(●^{m}) ∪ ι'(●^{m'})\) for the union of the two images, so that \(D\) is a closed subset of \(●^{n}\)
homeomorphic to the closed \(n'\)-disk; we must show \(\partial D ⊆ S\). Note first that \(S\) is closed in \(●^{n}\): by the closed map lemma, \(ι\) and \(ι'\) are closed maps, since
their domains are compact and codomains are Hausdorff, so both images, and hence their union, are closed.

Suppose, for contradiction, that some boundary point \(x ∈ \partial D ∖ S\) exists. Since \(D\) is a manifold with boundary, \(x\) admits a neighborhood basis in \(D\) by sets homeomorphic to closed half-balls of \(ℝ^{n'}\). Because \(x ∉ S\) and \(S\) is closed, we may therefore choose a closed cap neighborhood \(C ⊆ D\) of \(x\) with the following properties:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \(x ∈ C^{∘}\), the interior of \(C\) in \(D\);
\item \(C ∩ S = ∅\);
\item \(C\) is strictly contained in \(D\).
\end{enumerate}

Concretely, let \(φ\) be a chart carrying a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) in \(D\) homeomorphically onto a neighborhood \(V\) of the origin in a closed half-space of \(ℝ^{n'}\), with \(φ(x) = 0\). Then \(φ(U ∩ S)\) is closed in \(V\) and does not contain the origin; since \(ℝ^{n'}\) is \(T_{4}\), a small closed half-ball about the origin avoids it, and pulling this half-ball back along \(φ\) yields \(C\).

Now cut the cap off: set \(D' := D ∖ C^{∘}\). By (2) we have \(S ⊆ D'\), while \(x ∈ C^{∘}\) ensures that \(D'\) is a proper subset of \(D\) — geometrically, we have removed from \(D\) a small boundary cap at a point lying in neither image. Moreover, \(D'\) is closed in \(D\), hence in \(●^{n}\), and up to homeomorphism it is still an \(n'\)-disk; we may therefore regard it as the image of a closed embedding \(k{:} ●^{n'} ↪ ●^{n}\). Since the images of \(ι\) and \(ι'\) both lie within \(D'\), the two embeddings factor through \(k\) as subobjects of \(\mathbf{TDisk}\). Thus \(k\) is an \(n'\)-dimensional disk of \(●^{n}\) containing \(ι\) and \(ι'\) yet strictly smaller than \(ι ∨ ι'\), contradicting the defining property of the join as the smallest such disk.

The contradiction shows that no boundary point of \(D\) lies outside \(S\); that is,
\[\partial D = (ι ∨ ι')(∂ ●^{n'}) ⊆ S = ι(●^{m}) ∪ ι'(●^{m'}),\]
as claimed.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:33}
  In \cite{schreiberDifferentialCohomologyCohesive}, Schreiber uses the category \(\mathbf{CartSp}_{top}\), whose objects are the Cartesian spaces \(ℝ^{n}\) and whose morphisms are continuous
  functions, to construct a topological model for cohesion as developed by Lawvere in e.g. \cite{lawvereCohesiveToposesCantor1994}. The objects of \(\mathbf{TDisk}\) are compactifications of the spaces \(ℝ^{n}\) and the morphisms between them are also continuous
  functions, which are closed since each closed disk is compact Hausdorff. So \(\mathbf{TDisk}\) is the compact, i.e. universally closed, analogue of \(\mathbf{CartSp}_{top}\).
  \(\mathbf{TDisk}\) will be of importance in later texts due to its site structure. From that perspective, what \cref{xmp:63} shows to us is that there is an inherent conflict between a
  rich geometry and a manageable site structure, which was known before, albeit in different contexts.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:top-manifold-with-boundary}
  \index{manifold with boundary} Given \(n ∈ ℕ\), a \emph{(not necessarily Hausdorff or second-countable) topological \(n\)-manifold with boundary} is a topological space \(M\)
  such that for every point \(x ∈ M\) there exists

  \begin{itemize}
  \item an open neighborhood \(U \subseteq M\) of \(x\), and
  \item a homeomorphism (a \emph{chart}) \(φ {:} U \xrightarrow{\;\cong\;} V\) onto an open subset \(V \subseteq H^{n}\),
  \end{itemize}

  where the \emph{closed upper half-space} \(H^{n} \subseteq ℝ^{n}\) is defined by
  \[
    H^{n} := \{ (x_1, ..., x_n) ∈ ℝ^{n} \mid x_n ≥ 0 \}
  \]

  with the induced topology. The collection of such charts is called an \emph{atlas} for \(M\).

  A point \(x ∈ M\) is called an \emph{interior point} of \(M\) if there exists a neighborhood \(U_{x}\) of \(x\) and a homeomorphism \(φ{:} U_{x} \cong ℝ^{n}\) and a \emph{boundary
    point} otherwise.

  An \emph{embedding of topological manifolds} \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow M\) is a regular monomorphism of topological spaces, i.e. a continuous injection such that each open subset of
  \(A\) is the restriction of some open of \(M\). \(ι\) is \emph{closed} if its image in \(M\) is.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:31}
  The set of all interior points of a manifold with boundary \(M\) is denoted \(M^{\circ}\); it is an open subset of \(M\) and carries the structure of a (boundaryless) \(n\)-manifold.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\label{xmp:60}
  \index{small submanifold}
  For a manifold with boundary \(X\), write \(\mathbf{SOb}_{∂ \mathbf{Mfld}}(X)\) for the preorder of closed embedded submanifolds of \(X\), ordered by inclusion.
  Then a closed submanifold \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow X\) is small in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{∂ \mathbf{Mfld}}(X)\) precisely when \(\mathbf{dim} A < \mathbf{dim} X\).
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Write \(n = \mathbf{dim} X\).

  If \(\mathbf{dim} ι < n\) we have to show that a closed submanifold of lower dimension is nowhere dense in \(X\).
  Suppose \(κ \hookrightarrow X\) is another closed submanifold with \(ι ∨ κ = X\). Then the set-theoretic union \(ι \cup κ\) has to consist of all of \(X\). To see this, assume otherwise. Then there exists a
  \(p ∈ X ∖ ι \cup κ\). Since \(X\) is a manifold, there exists a local homeomorphism \(φ_{p}\) from a neighborhood \(U\) of \(p\) to \(D\), which is either \(ℝ^{n}\) or \(ℝ^{n}_{\geq 0}\) mapping \(p\) to \(0\). Since \(ι\) and \(κ\) are closed,
  \(ι \cup κ\) is as well, so that \(φ_{p}(ι \cup κ)\) is closed in \(D\) and does not contain \(0\). Since \(ℝ\) is regular, there exists a closed disk or half disk \(●_{p}\) around \(0\) that is disjoint
  from \(φ_{p}(ι \cup κ)\), so that \(φ_{p}^{-1}(●_{p})\) is disjoint from \(ι \cup κ\). Assume now that \(Y\) is a closed submanifold with boundary containing \(ι \cup κ\) and \(p\). Then
  \(\overline{Y ∖ ●_{p}}\) is also a closed submanifold with boundary that contains \(ι \cup κ\) but does not contain \(p\). Thus, \(p\) is outside of \(ι ∨ κ\) by the minimality of the join,
  so no such \(p\) can exist.

  Now, because \(ι\) is lower-dimensional, it is nowhere dense in each coordinate chart around its points and thus nowhere dense. Thus, the interior of \(ι ∪ κ\) coincides with the interior of \(κ\).
  Hence \(κ^{\circ}\) is dense in \(X\).  As \(κ\) is closed, this forces \(κ = X\).
  Thus the only subobject joining with \(ι\) to give \(X\) is \(X\) itself, so \(ι\) is small.

  \emph{If \(\mathbf{dim} ι = n\):}
  Then \(ι\) is a closed submanifold of full dimension. Choose a closed \(n\)-disk \(κ{:} ●^{n} → ι^{\circ}\). Then \(\overline{X ∖ κ}\) is a closed submanifold with boundary and \(ι ∨ \overline{X ∖ κ} = X\), showing that \(ι\) is not small.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
\label{xmp:17}
\index{dense subgraph}
\index{small subgraph}
  Let \(G\) be a (directed) graph with vertex set \(V(G)\) and edge set \(E(G)\). Let \(\mathbf{SOb}(G)\) denote the preorder of (directed) subgraphs of \(G\), ordered by inclusion of vertices and
  edges. This is an upward-bounded preorder with top element \(\top_G = G\) and bottom element \(\bot_G = ∅\) (the empty graph on the empty vertex set). Joins of finite families of subgraphs are given
  by set-theoretic unions on both vertices and edges:
  \[
    ι_1 ∨ ι_2 \;\;=\;\; ι_1 \cup ι_2,
  \]
  and meets are intersections \(ι_1 ∧ ι_2 = ι_1 \cap ι_2\).

  Applying \cref{defn_:58} to \(\mathbf{SOb}(G)\) gives concrete notions of small and dense subgraphs:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Small subgraphs.} A subgraph \(ι \hookrightarrow G\) is small in \(\mathbf{SOb}(G)\) if the only subgraph \(κ \hookrightarrow G\) with
    \[
      ι ∨ κ \;=\; ι \cup κ \;=\; G
    \] is \(G\). Assume now that \(ι\) contains no edges or isolated vertices in \(G\). Then, since \(ι \cup κ\) has to contain all edges and isolated vertices in \(G\), \(κ\) has to
    contain them as well, so that \(κ = G\) and
    \(ι\) is small. Conversely, if \(ι\) contains an edge or an isolated vertex \(a\), then \(ι \cup (G ∖ a) = G\), so that \(ι\) is not small.


  \item \textbf{Dense subgraphs.} It follows from the dual of \cref{■pn_:8} that a subgraph is dense if and only if it contains all vertices of \(G\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:monad}
\index{monad}
  A \emph{monad} on a category \(\mathcal{C}\) consists of
  \begin{itemize}
    \item an endofunctor \(T {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}\),
    \item a natural transformation \(η {:} \mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}} \Rightarrow T\) (the \emph{unit}), and
    \item a natural transformation \(\mu {:} T^{2} \Rightarrow T\) (the \emph{multiplication})
  \end{itemize}
  such that the following diagrams commute for every \(X {:} \mathcal{C}\):
  \[
  \begin{tikzcd}
    T^{3}(X) \ar[r, "\mu_{T(X)}"] \ar[d, "T(\mu_{X})"'] & T^{2}(X) \ar[d, "\mu_{X}"] \\
    T^{2}(X) \ar[r, "\mu_{X}"'] & T(X)
  \end{tikzcd}
  \qquad
  \begin{tikzcd}
    T(X) \ar[r, "T(η_{X})"] \ar[dr, "\mathbf{id}_{T(X)}"'] & T^{2}(X) \ar[d, "\mu_{X}"] & T(X) \ar[l, "η_{T(X)}"'] \ar[dl, "\mathbf{id}_{T(X)}"] \\
    & T(X) &
  \end{tikzcd}
  \]
  Equivalently, a monad is a monoid in the monoidal category \(([\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{C}], ⨾, \mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}})\) of endofunctors with composition.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:algebra-monad}
\index{Eilenberg-Moore algebra}
\index{algebra of a monad}
  Let \((T, η, \mu)\) be a monad on \(\mathcal{C}\). A \emph{\(T\)-algebra} (or \emph{Eilenberg-Moore algebra}) is a pair \((X, \xi)\) consisting of an object \(X {:} \mathcal{C}\) and a morphism \(\xi {:} T(X) \to X\) (the \emph{structure map}) such that the diagrams
  \[
  \begin{tikzcd}
    T^{2}(X) \ar[r, "T(\xi)"] \ar[d, "\mu_{X}"'] & T(X) \ar[d, "\xi"] \\
    T(X) \ar[r, "\xi"'] & X
  \end{tikzcd}
  \qquad
  \begin{tikzcd}
    X \ar[r, "η_{X}"] \ar[dr, "\mathbf{id}_{X}"'] & T(X) \ar[d, "\xi"] \\
    & X
  \end{tikzcd}
  \]
  commute.

  A morphism of \(T\)-algebras from \((X, \xi)\) to \((Y, θ)\) is a morphism \(f {:} X \to Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) satisfying \(\xi ⨾ f = T(f) ⨾ θ\). This forms the \emph{Eilenberg-Moore category} \(\mathcal{C}^{T}\).
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:monadic-category}
\index{monadic category}
  A category \(\mathcal{A}\) is called \emph{monadic} over \(\mathcal{C}\) (or \emph{monadic} with respect to a forgetful functor \(U {:} \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{C}\)) if there exists a monad \(T\) on \(\mathcal{C}\) and an equivalence of
  categories \(\mathcal{A} \simeq \mathcal{C}^{T}\) that commutes with the forgetful functors to \(\mathcal{C}\). A functor \(U {:} \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{C}\) is \emph{monadic} if it has a left adjoint \(F\) and the comparison functor \(\mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{C}^{T}\) (where \(T\) is the induced monad) is an equivalence.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rmk:2}
  The categories of many algebraic structures such as groups, rings, modules over a fixed ring, etc. are monadic over \(\mathbf{Set}\). \(F(S)\) is given by the free algebra generated by \(S\), \(U(M)\)
  by the projection onto the underlying set and an epimorphism \(F(S) → X\) a generalized quotient by some system of algebraic relations between the elements of \(X\). So what monads really
  describe from our perspective is the idea of generation, and this is what we can use to describe smallness and density.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
\label{xmp:49}
\index{dense submonoid}
  In the lattice of submonoids of a monoid \(M\), \(ι\) is dense
  if and only if for each non-identity element \(m\) of \(M\) a non-identity power \(m^{n}\) of \(m\) is in \(ι\) (or \(M\) is trivial). This is because each non-trivial submonoid of \(M\) has to contain
  a non-identity element and thus its powers, and each submonoid \(B\) generated by elements \(b_{i}\) contains the submonoid generated by each \(b_{i}\).
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prp:density-cyclic}
\index{density!cyclic-intersection criterion}
\index{dense subalgebra!cyclic-intersection criterion}
  Let \(M\) be an algebra in a monadic category over \(\mathbf{Set}\).
  A subalgebra \(A \le M\) is dense in \(M\) if and only if for every element \(x \in M\) that does not lie in the minimal subalgebra \(\bot_{M}\),
  the cyclic subalgebra \(\langle x \rangle\) has non-trivial intersection with \(A\):
  \[
    \langle x \rangle \cap A \;\neq\; \bot_M .
  \]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
If \(A\) is dense and \(x \notin \bot_M\), then \(\langle x \rangle \neq \bot_M\), so \(\langle x \rangle \cap A \neq \bot_M\).
  Conversely, let \(B \le M\) be a non-trivial subalgebra.  Choose any \(x \in B \setminus \bot_M\); then \(\langle x \rangle \le B\).
  The hypothesis gives \(\langle x \rangle \cap A \neq \bot_M\); hence \(B \cap A \neq \bot_M\).  Thus \(A\) is dense.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:29}
  Note that this proof works whether or not \(M\) has enough atoms. If it does however, then the dual of \cref{■pn_:8} shows that a subalgebra is dense if and only if it contains
  all atoms, which can be easier to check.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{dfn:20}
\index{anchored element}
  Let \(A \le M\) be a subalgebra.
  An element \(a \in A\) is called \emph{anchored} (in \(A\)) if there exists a proper subalgebra \(B < M\) such that
  \[
    ⟨A ∪ B⟩ = M \qquad\text{and}\qquad a \notin B .
  \]
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prp:3}
\index{small element!anchor criterion}
  \(A \le M\) is small in \(\mathbf{SOb}(M)\) if and only if \(A\) contains no anchored element.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
\label{prf:2}
  \((\Rightarrow )\): If \(A\) is small and \(a \in A\) exists with \(⟨A ∪ B⟩ = M\), then smallness forces \(B = M\) so \(a ∈ B\). Hence no element of \(A\) is anchored.

  \((\Leftarrow )\): Suppose \(A\) is not small. Then there exists a proper subalgebra \(B < M\) with \(⟨A ∪ B⟩ = M\).
  Since \(B \neq M\), \(A\) cannot be contained in \(B\); pick \(a \in A \setminus B\).
  This \(B\) witnesses that \(a\) is anchored.
  Thus \(A\) contains an anchored element.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:finitary-monad}
\index{finitary monad}
  A monad \(T\) on a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is called \emph{finitary} (or \emph{filtered-colimit preserving}) if its underlying endofunctor \(T {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}\) preserves filtered colimits.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{le↘_:2}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a finitary monadic category and \(M\) an object in \(\mathcal{C}\). Then every subalgebra in \(M\) is the join of its finitely generated subalgebras.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
\label{prf_:14}
  Let \(U {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}\) be the forgetful functor, with left adjoint \(F\). The monad \(T = F⨾ U\) is finitary, hence \(T\) preserves filtered colimits. A standard result about finitary
  monads on \(\mathbf{Set}\) states that \(U\) creates (and therefore preserves) filtered colimits (see Proposition 4.3.2 of \cite{borceuxHandbookCategoricalAlgebra1994}).

  Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be the set of all finitely generated subalgebras of \(M\) contained in some subalgebra \(A\). Order \(\mathcal{F}\) by inclusion. If \(F_{1}, F_{2} \in \mathcal{F}\) are generated by the finite sets \(S_{1}, S_{2} \subseteq U(A)\), then the
  subalgebra generated by \(S_{1} \cup S_{2}\) is again in \(A\), finitely generated and contains both \(F_{1}\) and \(F_{2}\); hence \(\mathcal{F}\) is a directed set.

  Consider the directed diagram \(D {:} \mathcal{F} \hookrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(M)\) that sends each finitely generated subalgebra to its inclusion in \(M\). Since \(U\) creates filtered colimits, the colimit
  \(A\) of \(D\) exists and is created by the set-theoretic colimit of the underlying sets. The underlying sets of the subalgebras in \(\mathcal{F}\) are subsets of \(U(A)\) and the union of the
  underlying sets of all \(F \in \mathcal{F}\) is exactly \(U(A)\) (every element \(a \in U(A)\) lies in the subalgebra it generates, which is finitely generated). Thus the colimit
  \(\varinjlim_{F \in \mathcal{F}} U(F)\) is equivalent to \(U(A)\) through the map induced by the canonical inclusions.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{dfn:22}
  \index{non-generator}\index{Frattini subalgebra}
  In an algebraic category \(\mathcal{C}\) an element \(g \in M\) is a \emph{non-generator} if for every subset \(S \subseteq M\)

  \[
    \langle S \cup \{g\} \rangle = M \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \langle S \rangle = M .
  \]

  The diagram of all finitely generated subalgebras of non-generators of \(M\) is finitely directed, so if \(\mathcal{C}\) is finitary, then its colimit is the union of its underlying sets. This is
  called the \emph{Frattini subalgebra} \(Φ(M)\) of \(M\).
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prp:frattini-nongenerator}
\index{non-generator!characterization}
In any finitary algebraic category \(\mathcal{C}\), let \(M\) be an object.  An element \(g \in M\) is a non-generator if and only if \(g\)
  belongs to every maximal proper subalgebra of \(M\).
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Denote by \(\mathbf{SOb}(M)\) the lattice of subalgebras of \(M\); its meet is intersection and the join of a set of subalgebras is the subalgebra generated by their union. Because
  \(\mathcal{C}\) is finitary, every subalgebra is the join of its finitely generated subalgebras.

  Let \(g\) be a non-generator and \(N < M\) a maximal proper subalgebra. If \(g \notin N\), then \(N \subsetneq \langle N \cup \{g\} \rangle\). By maximality the only larger subalgebra is
  \(M\), hence \(\langle N \cup \{g\} \rangle = M\). Since \(g\) is a non-generator, this forces \(\langle N \rangle = M\), contradicting that \(N\) is proper. Thus \(g\) is in every maximal proper subalgebra.

  Conversely, assume \(g\) lies in every maximal proper subalgebra of \(M\). For every subset \(S \subseteq M\) with \(\langle S \cup \{g\} \rangle = M\) but \(\langle S \rangle \neq M\) the subalgebra
  \(H := \langle S \rangle\) is proper and does not contain \(g\) (otherwise \(H = M\)). If \(H\) were in a maximal subalgebra \(H'\) then \(\langle S \cup \{g\} \rangle \subseteq H'\), so \(H\) cannot lie in any
  maximal subalgebra. Thus, there has to exist an infinite chain \(H < H_{1} < ... < M\) such that \(g\) is not in any \(H_{i}\). But by Zorn's lemma, the chain \(H_{i}\) has an
  upper bound, so any maximal such chain is bounded by a maximal subalgebra, which does not contain \(g\) since \(\mathcal{C}\) is finitary and is thus proper. Consequently no such \(S\)
  exists, so that \(g\) must be a non-generator.

  Note that this argument does not require the \emph{a
    priori} existence of any maximal proper subalgebra; if there are none, the condition is vacuously true for every \(g\), and the proof
  above shows that then every element is a non-generator — which matches the intersection over the empty family being the whole algebra.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:finitely-generated-algebra}
\index{finitely generated algebra}
  Let \(T\) be a finitary monad on \(\mathbf{Set}\). A \(T\)-algebra \((X, \xi)\) is called \emph{finitely generated} if there exists a finite set  \(K\) and an epimorphism of \(T\)-algebras \(F(K) \twoheadrightarrow (X, \xi)\) from the free \(T\)-algebra \(F(K)\) onto \((X, \xi)\).
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:enough-coatoms-fg}
  Let \(T\) be a finitary monad on \(\mathbf{Set}\) and \((X,\xi)\) a finitely generated \(T\)-algebra.
  Then the subalgebra lattice \(\mathbf{SOb}\bigl((X,\xi)\bigr)\) is coatomic.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Because \(T\) is finitary, the forgetful functor \(U {:} \mathbf{Set}^{T} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Set}\) creates filtered colimits; in particular, for any filtered family of subalgebras the underlying set
  of the colimit is the union of the underlying sets. Hence a chain of subalgebras of \((X,\xi)\) has a subalgebra as its union.

  Since \((X,\xi)\) is finitely generated, there exists an epimorphism \(e{:} F(K) \twoheadrightarrow (X,\xi)\). Since \(F\) is free, \(e\) is uniquely induced by a function
  \(\mathopen{∣}e\mathclose{∣}{:} K → \mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣}\) to the underlying set \(\mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣}\), so that \((X,\xi)\) itself is the only subalgebra that contains the set-theoretic image \(\mathopen{∣}e\mathclose{∣}(K)\) of \(K\).

  Let \(A \subsetneq X\) be a proper subalgebra. Consider the poset
  \[
    \mathcal{P} \;=\; \{\, B \le X \;|\; A \le B \;\text{and}\; B \neq X \,\},
  \]
  ordered by inclusion. That poset is non-empty because \(A \in \mathcal{P}\). Let \((B_{i})_{i \in I}\) be a chain in \(\mathcal{P}\) and set \(B := \bigcup_{i} B_{i}\) as the set-theoretic union. As noted,
  \(B\) is a subalgebra of \(X\) and clearly contains \(A\). If \(B = X\) then each of the finitely many generators \(k \in K\) lies in some \(B_{i}\); because the chain is totally ordered and
  \(K\) is finite, there exists an index \(i_{0}\) with \(K \subseteq B_{i_{0}}\). Since \(B_{i_{0}}\) is a subalgebra containing a generating set, we obtain \(B_{i_{0}} = X\), contradicting
  \(B_{i_{0}} \in \mathcal{P}\). Therefore \(B \neq X\) and \(B \in \mathcal{P}\); in other words, every chain in \(\mathcal{P}\) has an upper bound in \(\mathcal{P}\).

  By Zorn's Lemma, \(\mathcal{P}\) contains a maximal element \(M\). This \(M\) is a proper subalgebra of \(X\) that contains \(A\) and admits no proper intermediate subalgebra; hence \(M\) is a
  maximal proper subalgebra and so a co-atom of \(\mathbf{SOb}((X,\xi))\).
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prp:5}\index{smallness and the frattini subalgebra}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a finitary algebraic category and \(M{:}\mathcal{C}\). Let \(A\) be a subalgebra of \(M\).

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:108}   \(\mathbf{S}(M) \subseteq Φ(M)\).

  \item\label{item:132}    If \(M\) is coatomic (e.g. if \(M\) is finitely generated), then the converse holds and thus
    \[Φ(M) \subseteq \mathbf{S}(M)\].
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
\label{prf:7}
  Suppose \(A\) is small. Let \(N\) be any maximal proper subalgebra. If \(A \nsubseteq N\), then \(A ∨ N = M\) (by maximality of \(N\)), but \(N \neq M\), contradicting smallness of
  \(A\). Hence \(A ⊆ N\) for every maximal proper subalgebra, so \(A ⊆ Φ(M)\).

  \cref{item:132} follows from \cref{■pn_:8}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- example-10: body_md -->
\label{xmp:8}
  \index{small submonoid}
    In the lattice of submonoids of a monoid \(M\), the join \(ι ∨ κ\) is given by the completion of the set-theoretic union \(ι \cup κ\) under multiplication. By \cref{prp:3}, \(ι\) is small if
  and only if it contains no anchored element, and if \(M\) is finitely generated, this is the same as being in the intersection of all maximal subalgebras.
<!-- end example-10 -->
<!-- counterexample-1: body_md -->
\label{cxmp:7}
  Work in the finitary algebraic category of abelian groups and let \(M = \mathbb{Q}\).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \(\mathbb{Q}\) is divisible, hence so is every quotient. The only simple abelian groups are the cyclic groups \(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\) for primes \(p\), and none of these is divisible
    (multiplication by \(p\) is the zero map). Consequently \(\mathbb{Q}\) admits no maximal proper subgroup, and the Frattini subgroup \(Φ(\mathbb{Q})\) is the intersection over the empty family
    and thus \(\mathbb{Q}\) itself.

  \item Fix a prime \(p\) and set
  \[
    A \;=\; \mathbb{Z}_{(p)} \;=\; \left\{\frac{a}{b} \in \mathbb{Q} \;\middle|\; \gcd(b,\, p) = 1\right\}, \qquad
    B \;=\; \mathbb{Z}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{p}\right] \;=\; \left\{\frac{a}{p^{k}} \;\middle|\; a \in \mathbb{Z},\; k \geq 0\right\}.
  \]
  Both are proper subgroups of \(\mathbb{Q}\): \(\tfrac{1}{p} \notin A\) and \(\tfrac{1}{q} \notin B\) for any prime \(q \neq p\). Yet \(A ∨ B = A + B = \mathbb{Q}\). Indeed, any element of \(\mathbb{Q}\) can be written
  \(\frac{a}{p^{k}m}\) with \(\gcd(m,\, p) = 1\), and Bézout's identity supplies integers \(r,\, s\) with \(rm + sp^{k} = 1\), so that
  \[
    \frac{1}{p^{k}m} \;=\; \frac{r}{p^{k}} + \frac{s}{m} \;\in\; B + A.
  \]

\item Thus \(A\) joins with the proper subgroup \(B\) to the top element \(\top = \mathbb{Q}\), so that \(A\) is not small, even though \(A \subseteq \mathbb{Q} = Φ(\mathbb{Q})\).
  \end{itemize}
<!-- end counterexample-1 -->
<!-- example-11: body_md -->
\label{xmp:50}
  \index{small submodule}\index{dense submodule}
  In the module theory of rings, the joins are sums of submodules and meets are set-theoretic intersections. There, smallness is also called
  \emph{superfluousness} while density is called \emph{essentiality}.
<!-- end example-11 -->
<!-- example-12: body_md -->
\label{xmp:18}
  \index{small closed subscheme} Let \(X\) be an affine scheme represented by a ring \(R\) and \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) its lattice of closed subschemes. This is dual to the lattice of quotient
  rings of \(R\) and thus that of ideals in \(R\). Since these are modules, this is actually a special case of \cref{xmp:50}. So for any proper ideal \(ι{:} I \hookrightarrow R\) the
  corresponding subscheme \(\mathbf{Sch}(ι): \mathbf{Sch}(R / I) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{Sch}(X)\) is small if and only if \(ι\) is dense. Nevertheless, a general formula is still hard to pin down. The
  most important cases are clear however:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{item:18}
    If \(ι\) contains a non-zero-divisor \(a\), then for each \(κ{:} K \hookrightarrow R\) such that \(ι ∧ κ = ι \cap κ = \{0\}\) and each \(k \in K \setminus \{0\}\), it holds that \(ak \neq 0\) since \(a\) is a non-zero-divisor, yet \(ak \in ι \cap κ = \{0\}\), a contradiction. So \(κ =
    \{0\}\). So \(ι\) is dense.

    These ideals are of Krull height \(> 0\) and thus their subschemes are lower-dimensional, in line with the case of manifolds. The difficulty is with the zero-divisors.

  \item\label{item:19} If \(R\) is reduced, \(ι\) consists of zero-divisors and there exists a \(b ∈ \mathbf{Ann}(ι)\) that is not in \(ι\), then the intersection \((b) \cap ι\) of the ideal
    generated by \(b\) with \(ι\) consists of elements \(br = i\) with \(r ∈ R, i ∈ ι\). But also \(bi = 0\) since \(i\) is in \(ι\), so that \(bbr = 0\) and in particular
    \((br)^{2} = brbr = (bbr)r = 0\) by commutativity. So \(br = 0\) since \(R\) is reduced, and so \(i = 0\), which means that \((b) \cap ι = (b) \cap \{0\}\). Thus, \(ι\) is not dense.

    But not all ideals of zero-divisors have a non-empty annihilator. A ring in which every finitely generated ideal of zero-divisors has a non-empty annihilator is said to have
    \emph{Property A}. This includes all Noetherian rings but also many others, see \cite{azarpanahIdealsConsistingEntirely2000}. Geometrically, non-nilpotent zero-divisors correspond to
    pieces of \(X\) with the same dimension, so at least in the finite-dimensional case the pieces of \(X\) outside of  the subscheme \(\mathbf{Sch}(ι)\) can be brought into a
    common ideal. So an equidimensional piece is never small (if \(R\) is reduced and Noetherian, of course).

  \item\label{item:20} If on the other hand \(R\) is not reduced and \(ι\) contains its annihilator \(\mathbf{Ann}(ι)\), then for any other non-zero ideal \(κ\), \(ικ \subseteq ι \cap κ\). If \(ικ ≠ \{0\}\) then \(ι \cap κ ≠ \{0\}\); if \(ικ = \{0\}\) then \(κ \subseteq \mathbf{Ann}(ι) \subseteq ι\), so \(ι \cap κ = κ ≠ \{0\}\). Either way, \(ι\) is dense. This is the case for instance for \((x)\) in \(R[x] / x^{n}\) (or more generally \(R[x, \overline{y}] / x^{n}\)). Here, \((x)\) corresponds to the
    quotient \(R[x]/x^{n} → R{:} x ↦ 0\) and thus the embedding of the reduced part of an infinitesimally thickened point.

  \item\label{item:131} We can also ask for what happens when an infinitesimally thickened point is embedded into a line. This amounts to asking whether the ideal \((x^{n})\) is dense in
    \(R[x]\) and thus is a special case of \cref{item:18}. So even though an infinitesimal thickening appears higher-dimensional than its reduction in itself (\((x)\) has Krull height 1 in
    \(R[x] / x^{n}\)), it seems lower-dimensional within \(R[x]\).
  \end{enumerate}

  So the general pattern is clear: if an embedding is lower-dimensional or (relatively) reduced in an infinitesimally thickened scheme, then it is small, if it is some equidimensional
  equally infinitesimally extended part it is not, except perhaps with infinite-dimensional shenanigans.

  \index{Jacobson radical} On the other hand, note that by Zorn's Lemma every ideal is bounded by some maximal ideal, so that the collection of small elements is the set of those elements
  that are below every maximal ideal by \cref{■pn_:8}. Since ideals are stable under intersections, this set is an ideal, which is also known as the \emph{Jacobson radical} (at least in the
  commutative case). Note that this means that the dual of the Jacobson-radical is the smallest ``closed-dense'' subscheme of \(X\). By duality, this is the smallest subscheme of \(X\) that
  contains all points of \(X\) which are minimal in that their corresponding ideal is maximal (not the points of minimal primes!).
<!-- end example-12 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rmk:15}
  We can use the results of \cref{sec:inter-categ-size} to extend smallness and density into general schemes.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- example-13: body_md -->
\label{xmp:14}
  \index{semialgebraic set!smallness} Let \(\mathbf{SAlg}(R^{n})\) be the lattice of semialgebraic subsets of \(R^{n}\), so of finite unions of finite intersections of polynomial
  equalities \(p = q\) and strict polynomial inequalities \(p < q\). It is well-known that \(\mathbf{SAlg}(R^{n})\) is closed under (Boolean) complementation. As a consequence,
  (absolute) size is trivial in \(\mathbf{SAlg}(R^{n})\). But we can define a semialgebraic set as

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:109} \emph{open} if it can be defined solely through strict inequalities \(p < q\),

  \item\label{item:110} \emph{closed} if it can be defined solely through equalities \(p = q\) or inequalities \(p \leq q\).
  \end{enumerate}

  In particular, a closed semialgebraic subset \(ι\) is small in the lattice of closed semialgebraic subsets \(\mathbf{CSSAlg}(R^{n})\) if and only if it can be covered by a union
  of intersections of polynomial equalities, so if and only if it is lower-dimensional or equivalently if it can be contained in a finite number of algebraic varieties by
  \cref{prop:semialg-small-algebraic} below. Density meanwhile is trivial in \(\mathbf{CSSAlg}(R^{n})\) since it is atomistic, but of course the considerations for smallness in
  \(\mathbf{CSSAlg}(R^{n})\) are purely dual to those for density in the lattice of open semialgebraic subsets \(\mathbf{OSSAlg}(R^{n})\), which are only given through strict
  polynomial inequalities. Thus, \(\mathbf{SAlg}(R^{n})\) is kind of like a version of the topology of \(R^{n}\) that is small enough to be algebraically tractable. This is not a
  coincidence — semialgebraic subsets are a smaller but in some ways better-behaved version of the semi-analytic subsets that Grothendieck cites as a possible model for his vision
  of a tame topology in \emph{Esquisse
    d'un Programme}\cite{grothendieckSketchProgramme}:

  \begin{quote}
    It soon appeared that there could be no question of getting such an ambitious statement in the framework of topological spaces, because of the sempiternal ``wild'' phenomena… It was also clear that the contexts of the most rigid structures which existed then, such as the
    ``piecewise linear'' context were equally inadequate — one common disadvantage consisting in the fact that they do not make it possible, given a pair (U, S) of a ``space''
    \(U\) and a closed subspace \(S\), and a glueing map \(f {:} S → T\) , to build the corresponding amalgamated sum. Some years later, I was told of Hironaka's theory of what he
    calls, I believe, (real) ``semi-analytic'' sets which satisfy certain essential stability conditions (actually probably all of them), which are necessary to develop a usable
    framework of ``tame topology''.
  \end{quote}

  Both semialgebraic and semianalytic sets feature an instance of an open-closed duality in the sense that we will develop in \cref{sec:open-clos-dual}.
<!-- end example-13 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:semialg-small-algebraic}
\index{semialgebraic set!smallness characterization}
  Let \(\mathbf{CSSAlg}(R^{n})\) be the preorder of closed semialgebraic subsets of \(R^{n}\) ordered by inclusion, regarded as an upward-bounded preorder with top \(\top = R^{n}\).
  For \(A ∈ \mathbf{CSSAlg}(R^{n})\), the following are equivalent:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \(A\) is \emph{small} in the sense of \cref{defn_:58}.
  \item \(A\) has empty interior in \(R^{n}\).
  \item \(\mathbf{dim} A < n\).
  \item \(A\) is covered by a finite union of (real) proper algebraic subvarieties of \(R^{n}\), i.e. sets of the form
    \[
      V(p_{1},\dots,p_{k}) = \{x ∈ R^{n} \mid p_{1}(x)=\dots=p_{k}(x)=0\}.
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
We proceed in steps.

  \emph{(1) ⇔ (2).}
  In \(\mathbf{CSSAlg}(R^{n})\), finite joins are given by set-theoretic unions: if \(A,B\) are closed semialgebraic, then \(A ∨ B = A ∪ B\), since the union of closed
  semialgebraic sets is again closed semialgebraic and minimal with this property. Thus (1) says that the only closed semialgebraic \(B\) with \(B ⊇ R^{n} \setminus A\) is \(B=R^{n}\).
  This is equivalent to
  \[
    \overline{R^{n} \setminus A} = R^{n},
  \]
  where the closure is in the Euclidean topology. But \(\overline{R^{n} \setminus A} = R^{n}\) if and only if \(A^{\circ} = ∅\), since
  \[
    A^{\circ} = R^{n} \setminus \overline{R^{n} \setminus A}.
\]

  \emph{(2) ⇔ (3).}
  A semialgebraic subset \(A ⊆ R^{n}\) has nonempty interior if and only if
  \(\mathbf{dim} A = n\). This is a standard fact of semialgebraic geometry. For \(\Rightarrow\), take \(x ∈ A^{\circ}\). Then there exists a ball \(●_{x} \subseteq A^{\circ}\) since \(R^{n}\) is regular Hausdorff, so that \(\mathbf{dim}(A) = n\).
  Conversely, it follows immediately from the Euclidean topology that if \(\mathbf{dim}(A) < n\) then \(A\) has an empty interior.

  \emph{(3) ⇔ (4).}
  Suppose \(\mathbf{dim} A < n\) and \(A\) is closed semialgebraic. We may write \(A\) as a finite union of semialgebraic subsets \(P_{i}\) each of which is of codimension at least \(1\). Each such piece lies inside an
  algebraic hypersurface, meaning the zero set of a nonzero polynomial. Thus, there exist finitely many polynomial maps \(f_{1},\dots,f_{r}\) such that
  \[
    A \subseteq \bigcup_{j=1}^{r} V(f_{j}).
  \]

  Conversely, if \(A\) is covered by a finite union of algebraic varieties in \(R^{n}\), each such variety is a real algebraic set of dimension at most \(n\), and if \(A\) had dimension \(n\), one of its
  components would contain a nonempty open subset of \(R^{n}\), which is impossible unless that component is all of \(R^{n}\) since a proper real algebraic subvariety of \(R^{n}\) has dimension strictly less than \(n\). Thus if \(A\) is a
  proper closed subset and covered by a finite union of algebraic varieties, then \(\mathbf{dim} A < n\). Hence (4) implies (3) in the nontrivial case \(A ≠ R^{n}\); for \(A=R^{n}\) all four conditions fail.

  Combining the implications, we obtain (1) ⇔ (2) ⇔ (3) ⇔ (4).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- example-14: body_md -->
\label{xmp:3}
\index{subobject preorder!of preorders}
  Let \(\mathbf{PrO}\) be the category whose objects are preorders \((P, \le_P)\) and morphisms \(ι {:} P → Q\) are monotone (order-preserving) maps. Then for each \(P\), the subobject
  preorder \(\mathbf{SOb}(P)\) has as objects monomorphisms into \(P\), so order-preserving injections. This is a lattice where, given \(ι{:} Q \hookrightarrow P, κ{:} R \hookrightarrow P\):

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:4} the meet \(ι ∧ κ = ι \cap κ\) is given on elements by the intersection of the images of \(ι\) and \(κ\), such that for \(a, b ∈ ι ∧ κ\) it holds that \(a \leq b\) if and
    only if \(a \leq_{ι} b\) and \(a \leq_{κ} b\),

  \item\label{item:5} the join \(ι ∨ κ\) is the completion of the set-theoretic union under composition, so is given on elements by the set-theoretic union and such that for
    \(a, b ∈ ι ∨ κ\) it holds that \(a \leq b\) if and only if there exist families of elements \(c_{i} ∈ ι ∧ κ\) such that
    \(a \leq_{S} c_{0} \leq_{T} c_{1} ... \leq_{S} c_{n} \leq_{T} b\) with \(S = Q\) if \(a ∈ \mathbf{Im}(ι)\) and \(R\) otherwise, and similar for \(T\) and \(b\).
  \end{enumerate}

 We can describe the size of each
  \(ι{:} Q \hookrightarrow P\).

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{item:134} \textbf{Density} Since the meets in \(\mathbf{SOb}(P)\) are given by set-theoretic intersections, density is similar to \cref{xmp:17}. In particular,
    \(\bot\) is the empty embedding and \(\mathbf{SOb}(P)\) has enough atoms. So by the dual of \cref{■pn_:8}, \(ι\) is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}(P)\) if and only if it contains all
    atoms, i.e. one-element-embeddings into \(P\).

  \item \label{item:133} \textbf{Smallness} Since the join is given objectwise by the set-theoretic union and sequences of inequalities, any \(κ\) such that \(ι ∨ κ = \top\) has to
    generate all inequalities with \(ι\). Thus, \(κ\) has to contain all inequalities \(a \leq_{P} b\) with \(b ∈ ι\) such that there is no \(c ∈ ι\) such that
    \(a \leq c <_{ι} b\), so it has to contain each such \(b\). Thus, if \(ι\) does not contain any non-trivial inequalities and \(P\) does, then \(ι\) is small. More generally, let
    \(a < c < b\) in \(P\) be such that \(a <_{ι} b\) but not \(c ∈ ι\). Then \(κ\) has to contain all of \(a < c < b\) and thus \(a <_{κ} b\). Thus, if \(ι\) contains only
    morphisms in its image that are compositions of morphisms outside its image, then \(ι\) is small.

    Conversely, assume that \(ι\) contains a morphism \(a < b\) such that there
    does not exist a factorization of this morphism into morphisms outside the image of \(ι\) and let \(κ := \top ∖ (a < b)_{ι}\) be given by removing all morphisms from \(\top\) that
    \(a < b\) factors through and that are in the image of \(ι\). Then \(κ\) does not contain the chain of inequalities between \(a\) and \(b\) and thus \(a \cancel{<_{κ}} b\) but
    \(ι ∨ κ = \top\), so \(ι\) is not small.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end example-14 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:ff-es}
\index{fully faithful functor}
\index{full functor}
\index{faithful functor}
  Let \(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\) be categories and \(F {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) a functor.

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \(F\) is \emph{faithful} if for all objects \(X,Y {:} \mathcal{C}\) the function
    \[
      F_{X,Y} {:} \mathcal{C}(X,Y) \to \mathcal{D}(F(X),F(Y)),\quad f \mapsto F(f)
    \]
    is injective.  Equivalently, whenever \(f,g {:} X \to Y\) satisfy \(F(f) = F(g)\), we must have \(f = g\).

  \item \(F\) is \emph{full} if for all objects \(X,Y {:} \mathcal{C}\) the function \(F_{X,Y}\) is surjective.  Equivalently, every morphism \(h {:} F(X) \to F(Y)\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) is of the form \(h = F(f)\) for some \(f {:} X \to Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\).

  \item \(F\) is \emph{fully faithful} if it is both full and faithful, i.e. for every pair \(X,Y {:} \mathcal{C}\) the map
    \[
      F_{X,Y} {:} \mathcal{C}(X,Y) \to \mathcal{D}(F(X),F(Y))
    \]
    is a bijection.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- example-15: body_md -->
\label{xmp:4}\index{subcategory}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category and \(\mathbf{SOb}'_{\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}}(\mathcal{C})\) the preorder whose elements are faithful functors
  \(ι {:} \mathcal{D} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{C}\), ordered by \(ι \le κ\) if \(ι\) factors through \(κ\) up to isomorphism. The top element is \(\mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}}\); the bottom is the empty embedding.

  Joins in this preorder exist and are generated by the set-theoretic union by closure under morphisms. It follows again from the dual of \cref{■pn_:8} that a subcategory is dense if and only
  if it contains all objects of \(\mathcal{C}\).

  In general, \(\mathbf{SOb}'_{\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}}\) is a little pathological: for instance, the function between cardinals \([2] → [1]\) is a faithful functor (though it is not full) and
  thus in \(\mathbf{SOb}'_{\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}}\). But the defining condition makes it so that each faithful functor \(ι\) is equivalent to its image, literally given in
  terms of object and morphism sets. So for instance \(\mathbf{SOb}'_{\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}}([1])\) is not even a small category but equivalent to the one-object category. We
  can avoid this pathology by restricting to faithful functors that are also isomorphism-reflecting. So we define \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}}\) to consist of the
  isomorphism-reflecting faithful functors.
<!-- end example-15 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{defn_:12}
  A\emph{subcategory} \(ι{:} \mathcal{C} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{D}\) is an isomorphism-reflecting faithful.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{def:anchored-cat}
\index{anchored morphism}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category and let \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}}(\mathcal{C})\) as in \cref{xmp:4}. A morphism \(f\) of \(\mathcal{C}\) is \emph{anchored} relative
  to a subcategory \(ι{:} \mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{C}\) if there exists a subcategory \(κ\) such that in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}}(\mathcal{C})\)
      \[
        ι ∨ κ = \mathcal{C}
        \qquad\text{and}\qquad
        f \notin κ .
      \]
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{dfn:21}
\index{irreducible morphism}
  A morphism \(f\) of a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is called \emph{\(ι\)-irreducible} for a subcategory \(ι {:} \mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{C}\) if \(f\) is either an identity or cannot be written as a
  composite of the form  \(f = g⨾ h⨾ i\) where at least one of \(g, h, i\) is a non-identity in \(\mathcal{A}\).
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prp:7}\index{categorial smallness criterion}
  Let \(ι{:} \mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{C}\) be a faithful subcategory. Assume that every non-identity morphism \(f\) in \(ι\) admits a factorization
\[
  f \;=\; g_1 ⨾ g_2 ⨾ \dots ⨾ g_n
\]
into finitely many morphisms \(g_i\) that are \(ι\)-irreducible and not in \(ι\). Then \(ι\) is small in the
upward-bounded preorder of faithful subcategories of \(\mathcal{C}\).
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
\label{prf:5}
  We prove that under this hypothesis, \(ι\) cannot contain any anchored morphism.

  Given \(f\) in \(ι\) and a proper faithful subcategory \(κ \subsetneq \mathcal{C}\) such that \(ι ∨ κ \;=\; \mathcal{C}\) we may write \(f \;=\; g_1 ⨾ g_2 ⨾ \dots ⨾ g_n\) where each \(g_i\) is
  \(ι\)-irreducible. Hence \(g_i \notin ι\).

  Now, because \(ι ∨ κ = \mathcal{C}\), every morphism of \(\mathcal{C}\) can be expressed as a composition of morphisms taken from \(ι \cup κ\). In particular, for each \(i\) we can choose one such representation
  of \(g_i\):
  \[
    g_i \;=\; h_{i1} ⨾ h_{i2} ⨾ \dots ⨾ h_{ik_i}, \qquad h_{ij} \in ι \cup κ .
  \]

  Since morphisms are closed under composition and \(g_i\) is \(ι\)-irreducible, its representation cannot contain a non-identity factor from \(ι\). Therefore none of the \(h_{ij}\) belong to \(ι\). Consequently every \(h_{ij}\) lies in \(κ\).

  Thus each \(g_i\) is a composition of morphisms of \(κ\) and therefore belongs to the subcategory \(κ\). Finally \(f = g_1 ⨾ \dots ⨾ g_n\) is also a
  composition of morphisms in \(κ\), whence \(f \in κ\). Thus, no morphism of \(ι\) is anchored, so \(ι\) is small.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:4}
  This works great for preorders or deloopings of monoids without inverses but does not work for deloopings of groups or categories with non-trivial automorphism categories.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- example-16: body_md -->
\label{xmp:5}
\index{subobject preorder!2-categorical}
Given a category \(\mathcal{C}\), let \(\mathbf{SOb}_{f}\) be the preorder whose elements are subcategories and  \(ι \leq κ\) if and only if there exists a functor \(λ{:} \mathcal{D} → \mathcal{E}\) and a monic natural transformation \(Φ{:} ι \leq λ⨾ κ\):

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=small]
      \mathcal{E} \ar[dr, "κ"] & \\
      & \mathcal{C} \\
      \mathcal{D} \ar[uu, "λ"]\ar[ur, "ι"', ""{name=S}] \arrow[Rightarrow, from=S, to=1-1, "Φ", shorten >=6pt]
    \end{tikzcd}
                                 
  \end{figure}

  This is a less truncated structure than \cref{xmp:4}, but its smallness relations stay the same: \(\top\) is still \(\mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}}\), \(\bot = ∅\) and the join is given by the closure of the union of
  the subcategories under composition. The meet is interesting however: \(ι ∧ κ\) is the full subcategory on objects that are simultaneously subobjects of something in \(\mathcal{C}_{ι}\) and of something
  in \(\mathcal{C}_{κ}\) in some way. So the dense elements are different from those in \cref{xmp:4} : \(ι\) is dense if and only if it contains for each object \(X\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) some object \(A\) that
  is a subobject of \(X\). In particular, if \(\mathcal{C}\) contains an initial object whose universal morphisms are monic, then a subcategory is dense if and only if it contains that.

  Note that the
  dual statement is not true for the terminal object even if the morphisms into it are monic, which is also a much rarer assumption. This is because of the variance of the 2-cells in it
  (which would be necessary to define filters, for instance). \(\mathbf{SOb}_{f}\) will be central in \cref{sec:covar-repr-theor} but
  \cref{rmα_:9} would not work for either \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}}\) or the 2-dual of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{f}\). So here we can already begin to see that the entire structure
  we are describing is of one piece and it is all \emph{covariant} on the lowest level (the variance on higher levels will grow quite complex in \cref{sec:univ-char-mathbf}).
<!-- end example-16 -->
<!-- example-17: body_md -->
\label{xmp:29}
  Let \(\mathbf{SOb}_{ff}(\mathcal{C})\) be the quotient of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{f}(\mathcal{C})\) by the equivalence relation \(ι \sim κ\) if and only if \(ι\) and \(κ\) have the same fully faithful image. Then for each \(ι\) it
  holds that \(ι\) is equivalent to the embedding \(\mathopen{∣}ι\mathclose{∣}\) of the discrete subcategory on the objects in the image of \(ι\), and for \(\mathopen{∣}ι\mathclose{∣}\) and \(\mathopen{∣}κ\mathclose{∣}\) it holds that \(\mathopen{∣}ι\mathclose{∣} \leq \mathopen{∣}κ\mathclose{∣}\) if and only if there
  exists a function \(\mathopen{∣}ι\mathclose{∣} \hookrightarrow \mathopen{∣}κ\mathclose{∣}\) and monomorphism \(I{:} \mathopen{∣}ι\mathclose{∣}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathopen{∣}κ\mathclose{∣}(X)\). So \(ι \leq κ\) in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{ff}(\mathcal{C})\) holds if each \(X\) in the image of \(ι\) is the subobject of some \(Y\) in the image of
  \(κ\). We can similarly define a quotient \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathopen{∣}ff\mathclose{∣}}(\mathcal{C})\) of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}}(\mathcal{C})\), where \(ι \leq κ\) if and only if the objects of \(ι\) are contained in the objects of \(κ\) up to
  isomorphism.

  The joins and meets of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathopen{∣}ff\mathclose{∣}}(\mathcal{C})\) can be identified with set-theoretic unions and intersections, so that both smallness and density are trivial, but
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{ff}(\mathcal{C})\) has a more interesting structure. The joins \(ι ∨ κ\) can still be identified with set-theoretic unions of the object sets and thus the only subcategory that is
  small in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{ff}(\mathcal{C})\) is \(∅\). But the meet \(ι ∧ κ\) is again the full subcategory on objects that are simultaneously subobjects of something in \(\mathcal{C}_{ι}\) and of
  something in \(\mathcal{C}_{κ}\), which is not generally the set-theoretic intersection.
<!-- end example-17 -->
<!-- example-18: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:5}
\index{wide subcategory}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category and write \(\mathbf{Wide}(\mathcal{C})\) for the preorder of wide subcategories of \(\mathcal{C}\) (i.e. subcategories having all objects of
  \(\mathcal{C}\)), ordered by inclusion of morphism sets. We can construct this category as the preorder of faithful isomorphism-reflecting factorizations of the functor
  \(\mathbf{Disc}(\mathcal{C}){:} \mathbf{Ob}(\mathcal{C}) \hookrightarrow \mathcal{C}\). The top element is \(\mathcal{C}\) itself; the bottom is the discrete wide subcategory
  \(\mathbf{Disc}(\mathcal{C})\) containing only identities. A wide subcategory \(ι\) is again small in \(\mathbf{Wide}(\mathcal{C})\) if and only if it does not contain an anchor. \(ι\) is dense in \(\mathbf{Wide}(\mathcal{C})\) if and only if

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item every non-endomorphism of \(\mathcal{C}\) belongs to \(ι\), and
  \item for each non-identity endomorphism \(e {:} X → X\) of \(\mathcal{C}\) there exists an integer \(n \ge 1\) such that \(e^n\) is in \(ι\) with \(e^{n}\) not an identity.
  \end{enumerate}

  To see this, note that taking the wide subcategory generated by a single non-endomorphism forces all non-endomorphisms into \(ι\); taking those generated by an endomorphism \(e\) forces some
  power of \(e\) into \(ι\). The converse is a straightforward verification using the closure properties of wide subcategories.

  So on the level of wide subcategories density starts behaving as for monoids. Note that this is similar to how the periodic table for \(k\)-tuply \(n\)-monoidal categories only works when
  we take them as pointed.\cite{baezLecturesNCategoriesCohomology2007}
<!-- end example-18 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:64}
\index{unreachable preorder!representable presheaf}
\index{representable presheaf!unreachability}
  The subobject preorder of every representable presheaf is unreachable.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
\label{prf_:83}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category, \(X\) an object of \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(F \hookrightarrow \widehat{X}\) a proper subfunctor of the functor \(\widehat{X}\) represented by \(X\). We have to show that the only \(G \hookrightarrow \widehat{X}\) such that
  \(F ∨ G = \widehat{X}\) is \(\widehat{X}\) itself. For this remember that joins of presheaves are given by objectwise set-theoretic unions \(F(Y) \cup G(Y)\). Now \(\mathbf{id}_{X}{:} X → X\) is
  the only element of \(\widehat{X}(X)\) whose presence in a sub-functor forces that sub-functor to be all of \(\widehat{X}\). Since \(F\) is proper, it does not contain
  \(\mathbf{id}_{X}\) at \(X\). But \(F(X) \cup G(X) = \widehat{X}(X)\), so \(\mathbf{id}_{X} \in G(X)\). By Yoneda closure, this forces \(G = \widehat{X}\).
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:13}
  At least if \(\mathcal{C}\) is monic and \(X\) is Dedekind-finite, i.e. has no proper self-embeddings, we can construct a co-atom \(∂ X \hookrightarrow \widehat{X}\) as the presheaf with \((∂ X)(Y)\) given by the set of morphisms \(f{:} Y → X\) such that there exists a
  \(ι{:} Z \hookrightarrow X\) with \(Z \cancel{\simeq} X\) and a \(g{:} Y → Z\) with \(f = g⨾ ι\). So we can freely construct a boundary.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:41}
  This behavior is in contrast to that of density on representable presheaves: in \cref{rmk:1} we find that for a thin subcanonical site with an initial object the Yoneda embedding is a density-equivalence. The
  behavior on general categories is currently unknown but the mere fact that the structure of the base category matters independently of the coverage is already different from the case of
  smallness, where the coverage completely mediates what is small.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rmk:5}
  \cref{■pn_:64} recontextualizes \cref{obs_:1}: generally we would think that faces, being lower-dimensional, would be small. And they are — once we add enough unions to construct a
  boundary. It is the mark of the combinatorial that there are no subcanonical coverages on a combinatorial site \(⬢\) that would make some objects in the sheaf topos \(\mathbf{Sh}(⬢)\)
  small and others not: there is only the \emph{boundary coverage}, which identifies an object with its boundary — but this recreates the original site.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{def:lax-2-functor}
\index{sub-2-category}
\index{lax 2-functor}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) and \(\mathcal{D}\) be 2-categories. A \emph{lax 2-functor} \(F {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) consists of the following data:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item A function on objects, mapping \(X {:} \mathcal{C}\) to \(F(X) {:} \mathcal{D}\).
    \item for every pair of objects \(X, Y {:} \mathcal{C}\), a functor on hom-categories
      \[
        F_{X,Y} {:} \mathcal{C}(X, Y) \to \mathcal{D}(F(X), F(Y)),
      \]
      mapping a 1-cell \(f {:} X \to Y\) to \(F(f) {:} F(X) \to F(Y)\) and a 2-cell \(α {:} f \Rightarrow g\) to \(F(α) {:} F(f) \Rightarrow F(g)\).
    \item for every object \(X {:} \mathcal{C}\), a 2-cell (the \emph{lax unitor})
      \[
        ν_{X} {:} \mathbf{id}_{F(X)} \Rightarrow F(\mathbf{id}_X).
      \]
    \item for every pair of composable 1-cells \(f {:} X \to Y\) and \(g {:} Y \to Z\) in \(\mathcal{C}\), a 2-cell (the \emph{lax compositor})
      \[
        \mu_{f,g} {:} F(f) ⨾ F(g) \Rightarrow F(f ⨾ g).
      \]
  \end{enumerate}

  Subject to the same coherence conditions as pseudofunctors. An \emph{oplax 2-functor} is defined in the same way, but with dual unitors and compositors.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{defn_:15}
  Given a 2-category \(\mathcal{B}\), a \emph{sub-2-category} \(ι{:} \mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) is a 2-functor which is injective and isomorphism-reflecting on objects, 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms. A \emph{lax
    sub-2-category} is a lax 2-functor with the same properties and dually for oplaxity.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rmk:lax-vs-pseudo}
  A pseudofunctor is precisely a lax 2-functor for which the lax unitors \(ν_X\) and lax compositors \(\mu_{f,g}\) are invertible 2-cells (i.e. equivalences in the
  hom-categories). If these 2-cells are further constrained to be identity 2-cells, \(F\) reduces to a strict 2-functor. Laxifying a pseudofunctor thus amounts to replacing
  the requirement that composition and identities are preserved up to coherent isomorphism with the weaker requirement that they are preserved only up to coherent morphisms
  pointing in a specific direction. This process is known as \emph{laxification}. Now, consider this little-appreciated fact: laxification is evil.\footnote{To the knowledge of the
    author, this was first noticed by Chris Schommer-Pries \cite{schommer-priesLaxFunctorsEquivalence2009}.}

  Let \(I\) be the 2-category with two elements \(X, Y\), morphisms generated by \(f{:} X → Y, g{:} Y → X\) and 2-cells generated by \(\mathbf{id}_{X} < f⨾ g, \mathbf{id}_{Y} < g⨾ f\).
  Let \(I_{0} = \{X, Y\}\) be the set of objects of \(I\), and let \(\mathbf{CDisc}(I_{0})\) be the codiscrete category on \(X, Y\), consisting of two morphisms \([X, Y]{:} X → Y, [Y, X]{:} Y → X\) that compose to the identities. Then there
  exists an oplax functor \(F{:} \mathbf{CDisc}(I_{0}) → I{:} [X, Y] ↦ f, [Y, X] ↦ g, \mathbf{id}_{X} ↦ \mathbf{id}_{X}, \mathbf{id}_{Y} ↦ \mathbf{id}_{Y}\) that is not equivalent to
  any constant functor, even though \(\mathbf{CDisc}(I_{0})\) is equivalent to the point.

  What should we make of that?

  Should we use lax \emph{anafunctors} instead of lax functors? Or does laxification detect structure that is invisible to weakness? The following exposition suggests the latter.
  It also has to be noted that it is known that Lawvere had a negative opinion of \((∞, 1)\)-category theory. The exact reason why is less well-known but can to some extent be
  reconstructed: in \cite{lawvereWilliamLawvereAre}, Lawvere explicitly \emph{denies} that homotopy types are the same as infinitesimal skeleta because to him, they are an instance
  of an identity of opposites. Understanding this \emph{only} to an identity would seem like an undialectical collapse from this perspective. And we do have to ask ourselves: if,
  say, the codiscrete categories on different sets are just the same, \emph{then why are they different}? Because they do have different object cardinalities and, more saliently,
  different lax functors out of them.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- example-19: body_md -->
\label{xmp:12}
\index{geodesic!in metric space}
\index{metric space!as 2-category}
  Given a Lawvere metric space \((X, d)\) with its induced topology generated by \(U_{x, r} := \{y ∈ X | d(x, y) < r\}\) we can define a 2-categorical structure on \(X\) whose

  \begin{itemize}
  \item objects are the elements of \(X\),

  \item morphisms are the contracting functions \(f{:} [0, l] → X\) with \(l_{f} := l ∈ ℝ_{\geq 0}\) where \(ℝ_{\geq 0}\) has its usual metric and \([0, l]\) inherits it,

  \item \(f \leq g\) if \(l_{f} \leq l_{g}\),

  \item \(f⨾ g\) is the morphism \([0, l_{f} + l_{g}] → X\) given by \(f\) on \([0, l_{f}]\) and \(g\) on \([l_{f}, l_{f} + l_{g}]\),

  \item \(\mathbf{id}_{x} : [0, 0] → X\) is given by \(x{:} * \hookrightarrow X\) (since \([0, 0]\) is canonically equivalent to the terminal set),

  \item associativity and identity laws follow from pointwise evaluation.
  \end{itemize}

  This is kind of like the path groupoid of a topological space except that we don't assume any identifications whatsoever  and associativity holds without restraint because we
  don't normalize path lengths at all (i.e. not every path is a morphism from \([0, 1]\)).  Note
  also that no object of \(X\) has a non-contractible automorphism 2-group, so each natural isomorphism between paths is equivalent to an identity.

  Let us now consider the example of \(ℝ^{n}\) and the embedding of the codiscrete groupoid

  \[γ{:} \mathbf{CDisc}(ℝ^{n}) \hookrightarrow ℝ^{n}{:} x ↦ x, (f{:} x → y) ↦ [x, y]\]

 which maps the (unique) path from \(x\) to \(y\) to the (affine) line from \(x\) to \(y\). Then \(γ\) maps \(\mathbf{id}_{X}\) to \([x, x]\), which is the identity in \(ℝ^{n}\), and maps
  \(x \xrightarrow{f} y \xrightarrow{g} z\) to \([x, z]\), which is minimal in \(X(x, z)\), and is thus an oplax embedding of \(\mathbf{CDisc}(ℝ^{n})\) into \((ℝ^{n})^{[0, 1]}\). In
  other words, \(γ\) is the embedding of the geodesics between points in \(ℝ^{n}\).
<!-- end example-19 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
\label{dfn:19}
\index{convex sub-2-category}
\index{geodesic 2-category}
  An oplax sub-2-category \(ι{:} \mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) of a 2-category \(\mathcal{B}\) is \emph{convex} if for each 2-isomorphism
  \(σ{:} ι(f) \overset{\sim}{\Rightarrow} g⨾ h\) it holds that \(σ, g\) and \(h\) are in \(ι\).

  \(ι\) is \emph{convexly full} if for each \(f\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) such that  \(\mathbf{s}(f)\) and \(\mathbf{t}(f)\) are in (the image of) \(ι\) it holds that for each 2-isomorphism
  \(σ{:} f \simeq g⨾ h\) with \(\mathbf{t}(g) = \mathbf{s}(h)\) the cells \(σ\), \(g\) and \(h\) are in \(ι\).

  An object \(∅\) \emph{is sup-initial} if it has at most one morphism to every object (so if it is the dual of a subterminal object). \(∅\) is \emph{strict sup-initial} if it is
  sup-initial and each morphism with codomain \(∅\) is uniquely 2-isomorphic to the identity.

  A \emph{2-category with paths} is a pair of a 2-category \(\mathcal{B}\) and a wide convex oplax subcategory \(ι{:} \mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{B}\).

  A \emph{2-category with unique paths} is a 2-category with paths
  such that \(\mathcal{A}\) is the codiscrete groupoid \(\mathbf{CDisc}(\mathcal{B})\) on the objects of \(\mathcal{B}\).

  A \emph{2-category with geodesics} is a 2-category with paths
  \(ι\) such that each morphism \(p{:} X → Y\) in the image of \(ι\) is strict sup-initial in \(\mathcal{B}(X, Y)\).

  A \emph{geodesic 2-category} is a 2-category such that there
  exists a convex strict initial object \(γ{:} \mathcal{G} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) in the 2-category of wide oplax sub-2-categories of \(\mathcal{B}\) on
  \(\mathbf{CDisc}(\mathcal{B})\). Equivalently, \(\mathcal{B}\) is geodesic if each hom-category \(\mathcal{B}(X, Y)\) contains a strict initial object \(γ_{X, Y}\) such that each 2-isomorphism
  \(σ{:} γ_{X, Y} \simeq f⨾ g\) is an identity (since it is in the image of \(\mathbf{CDisc}(\mathcal{B})\)) and \(f = γ_{X, \mathbf{t}(f)}, g = γ_{\mathbf{s}(g), Y}\).
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rmk:16}
  So convex fullness is like fullness but only applies to morphisms that don't just go between objects in \(ι\) but also never factor through objects outside \(ι\) — no detours allowed!
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- example-20: body_md -->
\label{xmp:19}
  \index{convex space!2-categorical structure} In \cite{fritzConvexSpacesDefinition2015}, Fritz describes a convex space as a set \(X\) with a family of operations
  \(cc_{λ}{:} X × X → X\) for \(λ ∈ [0, 1]\) such that \(cc_{0}(x, y) = x\) and \(cc_{1}(x, y) = y\) (by commutativity). This is equivalent to a family of paths
  \(γ_{x, y}∈ X^{[0, 1]}{:} γ_{x, y}(λ) := cc_{λ}(x, y)\) where we don't assume any structure on \(X\) or \([0, 1]\). Fritz moreover introduces a commutativity axiom which ensures that
  the inverse of some path is literally the same path backwards, and an associativity axiom which regulates the continuous structure through combinatorial approximation. We reduce
  this to a discrete, i.e. categorical structure. This loses some geometry and there should be a continuous version of category theory that builds on that structure, but starting
  from a more basic perspective allows us to seamlessly integrate our theory with standard category theory before introducing more genuinely continuous considerations.

  Each convex space in the sense of \cite{fritzConvexSpacesDefinition2015} has an underlying convex 2-category \(\mathopen{∣}∏\mathclose{∣}(X)\) whose

  \begin{itemize}
  \item objects are the elements of \(X\),

  \item\label{item:38} morphisms are generated by \(γ_{x, y}\) (freely except for the 2-morphisms below),

  \item\label{item:59} 2-morphisms are the horizontal and vertical composites of the following two kinds:

    \begin{itemize}
    \item\label{item:62} 2-cells \(γ_{x, y}⨾ γ_{y, z} \geq γ_{x, z}\) for all \(x, y, z\),

    \item inverses \(γ_{x, z} \sim γ_{x, y}⨾ γ_{y, z}\) if \(y\) is in the image of \(γ_{x, z}\).
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}

  This is a 2-category whose identities are given by constant paths, which is both more rough and finer than the standard fundamental groupoid: it does not consider any
  higher-categorical structure (and there isn't really any unless it is induced by paths), but it also does not identify the composite \(γ⨾ \overline{γ}\) of a path
  \(γ{:} [0, 1] → X\) and its reflection \(\overline{γ}{:} [0, 1] \xhookrightarrow{\overline{x} := 1 - x} [0, 1] \xhookrightarrow{γ} X\) with \(\mathbf{id}(\mathbf{s}(x))\). It
  follows directly from the definition that each \(γ_{x, y}\) is the minimal path from \(x\) to \(y\), and that \(γ\) is convex (up to contractible homotopy).
  Thus, \(γ{:} \mathbf{CDisc}(X) → X\) is the \emph{underlying geodesic 2-category} of \(X\).
<!-- end example-20 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
\label{dfn:25}
\index{convex closure}
  Given a convex wide oplax sub-2-category \(λ{:} \mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) and a family of objects \(\mathcal{F}\) in \(\mathcal{B}\), the \emph{\(λ\)-closure} of
  \(\mathcal{F}\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) is the smallest convex and convexly full (weak) sub-2-category of \(\mathcal{B}\) containing the restriction of \(λ\) to the objects in \(\mathcal{F}\). A sub-2-category
  \(κ\) of \(\mathcal{B}\) is \emph{\(λ\)-convex} if it is equivalent to the \(λ\)-closure of a family of objects in \(\mathcal{B}\). If \(\mathcal{B}\) is geodesic, then \(κ\) is \emph{geodesically convex} if it is
  \(γ\)-convex (where \(γ\) is the oplax sub-2-category of geodesics of \(\mathcal{B}\)).
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rmk:19}
  Note in particular that we can identify each \(ι\)-convex sub-2-category of \(\mathcal{B}\) with its subset of objects. In particular, for a family
  \(s{:} S \hookrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) the geodesic closure \(\hat{s}\) has to be the smallest convex and convexly full weak subcategory of \(\mathcal{B}\) containing \(γ|_{s}{:} \mathbf{CDisc}(S) \hookrightarrow \mathcal{B}\).
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- example-21: body_md -->
\label{xmp:23}
  In a real vector space \(ℝ^{n}\) with its usual metric, let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a family of points. Applying \cref{xmp:12} we get that \(γ_{x, y}\) is the shortest path \([0, 1] → ℝ^{n}\) between
  \(x\) and \(y\), up to the points it contains. So the geodesic closure of \(\mathcal{F}\) contains \(\mathcal{F}\), \(γ_{x, y}\) for each \(x, y\) in \(\mathcal{F}\) and the shortest path between each pair of points in
  \(\mathcal{F}\), so concretely can be obtained from \(\mathcal{F}\) by adding each \(γ_{x, y}\), then adding all points on each obtained line, then adding the geodesics between each pair of new points and so
  on, then adding all paths that only cross points in that closure. Thus, \(\overline{\mathcal{F}}\) is indeed the convex closure of \(\mathcal{F}\) as traditionally understood.

  For instance if
  \(\mathcal{F}\) is given by function \(s{:} S \hookrightarrow ℝ^{n}\), with \(S\) a finite set, then \(\overline{s}{:} \mathbf{CDisc}(S) → ℝ^{n}\) is a (possibly degenerated) convex simplex in \(ℝ^{n}\) with vertices
  given by the images of the elements of \(S\). Note in particular that \(\mathbf{CDisc}([n])\) with \([n]\) a finite cardinal is the localization of the total order on
  the same elements, which is also known as the abstract \((n - 1)\)-simplex.

  Note also that a geodesic weak natural transformation \(η: ι_{0} \Rightarrow ι_{1}: I  
  \mathrel{\vcenter{\offinterlineskip
    \ialign{##\cr
       \hfil$\hookrightarrow$\hfil\cr
       \noalign{\vskip -0.3ex}
       \hfil$ 
  \scalebox{1}[-1]{\(\hookrightarrow\)}
$\hfil\cr
    }}} 
 ℝ^{n}\) between geodesic
  embeddings of the directed interval category, i.e. arrow category \(0 \hookrightarrow 1\), is a square with edges \(ι_{0}, ι_{1}, η_{0}, η_{1}\) such that

  \[\mathopen{∣}η_{0}⨾ ι_{1}\mathclose{∣} = \mathopen{∣}η_{0}\mathclose{∣} + \mathopen{∣}ι_{1}\mathclose{∣} = \mathopen{∣}ι_{0}\mathclose{∣} + \mathopen{∣}η_{1}\mathclose{∣} = \mathopen{∣}ι_{0} + η_{1}\mathclose{∣},\]

  i.e. an ex-tangential quadrilateral.
