<!-- end example-21 -->
<!-- example-22: body_md -->
\label{xmp:convex-small}
\index{convex cone!smallness}
\index{tablets!for convexity}
\index{small subobject!convex}
  Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be a geodesic \(2\)-category with distinguished geodesic morphisms
  \(γ_{x,y}{:} x → y\) for all objects \(x,y\). The geodesically convex sub-2-categories of \(\mathcal{B}\) form an upward-bounded preorder \(\mathbf{SOb}_{gcc}(\mathcal{B})\)
  under inclusion, with top element \(\mathcal{B}\) and bottom element the empty subcategory.
  Meets are given by intersections if they exist (which they often do not), and joins are
  geodesic closures of unions: \(ι ∨ κ \;=\; \overline{\mathbf{Ob}(ι) ∪ \mathbf{Ob}(κ)}\).

  Thus, smallness is not trivial in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{gcc}(\mathcal{B})\).
  A geodesically convex subcategory \(ι\) is not small if and only if there exists a proper geodesically convex \(κ\) such that \(\overline{ι ∪ κ} = \mathcal{B}\). Since both \(ι\) and \(κ\) are geodesic
  closures of objects \(ι_{0}, κ_{0}\), this closure is equivalent to \(\overline{ι_{0} \cup κ_{0}}\). Thus, \(ι\) is not small if there exists a \(κ_{0}\) such that each object of \(\mathcal{B}\)
  can be obtained by repeatedly taking geodesics of points on geodesics... between \(ι_{0}\) and \(κ_{0}\), but there is a point in \(ι_{0}\) that cannot be obtained from repeated geodesics between
  points in \(κ_{0}\).

  So for instance in a non-trivial convex cone in \(ℝ^{n}\) with the convex 2-categorical structure from \cref{xmp:12}, the one-point subset on the tip is not small while all other points are small.
<!-- end example-22 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:1}
  We might expect smallness in \cref{xmp:convex-small} to be given by ``A is contained in the closure of its set-theoretic complement'', but the notion we derived is generally
  stronger than that. This is roughly because smallness is derived using both the fewer subobjects that are convex subspaces and their more expansive join. In
  \cref{xmp_:15} we will learn how to use only one of these at a time, recovering a weaker notion of smallness.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- example-23: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:9}
\index{stochastic matrix!simplicial structure}
  \index{stochastic matrix!smallness}
  Let us look at the category \(\mathbf{FStoch}\) whose objects are finite sets and whose morphisms are stochastic matrices. Recall that
  stochastic matrix \(M{:} X → Y\) is a function \(f(- \mid -){:} X × Y → [0, 1]\) such that for each \(x ∈ X\) it holds that

  \[∑_{y ∈ Y} f(y \mid x) = 1.\]

  \(f\) here is a synthetic descriptor of conditional probability, where the defining equation says that each conditional probability is a probability function. However, \(M\) is
  also the descriptor of an affine transformation that maps a unit simplex \(▲^{X}_{1} \subseteq ℝ^{X}\), which is the convex hull of the unit vectors \(δ_{i}\) in \(ℝ^{X}\), into
  \(▲^{Y}_{1} \subseteq ℝ^{Y}\), given by multiplying \(δ_{i}\) with \(M\). Thus, we can identify \(X{:} \mathbf{FStoch}\) with the \((\mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣} - 1)\)-dimensional unit simplex \(▲^{X}_{1}\) and the
  subobjects \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) with the affine sub-simplices of \(▲^{X}_{1}\).\footnote{This geometric interpretation was pointed out to me by Fritz.} Since each point is an affine
  sub-simplex, \(\mathbf{SOb}(▲^{X}_{1})\) is atomistic by \cref{coR_:3}, so density is trivial; the question is again smallness. For joins, \(σ ∨ τ = ▲^{X}_{1}\) holds if and only if
  \(▲^{X}_{1}\) is the only subsimplex of \(▲^{X}_{1}\) containing the union \(σ \cup τ\).

  Dimension 0 is clear. In dimension 1 the only sub-simplex of \(▲^{1} = [0, 1]\) that contains both \(0\) and \(1\) is \(\top = \mathbf{id}_{[0, 1]}\) itself, so the join \(ι ∨ ι'\) of
  two affine sub-simplices \(ι, ι'\), i.e. sub-lines, is \(\top\) if and only if both \(0\) and \(1\) are in the union \(ι \cup ι'\). Thus, \(ι\) is small if and only if it does not
  contain either \(0\) or \(1\).

  For dimension \(> 1\)  we claim that the only small subobject in \(\mathbf{SOb}(X)\) is \(\bot\). To prove this, we treat \(▲^{X}_{1}\) as embedded into \(ℝ^{X}\) and construct for each
  \(p ∈ ▲^{X}_{1}\) a full-dimensional, maximal
  proper subsimplex that does not contain \(p\). For this, take some maximal face \(τ\) such that \(p\) is not in \(τ\). Since each simplex is \(T_{4}\) and both \(p\) and \(τ\)
  are closed and disjoint in \(▲^{X}_{1}\) there exists some open neighborhood \(U_{τ}\) of \(τ\) that does not contain \(p\) and thus, by the definition of the restricted Euclidean
  topology, an \(ε > 0\) such that the \(ε_{p}\)-thickening \(ε_{p}τ \cap ▲^{X}_{1}\) of \(τ\) does not contain \(p\). Let now \(τ_{p}\) be the sub-simplex of \(▲^{X}_{1}\) parallel to \(τ\)
  in \(▲^{X}_{1}\) whose orthogonally measured distance from \(τ\) is \(ε_{p}\). This is a shrunken but otherwise undeformed copy of \(τ\) and thus each of its vertices is linearly
  independent and independent of each vertex in the interior of \(τ\). Thus, the simplex \(τ_{p}'\) spanned by \(τ_{p}\) and the barycenter of \(τ\) is maximal (since it is
  equidimensional and each of its vertices in on the boundary) and proper in \(▲^{X}_{1}\) and does not contain \(p\), so that \(\{p\} ∨ τ'_{p} = \top\).
<!-- end example-23 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:32}
  \cref{xmp_:9} would seem like a trivialization of our theory in a part of synthetic probability theory; and it is — on its own. But it is re-contextualized by \cref{■pn_:64}, which shows
  that smallness in the sheaf topos of a site \(\mathcal{S}\) only depends on the coverage on \(\mathcal{S}\). So for a site, having rough smallness relations is in a sense welcome as long as the coverages on
  it are interesting. So the key point of \cref{xmp_:9} is not that smallness in \(\mathbf{FStoch}\) is trivial but that its structure is very similar to that of \(\mathbf{TDisk}\) from
  \cref{xmp:63}, which is quite important, as mentioned in \cref{rmα_:33}. We will show in later work that this similarity of site structures descends to one of topoi, which opens up a
  connection of synthetic probability theory to cohesion and closed geometric logic that could be of interest.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{defn_:7}
  \index{reduced element}\index{sated element}
  An element \(a\) of an upward-bounded preorder \(P\) is \emph{reduced} if for any small \(b\)  and arbitrary \(c\) such that \(a \leq b ∨ c\) it holds that \(a \leq c\).

  Dually, \(a\) is \emph{sated} if for every dense \(b\) and \(c\) such that \(a \geq b ∧ c\) it holds that \(a \geq c\).
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- example-24: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:27}
\index{reduced element!topological}
A paradigmatic example are the closed subsets \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) of a topological space: each closed \(C\) is equal to the union \(\mathopen{∣}C\mathclose{∣} \cup \mathbf{s}(C)\) where \(\mathopen{∣}C\mathclose{∣}\) is the
reduction of \(C\), i.e. the closure of its interior, and \(\mathbf{s}(C)\) is the closure in \(C\) of the complement \(C ∖ \mathopen{∣}C\mathclose{∣}\). Thus, if \(C\) is reduced, then
\(C \leq \mathopen{∣}C\mathclose{∣}\) and hence \(C = \mathopen{∣}C\mathclose{∣}\). Conversely, if \(C \leq D \cup E\) with \(D\) small, then the interior \(C°\) is contained in the interior \((D \cup E)°\), which is equal to \(E\) by
smallness. Thus, in the lattice of closeds of a topological space an element is reduced if and only if it is the closure of an open subset, so if it is regular. Dually, an open subset is sated if and only if it
  is the interior of some closed subset, so also if it is regular.
<!-- end example-24 -->
<!-- example-25: body_md -->
\label{xmp:54}
\index{radical ideal!satedness}
  In \cref{xmp:49} we saw that a submonoid \(C\) is dense if and only if it contains a power of each element in \(M\). So \(A\) is sated if and only if whenever \(A \geq B \cap C\) for some dense
  \(C\), then \(A \geq B\), or equivalently if and only if it contains each root of its elements. In particular each (ring-theoretic) ideal in a ring \(R\) is sated as a multiplicative
  submonoid of \(R\) if and only if it is a radical
  ideal.\footnote{Regrettably for our nomenclature this is also called a ``reduced ideal'', though our terminology is arguably more accurate since a radical ideal is ``complete under radicals'' and
    thus ``large enough to be sated over
    everything it contains'', not ``reduced'', i.e. obtained by shaving away all small parts.}
<!-- end example-25 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:5}
\index{small element!exclusivity with reducedness}
  Let \(P\) be a bounded preorder. Then \(a\) is both small and reduced if and only if \(a = \bot\).
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Because \(P\) is bounded, \(\bot\) exists.
  \(\bot\) is small: \(\bot ∨ b = b\), so \(\bot ∨ b = \top \Rightarrow b = \top\).
  \(\bot\) is reduced: if \(b ∨ c \geq \bot\) with \(b\) small, then also \(c \geq \bot\) by the minimality of \(\bot\).

  For the converse, assume \(a\) is both small and reduced.  Choose \(b = a\) (which is small) and \(c = \bot\).  Then \(a \leq a ∨ \bot\), so by reducedness \(a \leq \bot\), so \(a = \bot\).
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{dfn:7}
  \index{smallness fibration} \index{n-small element}
  Given an upward-bounded preorder \(P\), every element \(a ∈ P\) is \emph{\(0\)-small}. \(a\) is \emph{\(n\)-small} for \(n\) a successor ordinal if there is an \((n - 1)\)-small element \(b \geq a\) such that \(a\) is small in the (restriction of
  \(P\) to the) principal ideal \((b)\) of \(b\). \(a\) is \emph{purely \(n\)-small} if \(a\) is \(n\)-small but not \((n + 1)\)-small. \(a\) is \emph{\(ω\)-small} for \(ω\) a limit ordinal if it is \(n\)-small
  for all \(n < ω\).
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
\label{dfn:8}
  \index{smallness stratification}
  Let \(\mathbf{Ord}\) be the large preorder of ordinals. Given an upward-bounded preorder \(P\) the \emph{smallness stratification} \(\mathbf{small}{:} P → \mathbf{Ord}\) is the order morphism given by mapping \(a ∈ P\) to
  \(n\) if and only if \(a\) is purely \(n\)-small, and to \(\omega\) if \(a\) is \(\omega\)-small. The \emph{smallness fibration} is the morphism \(∐_{n ∈ \mathbf{Ord}} \mathbf{small}^{-1}(n) → P\) classified by
  \(\mathbf{small}\). We define the \emph{density stratification} and \emph{density fibration} dually.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:strat-welldef}
  \index{smallness stratification!well-definedness}
  Let \(P\) be a (small) upward-bounded preorder. For every \(a ∈ P\), there exists an ordinal \(n\) such that \(a\) is purely \(n\)-small.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
\label{prf:1}
  Assume that \(a\) is not purely \(n\)-small for any \(n\). By definition \(a\) is 0-small. To not be purely 0-small, \(a\) must be 1-small, meaning \(a\) is small in some 0-small principal ideal. Proceeding by induction, \(a\) is \((n+1)\)-small for each \(n\). For each limit ordinal \(ω\), if \(a\) is \(n\)-small for all \(n < ω\), then \(a\) is \(ω\)-small by definition. Thus, by transfinite induction, \(a\) is \(α\)-small for every ordinal \(α\). But \(α\)-smallness requires \(a\) to be small within some \((α-1)\)-small principal ideal, which itself must be small within some \((α-2)\)-small principal ideal, and so on. This creates a strictly ascending chain of principal ideals of length \(α\) for each ordinal \(α\), so there exists an injection \(\mathbf{Ord} \hookrightarrow P\). Consequently, \(P\) cannot be small.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- example-26: body_md -->
\label{xmp:107}
  In \cref{xmp:60} we saw that a (topological) sub-manifold with boundary \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) is small in a manifold with boundary \(X\) if and only if
  \(m := \mathbf{dim}(A) < n := \mathbf{dim}(X)\). If \(A\) is non-empty then there exists \(p ∈ A\), and thus a local isomorphism \(σ_{p}\) from some open \(U_{p}\) in \(X\) to either \(ℝ^{n}\) or
  \(ℝ^{n}_{\geq 0}\), which without loss of generality we can choose so that \(ι|_{U_{p}}⨾ σ\) is isomorphic to \(ℝ^{m}\). In particular we can for each \(m < n' < n\) find an
  \(n'\)-dimensional disk or half-disk \(D_{p}\) around \(ι|_{U}⨾ σ(p)\). Let us take the union \(κ := \bigcup_{p ∈ A} D_{p}\) in \(X\). Then the \(σ_{p}|_{D_{p}}\) provide an atlas for
  \(κ\), so that \(κ\) is an \(m\)-dimensional submanifold with boundary of \(X\). Thus, the smallness fibration in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{∂ \mathbf{Mfld}}(X)\) agrees with the dimensional fibration.
<!-- end example-26 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
\label{defn_:24}
\index{monoidal smallness}
An element \(a\) of an ordered monoid \(M\) with a product \(+\) and a top element \(\top\) is \emph{\(+\)-small} if and only if for each \(b ∈ M\) such that \(a + b = \top\)
  it holds that \(b = \top\). Dually, an element \(a\) of an ordered monoid \(M\) with a contravariantly monotone monoidal product \(\otimes\) and a bottom element \(\bot\) is \emph{\(\otimes\)-dense} if and
  only if for each \(b ∈ M\) such that \(a \otimes b = \bot\) it holds that \(b = \bot\).
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
\label{defn_:14}\index{small under a tablet}\index{reduced under a tablet}\index{tablets}
  Let \(τ{:} T → P\) be a morphism of upward-bounded preorders and \(a\) an element of \(P\).
  We call \(τ\) the \emph{tablets} we use.

  \(a\) is \emph{small under \(τ\)} if for each join \(a ∨ τ(b) = \top_{P}\) it holds that \(b = \top_{T}\).

  \(a\) is \emph{reduced under \(τ\)} if for each element \(b ∈ P\) that is small under \(τ\) and each \(c ∈ T\) it holds that

  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:2}
    \text{if } a \leq b ∨ τ(c) \text{ then } a \leq τ(c).
  \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:3}
  The use of inequalities for reducedness in \cref{defn_:14} allows us to bound the fuzziness between the images of elements of \(T\). Note that the formula \(a ∨ τ(b) = \top_{P}\) is already equivalent
  to \(a ∨ τ(b) \geq \top_{P}\) due to the definition of a top, so for smallness the question of whether to use an inequality doesn't arise.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- example-27: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:20}
  \cref{defn_:14} reduces to \cref{defn_:58} and \cref{defn_:7} when \(τ = \mathbf{id}_{P}\), i.e. each subobject of \(P\) is a tablet.
<!-- end example-27 -->
<!-- example-28: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:26}
\index{Cauchy completeness!generalized}
\index{tablets!topological}
   Building on \cref{xmp_:27}, consider the inclusion \(ι_{\mathbf{C},X}{:}\mathbf{C}(X)\hookrightarrow\mathbf{P}(X)\) of the closed subsets of a topological space \(X\) into all subsets. A subset
  \(a \subseteq X\) is small under \(ι_{\mathbf{C},X}\) if and only if \(X\) itself is the only closed subset \(c\) such that \(a \cup c = X\), so if its closure is small, i.e. nowhere dense. A subset
  \(b \subseteq X\) is reduced under \(ι_{\mathbf{C},X}\) if and only if whenever \(b \leq a \cup c\) with \(a\) nowhere dense and \(c\) closed, then already \(b \leq c\), so if
  the closure \(\overline{b}\) is regular. So our tablets allow us to bound the sets in \(\mathbf{P}(X)\) by those in \(\mathbf{C}(X)\).

  Dually, if we take \(ι_{\mathbf{O}, X}{:} \mathbf{O}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(X)\) as the tablets, then a subset \(a\) of \(X\) is dense under \(ι_{\mathbf{O}, X}\) if and only if its meet with every open subset is non-empty,
  so if it is dense in the topological sense. \(b\) is sated if and only if whenever \(b\) is locally dense in that \(b \geq a \cap c\) with \(a\) open and \(c\) dense, then \(b\) just contains
  \(a\).

  In particular, let \(X\) be a metric space with its underlying topology and the tablets \(τ\) again given by the opens of \(X\). Then a subset \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) is \(τ\)-dense if and only if
  for each \(x ∈ X, r ∈ ℝ_{> 0}\) the intersection \(ι \cap U_{x, r}\) with the open ball around \(x\) with radius \(r\) is nonempty, i.e. if for each \(x\) there exists some Cauchy sequence
  converging to \(x\). Thus, \(ι\) is sated if and only if for each union of Cauchy sequences \(δ\) that converge to all of \(X\), if \(ι\) contains the restriction of \(δ\) to some open
  \(U\), then \(ι\) contains all of \(U\). So our notion generalizes a topological relative version of Cauchy completeness.

  We can also zoom into a point \(x\) by reducing our collection of tablets to the opens of \(X\) containing \(x\). This allows us to say that \emph{\(ι\) is \(τ\)-dense at \(x\)} if it
  contains some sequence converging to \(x\). But actual Cauchy completeness is not straight-forwardly described as satedness in this way, which makes sense since it is not
  homeomorphism-invariant.
<!-- end example-28 -->
<!-- example-29: body_md -->
\label{xmp:monoid-action-density}
\index{monoid action!density and satedness}
\index{radial density}
  Let \(M\) be a monoid and \(X\) a set with a left action \(λ{:} M \hookrightarrow \mathbf{End}(X)\). Write \(\mathbf{SOb}_λ(X)\) for the preorder of sub-\(λ\)-sets of \(X\), ordered by inclusion; it is a bounded lattice with meets given by
  intersection and joins by union (since each union of \(λ\)-sets is a \(λ\)-set).

  Consider the tablets given by the inclusion \(τ_{\mathbf{SOb}_λ} {:} \mathbf{SOb}_λ(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(X)\) of sub-λ-sets. Applying the definitions of density and satedness from
  \cref{rmk:dual-sigma-mu} we obtain that:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item A subset \(D \subseteq X\) is dense under \(τ_{\mathbf{SOb}_λ}\) if and only if every sub-\(λ\)-set \(S \subseteq X\) such that \(D ∩ S = ∅\) is equal to
    \(\bot_{τ} = \bigcap_{ι ∈ \mathbf{SOb}_{λ}(X)} ι = ∅\) since the empty set is closed under the action of \(λ\). Equivalently, \(D\) meets every orbit.

    If \(k\) is a ring and \(X\) a \(k\)-module, then we can further restrict the tables \(τ'\) to be sub-modules of \(X\). Then \(\bot_{τ'}\) is no longer empty however, since each
    submodule of \(X\) contains a neutral element. In particular let \(k\) be a field and \(V\) a \(k\)-vector space equipped with the action of \(k\) by multiplication. The orbits are \(\bot_{τ} = \{0\}\) and the lines
  \(\mathcal{O}_v = \{ λv \mid λ ∈ k\}\) for \(v \neq 0\). Thus a subset \(D \subseteq V\) is dense if and only if \(D \cap \mathcal{O}_v \neq ∅ \text{ for every } v \neq 0\). One simple way this can happen is when
  \(0\) is in \(D\), otherwise \(D\) has to intersect all orbits individually.

    For instance if we take \(k = ℝ\) and \(V = ℝ^n\), the nonzero orbits are the lines through the origin, which correspond bijectively to points of the real projective space \(ℝ\mathbf{P}^{n-1}\) via the direction map
  \[
    q {:} ℝ^n \setminus \{0\} → R\mathbf{P}^{n-1},\quad v \mapsto [v],
  \]
  where \([v]\) denotes the equivalence class of \(v\) under scalar multiplication. If we instead take \(k\) as \(ℝ_{\geq 0}\) (but leave \(V\) the same), then \(q\) goes to \(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\). Hence \(D\) is dense precisely when it contains the origin or its image under \(q\) is all of \(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\); in geometric language, \(D\) is \emph{radially dense}: it is either at the center
  or has at least one point in every direction from the origin.

  \item A subset \(A \subseteq X\) is sated under \(τ_{\mathbf{SOb}_λ}\) if and only if whenever \(A \supseteq D ∩ B\) with \(D\) dense and \(B\) an \(λ\)-subset of \(X\), then already
    \(A \supseteq B\).
    If now \(a\) is some element of \(A\) and \(O\) an orbit that contains \(a\), then \((\{a\} \cup \bigcup_{\mathcal{O}'} \mathcal{O}') ∖ \bot_{τ}\) is dense, where
    \(\mathcal{O}'\) ranges over the orbits of \(X\) that do not contain \(a\) and the complement is set-theoretic. Moreover, if \(O\) is an orbit that contains \(a\) and whose intersection with any
    orbit that does not contain \(a\) factors through \(\bot_{τ}\), then \(O \cap (\{a\} \cup \bigcup_{\mathcal{O}'} \mathcal{O}') = \{a\} \subseteq A\), so that \(O \subseteq A\). In particular, if \(λ\) is a group or the action is one of a
    field on a vector space, then all orbits fulfill this condition , so that \(A\) has to contain every orbit it intersects.

  \item\label{item:55} \(S \subseteq X\) is small under \(τ_{\mathbf{SOb}_λ}\) if the smallest \(λ\)-set \(T\) whose union with \(S\) is \(X\) is the largest \(λ\)-subset, which is \(X\) itself, so if
    the complement of \(S\) is in no proper \(λ\)-subset of \(X\), meaning that the closure of \(¬ S\) under the action of \(λ\) contains \(S\), so if each element of \(S ∖ \bot_{τ}\) is a multiple of
    one outside it. If \(M\) is a group then its orbits are disjoint partitions, so that \(S\) is small if and only if it does not contain an orbit. So in \(ℝ^{n}\) as an \(ℝ\)-module \(S\)
    is small if it does not contain a (linear) line. But in a general monoid the property is looser: for instance in \(ℝ^{n}\) as a \(ℤ\)-module no central \(n\)-disk of radius \(> 0\) is small, since its
    elements cannot be generated by elements outside it.

  \item\label{item:56} \(R \subseteq X\) is reduced if for each small \(S\) and \(λ\)-set \(Q\) if \(R \subseteq S \cup Q\), then \(R \subseteq Q\). Now, if \(R \subseteq S \cup Q\), then \(R \subseteq \overline{S} \cup Q\), where \(\overline{S}\) is
    the closure of \(S\) under the action of \(λ\), so \(R\) is reduced if any part of \(R\) that is in a small \(λ\)-subset is also in any \(λ\)-subset that contains the rest of \(R\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end example-29 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:28}
  In \cref{defn_:14} we use the same set of tablets for both the definition of smallness and reducedness. Most of our examples work fine like this, but it is possible to use a
  second set of tablets for reducedness instead of those used for smallness, i.e. use a second morphism \(τ'{:} T' → P\) to quantify \(\)
  second relativization so generally remain with the \(P\)-quantified case for simplicity, but occasionally the twice-relativized notion is necessary, e.g. in \cref{xmp_:22}.

 in \cref{eq:2} is ``absolute'', i.e. quantified over \(P\). Quantifying it over \(T\)
  does not generally yield good results, but we \emph{could} introduce a second set of tablets \(τ'{:} T' → P\) to quantify over \(c\). This further degree of generality can
  sometimes be both necessary and sufficient to achieve nice results, see in particular the results for satedness in \cref{xmp_:22}.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- example-30: body_md -->
\label{xmp:21}
\index{abstract polytope!smallness and density}
\index{universal vertex}
  In \cref{coR_:3} we found that if a preorder \(P\) is atomistic, then its notion of density is trivial, and similar for smallness. However, if \(P\) is bounded in both directions
  we can obtain an interesting notion of density by considering the embedding \(ι_{cat}{:} P_{cat} \hookrightarrow P\) of the bounded preorder on co-atoms \(P_{cat}\) into \(P\). Density with
  respect to these tablets is more about the position in the preorder than dimension: an element is \(ι_{cat}\)-dense if and only if its intersection with every co-atom is
  non-empty. Dually, an element is \(ι_{at}\)-small if and only if it is in a proper face with every other atom. For points in a polytope this is a known property and a vertex that
  fulfills it is called a \emph{universal vertex} or \emph{dominating vertex}.

  If we apply this to the objects of the sites in \cref{obs_:1} an interesting split emerges:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:28} In globes and simplices (above dimension one), every (maximal) face touches every other face and thus all are \(cat\)-dense, but no other faces are
    \(cat\)-dense. On the other hand, every non-empty proper face shares some non-empty non-maximal face with any vertex, so all are small, while every maximal face shares no
    proper face with the vertex opposite to it, and thus is not small.

  \item\label{item:29} In cubes over dimension one, every proper face has an opposite face which it does not touch and thus is not small or dense. So no non-trivial faces or points
    are \(cat\)-dense or \(at\)-small.

  \item\label{item:30} In abstract polytopes, any case can arise. Moreover, while the abstract duality of the two makes it so that in many cases, such as the above, the two develop
    analogously, this is not according to any straightforward formal duality. For instance, consider an \(n\)-ary pyramid, consisting of a tip \(τ\), an opposite face \(ω\), \(n\)
    rays \(ρ_{i}\) between them and the \(n\) induced faces \(φ_{i}\). In this, there is a clear duality: there is one \(at\)-small vertex \(τ\) and one \(cat\)-dense maximal face
    \(ω\) and for \(n > 3\) no other faces are \(cat\)-dense or \(at\)-small. But if we now take any ray \(ρ_{i}\) and put a small digon into the middle of it in such in a way that
    it does not touch anything except \(ρ_{i}\) and its two adjacent faces, then \(τ\) remains small but (again for \(n > 3\)) there is no dense face anymore.
  \end{enumerate}

  This points again at the interesting geometry of abstract polytopes, which will be featured more in future work.
<!-- end example-30 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:4}
  Let \(L\) be an upward-bounded preorder and \(T' \xrightarrow{τ'} T \xrightarrow{τ} L\) be morphisms of preorders of \(L\) such that \(τ\) and \(τ'\) reflect tops . If \(b ∈ L\) is \(τ\)-small, then it is \((τ'⨾ τ)\)-small. Moreover, if
  \(τ'\) is surjective, then \((τ'⨾ τ)\)-smallness and \(τ\)-smallness are equivalent. Thus, the smallness of \(b\) only depends on the underlying set of \(T\). In particular, we can assume without loss of
  generality that \(τ, τ'\) are order-reflecting embeddings (and thus fully faithful).
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
\label{prf_:6}
  If the only \(a ∈ T\) such that \(τ(a) ∨ b = \top_{L}\) is \(\top_{T}\), then if \((τ'⨾ τ)(a') ∨ b = \top_{L}\) it follows from \(τ\)-smallness that \(τ'(a') = \top_{T}\) and since \(τ'\)
  reflects \(\top_{T}\), \(a' = \top_{T'}\). Moreover, since the join is taken in \(L\), the order-theoretic structure of \(T\) does not matter.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:lax-smallness}
  Let \(L\) be an upward-bounded preorder, and let \(τ {:} T → L\) and \(τ' {:} T' → L\) be monotone maps. Suppose there exists a monotone map \(f {:} T' → T\) such that:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item\label{item:78} \(τ' \le f⨾τ\), i.e. \(τ'(t') \le τ(f(t'))\) for all \(t' ∈ T'\);
    \item\label{item:111} if \(τ(f(t')) = \top_L\) then \(t' = \top_{T'}\).
  \end{enumerate}
  Then every \(τ\)-small element of \(L\) is also \(τ'\)-small.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Assume \(b ∈ L\) is \(τ\)-small, and let \(t' ∈ T'\) satisfy \(b ∨ τ'(t') = \top_L\).
  From \(τ'(t') \le τ(f(t'))\) we obtain \(b ∨ τ(f(t')) = \top_L\).
  By \(τ\)-smallness of \(b\), we must have \(τ(f(t')) = \top_L\).
  But \cref{item:111} then forces \(t' = \top_{T'}\), which is exactly what is required for \(b\) to be \(τ'\)-small.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
In the special case where \(f\) is surjective and \(τ' = f⨾τ\) so the inequality in \cref{item:78} becomes an equality \cref{item:111} is trivial, we recover the original statement of
  \cref{■pn_:4}.
  When \(τ\) and \(τ'\) are order-embeddings, \cref{item:111} simply says that if \(τ\) contains the top of \(L\), then \(τ'\) does as well.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- example-31: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:25}
  We found in \cref{xmp:17} that a subset of a graph is small if and only if contains no edges or isolated vertices. Given a preorder \(P\), let
  \(ι_{\mathbf{non\text{-}small_{G}}}{:} \mathbf{non\text{-}small_{G}}(P) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}(P)\), be the embedding of all full sub-preorders of \(P\) that are not small in the
  underlying graph of \(P\) (without identities in \(P\)). Then \(\mathbf{non\text{-}small_{G}}(P)\) contains all isolated vertices and proper intervals in \(P\), i.e. the full
  sub-preorders \([a, b]\) for \(a < b\) consisting of all elements \(c\) in \(P\) such that \(a \leq c \leq b\). Thus, a sub-preorder of \(P\) is
  \(ι_{\mathbf{non\text{-}small_{G}}}\)-dense if and only if it meets isolated vertex and every proper interval in \(P\) non-trivially, so if it is dense in the order-theoretic
  sense.
<!-- end example-31 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
\label{defn_:1}
\index{scale}
  A \emph{scale} on an upward-bounded preorder \(P\) is a map \(P \overset{σ}{→} S\) into some preorder \(S\). An element \(a\) of \(P\)  is \emph{small over \(σ\)} if for each \(b ∈ P\) and join
  \(a ∨ b= \top_{P}\) it holds that \(σ(b) = \top_{σ}\) where \(\top_{σ}\) is the top of the image of \(σ\). Dually for density.

  \(c\) is \emph{reduced over \(σ\)} if for each \(a\) that is small over \(σ\) and \(b ∈ P\) such that
  \(a ∨ b \geq c\)
 it holds that
  \(σ(b) \geq σ(c)\). Dually for satedness.
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:6}
  Unlike with tablets and \(P\) itself we do not necessarily assume that scales are upward-bounded. The difference is small, but conceptually a scale need not come from the
  subobjects of some object.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- example-32: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:21}
  Similarly to \cref{xmp_:20}, \cref{defn_:1} reduces to the absolute definition of the fourfold calculus when \(σ = \mathbf{id}_{P}\).
<!-- end example-32 -->
<!-- example-33: body_md -->
\label{xmp:28}
\index{measure!as scale}
  Let \(σ{:} \mathbf{M}(X) → ℝ_{\geq0, ∞}\) be a measure on the \(σ\)-algebra of a measure space \(X\). A set \(S\) in \(M\) is small over \(σ\) if and only if for each \(T\) such that
  \(S \cup T = X\) it holds that \(σ(T) = σ(X)\). There is a minimal such choice, which is the Boolean negation \(¬ X\), so \(S\) is small when \(σ(¬ S) = σ(X)\). By binary
  additivity, \(σ(S) + σ(¬ S) = σ(X)\), so when \(σ(X)\) is finite we can form \(σ(S) = σ(X) - σ(¬ S) = 0\) since \(ℝ_{\geq 0}\) is cancellative, so \(S\) is not \(σ\)-small if and
  only if \(σ(S) = 0\), so if it is negligible. But if \(σ(X) = ∞\), then

  \begin{itemize}
  \item each finite \(S\) is small by additivity,
    
  \item it does not hold that each \(S\) with \(σ(S) = ∞\) is not small: \(σ(¬ S)\) can still be infinite. So \(S\) is only small if and only if it is co-finite.
  \end{itemize}

  so our notion is not \emph{exactly} the same as negligibility, but we can derive measure-theoretic negligibility from \(σ\)-smallness by defining it
  through restriction to finite-measure subspaces. What is interesting however is the our notion of density \emph{does} reduce to having a negligible complement:
  \(D\) is dense over \(σ\) if for each \(T\) such that \(D \cap T = ∅\) it holds that \(σ(T) = 0\), so if its complement is negligible. Moreover, \(A\) is sated if for each such dense subset
  \(D\) it holds that if \(A\) contains \(D \cap T\) with \(D\) dense, then \(σ(A) \geq σ(T)\). Since \(σ(T) = σ(T \cap D) + σ(T \cap ¬ D) \leq σ(A) + σ(¬ D) = σ(A)\), this holds trivially in our case.

  Now, \(R\) is reduced over \(σ\) if for each small \(S\) and arbitrary \(T\) if \(R \subseteq S \cup T\) then \(σ(R) \leq σ(T)\). It follows from additivity that \(σ(S \cup T) \leq σ(S) + σ(T)\), so
  if \(σ(X)\) is finite then each non-negligible element of \(\mathbf{M}(X)\) is reduced. But also, if \(σ(R) = 0\), then \(σ(R)\) is minimal, so that \(R\) is \emph{also} reduced.
  So actually \emph{every} subset of \(X\) is reduced.

  If \(σ(X)\) is \(∞\) then we have to think some more. If \(R\) is small, then \(R \subseteq R \cup ∅\), so \(σ(R) \leq σ(∅) = 0\), so \(R\) is negligible. So to be non-negligible, \(R\) has to
  be non-small i.e. co-finite. But then if \(R \subseteq S \cup T\), then \(∞ = σ(R) = σ(T)\) since \(∞ = \top\). So \(\mathbf{M}(X)\) is the union of small and reduced elements, with the
  intersection of the two being negligible ones.

  Note in particular that we can do this for the linear
  extension \(\mathopen{∣}-\mathclose{∣}: \mathbf{P}(ℕ) → ℕ_{∞}\) of the unit measure, i.e. cardinality for finite sets and \(∞\) for infinite ones. Then a subset \(S\) of \(ℕ\) is \(σ\)-small if and only if each \(T\) such that
  \(S \cup T = ℕ\) has infinite cardinality, so if the complement of \(S\) is infinite, so if \(S\) is co-infinite.
<!-- end example-33 -->
<!-- definition-27: body_md -->
\label{defn_:21}
  \index{small under a tablet over a scale}\index{reduced under a tablet over a scale}
  Let \(T \overset{τ}{→} P \overset{σ}{→} S\) be a triple of maps of preorders where we assume that \(T\) and \(P\) are upward-bounded, and let \(a\) be
  an element of \(P\). Then \(a\) is \emph{small under \(τ\) over \(σ\)} if for each join \(a ∨ τ(b) = \top_{P}\) with \(b\) in \(T\) it holds that \((τ⨾ σ)(b) = \top_{σ}\) where
  \(\top_{σ}\) is the top of the image of \(σ\). Dually for density.

  \(c\) is \emph{reduced under \(τ\) over \(σ\)} if for each \(a\) that is small under \(τ\) over \(σ\) and \(b ∈ T\) such that \(a ∨ τ(b) \geq c\) it holds that
  
  \[(τ⨾ σ)(b) \geq σ(c).\]

  Dually for satedness.
<!-- end definition-27 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:38}
  As in \cref{rmα_:28} we can quantity \(b\) in \cref{defn_:21} for reducedness and satedness with a second set of tablets.
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- notation-1: body_md -->
\label{ntn:1}
  As a convenient shorthand, we just write the parameters next to each other separated by \(|\)-signs. So we write ``\((τ \mid σ)\)-small'' for ``small under \(τ\) over \(σ\)''. Since all
  parameters are optional we leave those out that we don't need.
<!-- end notation-1 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:lax-scale}
  Let \(P\) be an upward-bounded preorder, let \(τ {:} T → P\) be a monotone map of tablets and \(σ {:} P → S\), \(σ' {:} P → S'\) monotone maps of scales. Suppose there is a monotone
  map \(g {:} S → S'\) such that:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item \label{item:57} \(σ' \ge σ⨾ g\), i.e. for all \(p ∈ P\),
      \[
        g(σ(p)) ≤_{S'} σ'(p),
      \]
    \item \label{item:58} the top elements of the images of \(σ\) and \(σ'\) correspond:
      \[
        g(\top_{σ}) = \top_{σ'},
      \]
      where \(\top_{σ}\) and \(\top_{σ'}\) denote the top elements of the images \(\mathbf{Im}(σ)\) and \(\mathbf{Im}(σ')\), respectively.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then any element of \(P\) that is \((τ \mid σ)\)-small is also \((τ \mid σ')\)-small.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Let \(a ∈ P\) be \((τ \mid σ)\)-small. By \cref{defn_:21}, this means:
  \[
    (\forall b ∈ T)\; \bigl(a ∨ τ(b) = \top_P\bigr) \Rightarrow σ\bigl(τ(b)\bigr) = \top_{σ}.
  \]
  Now suppose \(b ∈ T\) satisfies \(a ∨ τ(b) = \top_P\). Then by \((τ \mid σ)\)-smallness,
  \[
    σ\bigl(τ(b)\bigr) = \top_{σ}.
  \]
  Applying \(g\) and using \cref{item:58} gives
  \[
    g\bigl(σ(τ(b))\bigr) = g(\top_{σ}) = \top_{σ'}.
  \]
  Using \cref{item:57}, we also have
  \[
    g\bigl(σ(τ(b))\bigr) \le σ'(τ(b)).
  \]
  Since \(\top_{σ'}\) is the maximum element in the image of \(σ'\), this inequality forces
  \[
    σ'(τ(b)) = \top_{σ'}.
  \]
  This is exactly the condition that \(a\) is \((τ \mid σ')\)-small.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{coR_:4}
  Given \(σ{:} P → S\) and an  order-preserving injection \(f{:} S → S'\), smallness over \(σ\) and \(σ⨾ f\) are equivalent.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- remark-22: body_md -->
\label{rmk:dual-sigma-mu}
  By order-theoretic duality, one obtains analogous notions for downward-bounded preorders, which we call \emph{density} and \emph{satedness} under a tablet and over a scale.
  Explicitly, let \(T \xrightarrow{τ} P \xrightarrow{σ} S\) be morphisms of preorders, and assume that \(P\) and \(S\) are downward-bounded (with bottoms \(\bot_P\) and \(\bot_S\))
  and that the image of \(σ\) has a bottom element \(\bot_σ\).

  An element \(d \in P\) is \emph{dense under \(τ\) over \(σ\)} if for every \(b \in T\) with \(d ∧ τ(b) = \bot_P,\) it holds that
  \((τ⨾σ)(b) = \bot_σ\). An element \(e \in P\) is \emph{sated under \(τ\) over \(σ\)} if for every \(d \in P\) that is dense under \(τ\) over \(σ\) and every \(b \in T\) such that \(d ∧ τ(b) \le e\)
  we have \((τ⨾σ)(b) \le σ(e)\).
<!-- end remark-22 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:13}
  Let \(T \xhookrightarrow{τ} P \xhookrightarrow{σ} S\) be tablets and a scale with \(T\) being a bounded preorder (and \(P\) upward-bounded). Then \(a\) is \((τ, σ)\)-small and
  \((τ, σ)\)-reduced if and only if \(σ(a) \leq \bot_{τ⨾ σ}\).
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
\label{prf_:5}
  The proof of \cref{■pn_:5} mostly carries over:

  Because \(T\) is bounded, \(\bot_{τ⨾ σ} := σ(τ(\bot))\) exists.
  If \(σ(a) \leq \bot_{τ⨾ σ}\), then \(a\) is \((τ, σ)\)-small: if \(a ∨ τ(b) = \top_{P}\), then

  \[\top_{σ} = σ(\top_{P}) = σ(a ∨ τ(b)) \leq σ(a) ∨ σ(τ(b)) \leq  σ(τ(\bot_{T})) ∨ σ(τ(b)) = σ(τ(b)),\]

  and thus \(\top_{σ} = σ(τ(b))\).
  
  If \(σ(a) \leq \bot_{τ⨾ σ}\), then \(a\) is \((τ, σ)\)-reduced:\(\bot\) is reduced: if \(τ(b) ∨ c \geq a\) with \(b\) small, then \(σ(τ(b)) \geq σ(τ(\bot_{T})) = \bot_{τ⨾ σ}\) by the universal property
  of \(\bot_{T}\).
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:12}
  Let \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow P\) be a proper full sub-preorder in \(\mathbf{UBP}\) such that for each \(a, b ∈ ι\) there exists a \(c\) in \(ι\) such that \(a \leq c, b \leq c\). Then there exists a scale \(σ{:} P → S\)
  such that \(d ∈ P\) is small if and only if there exists an \(a ∈ ι\) such that \(d \leq a\).
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
\label{prf_:3}
  Take \(S\) to be the two-element total order and define \(σ\) by

  \[σ(d) := \begin{cases}
      \bot \text{ if and only if there exists some \(a ∈ ι\) such that} d \leq a, \\
      \top \text{ else}
    \end{cases}.\]

  This is a preorder morphism by definition. Since \(P\) has a top element and \(ι\) is proper, the fiber \(σ^{-1}(\bot)\) over \(\top\) is inhabited, and by assumption \(σ^{-1}(\bot)\) is
  closed under binary joins, so each element in it is \(σ\)-small.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- example-34: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:18}
  In \cref{xmp_:26} we saw that a subset of a topological space \(X\) is small with respect to the tablets consisting of closed subsets of \(X\) if and only if it is nowhere dense.
  We can define a scale \(σ{:} \mathbf{P}(X) → S\) on \(\mathbf{P}(X)\) where \(S\) consists of the nowhere dense subsets of \(X\) and a freely added top \(\top\), and scale is the
  identity on nowhere dense subsets and maps every other subset to \(\top\).
<!-- end example-34 -->
<!-- counterexample-2: body_md -->
\label{cxmp_:1}
  Let \(P\) be the upward-bounded preorder on elements
  \(\top, a, b, c, d, e\) with relations \(a \leq d, b \leq e, c \leq d, c \leq e\) and, of course, \(\top\) above everything. Then \(a ∨ c = d\) and \(b ∨ c = e\). Let moreover \(τ\) be the embedding of
  \(\{c, \top\}\). Then both \(a\) and \(b\) are \(τ\)-small but the join of \(a\) and \(b\) is \(\top\), so that they are not small under any scale that trivializes \(d\) and \(e\) by mapping them to
  \(\top{σ} := σ(\top_P)\) but preserves \(a\) and \(b\) by mapping them below \(\top_{σ}\). The underlying reason for this is that, unlike in the absolute case, where the tablets are
  \(id_{P}\) where smallness is stable under joins, this is not always the case for non-trivial tablets. So in particular \(τ\)-small elements are can be non-small against each other.
<!-- end counterexample-2 -->
<!-- example-35: body_md -->
\label{xmp:2}
\index{density!topological-measure-theoretic}
\index{fat Cantor set}
  A (not necessarily open) subset \(ι\) of \(X\) is dense with respect to the morphism triple
  \(\mathbf{O}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{M}(X) → ℝ_{∞, \geq 0}\), where \(\mathbf{M}(X)\) are the measurable subsets of \(X\), if and only if for each open subset \(κ\) of \(X\) it holds that if
  \(ι ∧ κ = ∅\) in \(\mathbf{M}(X)\), then \(κ\) has measure \(0\). So \(ι\) is dense if and only if the only open subsets that it does not intersect with are measure-theoretically negligible.

  If we take, for concreteness, \(X = ℝ^{n}\) with its usual measure and topology, then this is a slightly disappointing example since no non-trivial open subset of \(ℝ^{n}\) has measure \(0\).
  But what if we switch out \(\mathbf{O}(X)\) with \(\mathbf{C}(X)\)? Then \(ι\) is dense if and only if each closed subset \(κ\) of \(ℝ^{n}\) that \(ι\) does not intersect with has measure
  \(0\). Now, if \(κ\) is regular, so if it is the closure of a non-trivial open, then its measure is surely not \(0\), so it has to intersect with \(ι\). But there are small (and so in
  particular non-regular) closed subsets of \(ℝ^{n}\) that do not have measure \(0\), such as a \emph{fat Cantor set} (or \emph{Smith-Volterra-Cantor set}), which is closed, nowhere dense,
  yet has positive Lebesgue measure.

  Thus, the density condition with respect to closed tablets and the Lebesgue scale is sensitive to these ``thick'' nowhere dense sets while also excluding subsets that are too small such as
  atoms. In any case, it is a different and unexpected notion. Now, what does completeness mean? Well, if \(ι \supseteq κ \cap λ\), with \(κ\) closed-dense and \(λ\) closed, then \cref{rmk:dual-sigma-mu} tells
  us that \(σ(ι) \geq σ(λ)\), so completeness says that if \(ι\) is dense in a closed \(λ\), then \(ι\) is at least as big as \(λ\) when measured.

  Dually, \(ι\) is closed-\(σ\)-small if and only if each closed \(κ\) such that \(ι \cup κ = X\) has the same measure as \(X\) and similar for opens, and \(ι\) is closed-reduced if for each
  closed \(κ\) and small \(λ\) it holds that if \(ι\) is contained in \(κ \cup λ\) then \(σ(ι) \leq σ(κ)\) and similar for opens.
<!-- end example-35 -->
<!-- example-36: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:10}
  Let \(S\) be a set, \(w{:} S → ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞}\) an arbitrary weighting function and \(\overline{w}{:} \mathbf{P}(S) → ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞}\) be defined by linear extension, i.e. for some subset
  \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow S\) of \(S\) and well-ordering \(\overset{>}{A}\) of \(A\) the limit \(\mathbf{lim}_{a ∈ \overset{>}{A}} ∑_{b ∈ (a)} w(ι(b))\), with that being \(∞\) if that series
  diverges. Note that since the reals are Cauchy-complete and \(w\) is positively valued, each such \(\overline{w}\) on each \(ι\) either goes to infinity for every well-ordering
  of \(A\) or is absolutely convergent on some well-ordering, which implies that it is so on every well-ordering. In other words, this definition is independent of the chosen
  order. Since \(\overline{w}\) is given by linear extension, it is binarily additive, so smallness and density are special cases of \cref{xmp:28}.
<!-- end example-36 -->
<!-- example-37: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:12}
  In the situation of \cref{xmp:28} let \(\lfloor - \rfloor_{c}{:} ℝ_{\geq0, ∞} → ℕ_{\geq0, ∞}\) be given on \(r ∈ ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞}\) by the largest \(n ∈ ℕ_{\geq0, ∞}\) such that
  \(r \geq nc\). Note that these definitions also work for \(r = ∞\) and \(c = ∞\). Then \(ι\) is \((σ⨾ \lfloor - \rfloor_{c})\)-small if and only if
  \(\lfloor σ(X) \rfloor_{c} = \lfloor σ(¬ ι) \rfloor_{c}\). So since \(σ(X) = σ(¬ ι) + σ(ι)\) we have that \(ι\) is
  \((σ⨾ \lfloor - \rfloor_{c})\)-small if and only if

  \[\lfloor σ(¬ ι) + σ(ι) \rfloor_{c} = \lfloor σ(¬ ι)\rfloor_{c}\].

  So basically \(ι\) is small if and only if it fits within a rounding error.

  Dually, \(ι\) is dense if its intersection with each \(\geq c\)-large subset is non-nil, and sated if for every dense \(κ\) and \(λ\), if \(ι\) contains \(κ\) in \(λ\), then the
  measure of \(ι\) is as large or larger as the measure of \(λ\), up to rounding downwards.
<!-- end example-37 -->
<!-- example-38: body_md -->
\label{xmp:106}
  Let \(ι{:} \mathbf{P}_{inf}(ℕ) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(ℕ)\) be the embedding of the sub-preorder of \(\mathbf{P}(ℕ)\) whose non-trivial elements are the infinite subsets of \(ℕ\). Then \(S \subseteq ℕ\) is \(ι\)-dense if
  and only if its intersection with each infinite subset of \(ℕ\) is infinite, i.e. if its complement is finite, so if \(S\) is co-finite. \(S\) is \(ι\)-sated if and only if whenever
  \(S \supseteq Q \cap T\) with \(Q\) infinite and \(T\) co-finite, then \(S \supseteq Q\). This holds trivially for finite sets. If \(S\) is infinite but not \(ℕ\), choose \(x ∉ S\). Set \(Q = S ∪ \{x\}\)
  (infinite) and \(T = ℕ \setminus \{x\}\) (co-finite). Then \(Q ∩ T = S\) but \(Q ≠ S\), violating satedness. For \(ℕ\), satedness holds again.
<!-- end example-38 -->
<!-- example-39: body_md -->
\label{xmp:6}
  Let \(ι{:} \mathbf{P}_{\cancel{∂}}(ℝ^{n}) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(ℝ^{n})\) be the embedding of unbounded subsets of \(ℝ^{n}\). Then \(S \subseteq ℝ^{n}\) is \(ι\)-dense if and only if its intersection with every unbounded
  subset of \(ℝ^{n}\) is non-empty, so if its complement is bounded. We can again prove as in \cref{xmp:106} that the only subsets of \(ℝ^{n}\) that are \(ι\)-sated are bounded or
  \(ℝ^{n}\) itself.
<!-- end example-39 -->
<!-- example-40: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:15}
  In \cref{dfn:25} we defined geodesically convex sub-2-categories in such a way that each geodesically convex \(ι{:} \mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) is uniquely determined by the objects it contains. Thus,
  there exists a preorder morphism \(τ_{conv}{:} \mathbf{Conv}(\mathcal{B}) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{Ob}(\mathcal{B})\) from the convex sub-2-categories of \(\mathcal{B}\) forward ordered by inclusion
  (which is non-evil if \(\mathcal{B}\) has no non-trivial isomorphisms like the examples we looked at in \cref{sec:other-examples}). so that a subset of the objects of \(\mathcal{B}\) is
  \(τ_{conv}\)-small if and only if the smallest geodesically convex sub-2-category of \(\mathcal{B}\) that contains all objects outside \(ι\) is \(\mathcal{B}\) itself.
<!-- end example-40 -->
<!-- example-41: body_md -->
\label{xmp:30}
  If the tablets \(τ{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathbf{Mon}}(M) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(M)\) are given by the embedding of the sub-monoids of a monoid \(M\), then a subset \(ι\) of \(M\) is
  \(τ\)-small if and only if its complement \(¬ ι\) is not contained in a proper submonoid. So for
  instance in \(ℕ\) the even numbers are small while the odd numbers are not. \(ι\) is \(τ\)-reduced if whenever \(ι\) is contained in the union of a submonoid and a small subset, then
  \(ι\) is in the submonoid.

  Note that \(\bot_{τ}\) is \(\{e\}\), not \(\emptyset\) (the bottom of \(\mathbf{P}(M)\)), so that \(ι\) is \(τ\)-dense if for each non-trivial submonoid \(κ\) the intersection of \(ι\) with \(κ\) contains an
  element outside \(\{e\}\). It suffices to test this on principally generated submonoids, so \(ι\) is \(τ\)-dense if its intersection with each orbit \(⟨a⟩\) contains a non-zero
  power of \(a\). \(ι\) is \(τ\)-sated if for each \(τ\)-dense \(κ\) and submonoid \(λ\) it holds that \(ι\) contains \(κ \cap λ\) if and only if \(ι\) contains \(λ\). Given now \(a ∈ M\) such
  that \(ι\) contains \(a^{n}\) let \(κ\) consist of \(a^{n}\) and all \(b\) such that \(a\) is not in the orbit of \(b\). Then \(κ\) is \(τ\)-dense and \(ι\) contains \(a^{n}\); so that \(ι\) is
  again \(τ\)-sated if and only if it contains each radical of its elements and thus if it is reduced in the monoid-theoretic sense.
<!-- end example-41 -->
<!-- example-42: body_md -->
\label{xmp:1}
\index{cost!as scale}
\index{smallness!applied to machine parts}
  Let \(M\) be some kind of machine and \(\mathbf{SOb}(M)\) the preorder of parts of \(M\) where \(a \leq b\) if and only if \(b\) is not functional without \(a\). Then \(a\) is small
  if and only if it factors through each maximal part of \(M\) by \cref{■pn_:8} and the finitude of real-world machines.
  Now let \(τ{:} \mathbf{T}(M) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}(M)\) be the embedding of those parts that can be bought stand-alone. Then a part \(ι\) is \(τ\)-dense if and only if it factors through each part of
  \(M\) that can be bought, so if we get it delivered each time we buy a replacement. Notice that the embedding \(τ\) is connected to the material we exposed in
  \cref{sec:monoidal-smallness}: \(τ\) embeds those parts that can be duplicated, so for which addition makes sense (and arises, for instance if \(b\) is broken and we buy a replacement
  \(b'\), but \(a \leq b\) is fine, so we obtain an \(a\)-spare \(a'\)).

  But because \(\mathbf{SOb}(M)\) is elementary, i.e. consists of parts and not families of parts, its smallness relations are somewhat rough. So let us endow
  \(\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{SOb}(M))\) with the relation \(F \leq G\) if and only if for each \(a ∈ \mathbf{SOb}(M)\) such that each element of \(G\) is \(\leq a\) it holds that each
  element of \(F\) is \(\leq a\). So in particular if \(a = \bigvee B\) then \(a = B\) in this order up to univalence, so as a category this preorder is actually in part a weak quotient and
  equivalent to the ideal completion.

  Now, smallness under the powerset-induced function
  \(\mathbf{P}(τ){:} \mathbf{P}(\mathbf{T}(M)) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(\mathbf{SOb}(M))\) gives us a more useful size measure. Then a family of parts \(F\) of \(M\) is
  not small if and only if we can buy a family \(G\) that contains all parts of \(M\) missing in \(F\) but not all parts of \(M\) in itself, so that we can assemble \(M\) from \(F\) and \(G\), given the
  necessary skill and machinery.

  But of course there is a \emph{cost} associated with duplication. So let \(σ{:} \mathbf{T}(M) → ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞}\) be given by the price of each part and
  \(\overline{σ}{:} \mathbf{SOb}(M) → ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞}\) by \(\overline{σ}(a) := \bigwedge_{a' ∈ \mathbf{T}(M){:} a \leq τ(a')} σ(a')\) so basically the least cost we have to pay for \(a\). Finally, let \(\hat{σ}\) be
  given by  \(\hat{σ}(F) := \bigwedge_{F \simeq G} ∑_{ι ∈ G} \overline{σ}(ι)\), so the least cost we have to pay for the parts of \(F\).  Then \(F\) is \((\mathbf{P}(τ) \mid \hat{σ})\)-small if and only if
  each family of parts of \(M\) that we can buy costs at least much as \(M\) itself — a frequent occurrence when one tries to repair something. If we combine this scale with the rounding we
  introduced in \cref{xmp_:12}, we can further refine smallness so that a family is small if and only if the cheapest way to complete it is as expensive as \(M\) up to a rounding error.
<!-- end example-42 -->
<!-- example-43: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:1}
\index{infinitesimal}
\index{nonstandard analysis!infinitesimality}
\index{density function!for gases}
  As noted in the introduction, our notion of density is motivated by the topological one, which is binary. Here we want to sketch out the connection to the treatments of density
  through continuous functions, as arise in chemistry. So let \(X\) be spacetime and \(γ\) some gas. When should we say that \(γ\) is dense in \(X\)? This question is tricky
  because \(γ\) has, strictly speaking, only finitely many atoms while \(X\) is continuous; and often glanced over. Arguably the most conceptually thorough way to handle such
  questions is through Robinson's nonstandard analysis,\cite{robinsonNonstandardAnalysis1974} or even more particularly through Nelson's internal set
  theory.\cite{nelsonInternalSetTheory} In these, the ``standard'' natural numbers \(ℕ\) are embedded in a \emph{nonstandard} extension \(\overline{ℕ}\) which fulfills the same
  algebraic axioms but contains additional numbers \(N > ℕ\), which are larger than any standard natural number (this is called \emph{hyperfinite}). So a nonstandard number is a
  number that is larger than any finite number but acts in essentially the same way. As Nelson worked out, this gives a rigorous idealization of what it means that ``a number
  beyond the standard range'', as is often assumed in the natural sciences. Similarly the ``standard'' real numbers \(ℝ\) are embedded into a nonstandard extension \(\overline{ℝ}\)
  that also contains the nonstandard natural numbers \(\overline{ℕ}\), so that there exists for each nonstandard number \(N\) an inverse \(\frac{1}{N}\) and thus an
  \emph{infinitesimal number} \(δ\) such that \(0 < δ < ℝ_{> 0}\).  We can define a scale \(\mathbf{st}_{∞}{:} \overline{ℝ} → ℝ_{\pm ∞}\), given by assigning to each
  extended real \(r\) its standard part, and a scale \(\mathbf{infl}{:} \overline{ℝ} → \mathbf{h}(0)_{\pm ∞}\) to the \emph{halo} \(\mathbf{h}(0)\) of such infinitesimal numbers
  around \(0\), given by the identity on \(\mathbf{h}(0)\) and \(\pm ∞\) otherwise. These two jointly
  describe non-standard finitude and infinitesimality through smallness.

  It is also well-known (see for instance \cite{alamApplicationsNonstandardAnalysis2021}) that in such a setting each Hausdorff space admits a nonstandard extension, so if we
  assume that our spacetime is Hausdorff, which seems reasonable, then there exists an extension \(ξ_{X}{:} X \hookrightarrow \overline{X}\) and a partial function
  \(\mathbf{st}{:} \overline{X} → X\) such that \(ξ_{X}⨾ \mathbf{st} = \mathbf{id}_{X}\). So \(\overline{X}\) houses \(X\) but also for each point \(x\) of \(X\) a \emph{monad} or
  \emph{halo} \(\mathbf{h}(x) := \mathbf{st}^{-1}(x)\) filled with nonstandard elements around \(X\).

  A very simple definition for ``γ is dense in \(X\)'' is then that each open subset of \(X\) contains some atom in \(γ\). If we assume that the spatial extension of each atom is
  0,\footnote{More generally if we assume that the diameter of each atom is infinitesimal.}, then this is impossible if \(γ\) has only a standard amount of atoms (since \(X\) is
  continuous), but quite possible if \(γ\) contains a nonstandard set \(G\) of them. It makes sense then to treat \(γ\) as a function \(γ{:} G \hookrightarrow \overline{X}\) which assigns to each
  atom of \(γ\) its position. But this just says that \(γ\) is dense with respect to the collection of tablets given by the composite
  \(\mathbf{O}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(\overline{X})\).

  The question is now whether we can derive from such a nonstandard gas a function which assigns to each point \(x\) in \(X\) a density of \(γ\) at \(x\), which would complete the
  bridge from our notion to density functions. An easy approach in line with our notion of density would be to first fix a
  \(δ ∈ \mathbf{h}(0)\) that we use to scale infinitesimal
  lengths to normal ones. We can derive a density function \(δ_{γ}'(x) := \frac{1}{\mathbf{min}\{r ∈ ℝ_{∞} | ∃ g ∈ G{:} γ(g) ∈ ●^{δr}_{x}\}}\) where \(●_{x}^{δr}\) is the ball around
  \(x\) of radius \(δ r\), so by finding the smallest ball around each \(x\) that does not contain any elements of \(γ\) and thus the representators of the smallness-ideal. This
  gives us the right result at \(x\) in that if there is an atom of \(γ\) precisely at \(x\) then the density function maps to \(∞\) and the function decreases with the perimeter.

  But in chemistry a density function is dependent on both the local number of atoms and
  their distance, and this introduces a parameter that cannot cleanly be handled just by the current framework. We could try to sum over all atoms in \(\mathbf{h}(x)\), perhaps
  scaled by their mass and inversely scaled by their distance to \(x\), but this sum is ill-defined in non-standard analysis. What we can do is fix a nonstandard \(δ\) and sum over
  all atoms in the \(δ\)-ball around \(x\). But the result of this sum would, without further assumptions, depend on \(δ\), and not necessarily just up to a nonstandard part. So
  sadly it seems like non-standard analysis cannot be used to derive a density function in a way that accounts for both the mass of atoms and their distance from \(x\) without some
  arbitrariness, even in an idealized way.
<!-- end example-43 -->
<!-- example-44: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:22}
  \index{digitization!as tablets}
  \index{density function!from lattices}
  Digitization, such as pixellation, is ubiquitous in the modern world, and we often test things up to pixels, e.g. when we film with a digital
  camera. Abstracting a little we can describe this by taking the inclusion of the (order-theoretic) subobject lattice
  \(\mathbf{P}(λ){:} \mathbf{P}(Λ) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(M)\) as tablets, where \(λ\) is the embedding of a (module-theoretic) lattice, i.e. additive sub-monoid
  \(λ{:} Λ \hookrightarrow M\) into some module \(M\) over some semiring or ring. So we use \(λ\) to digitize \(M\). For \(V = R^{n}\) with \(R\) a ring we always have a canonical such
  sub-monoid given by the embedding \(⟨1⟩^{n}{:} ℤ^{n} \hookrightarrow R^{n}\) that is the \(n\)-fold power of the initial ring-morphism into \(R\) (i.e. the submonoid additively generated by
  \(1 ∈ R\)), but we can also use other lattices. Then a subset of \(V\) is \(λ\)-dense if and only if it contains all elements of \(λ\). Often we are only interested in the density of a
  subobject \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow V\) in some neighborhood \(U\), such as the convex closure of \(ι\), which we can evaluate by restricting \(λ\) to \(U\). Then \(ι\) is
  \(λ|_{U}\)-dense if and only if it contains all elements of \(λ\) in \(U\).

  Now, many module-theoretic lattices are structured into parameter-dependent families which we can use to define density functions. For instance, \(⟨1⟩\) generalizes to the
  \(R\)-parameterized family \(⟨-⟩^{n}\) of \(n\)-cubic lattices of \(R\). So if \(R\) is also complete and totally ordered, i.e. \(ℝ\), then we can define a density function
  \(δ{:} \mathbf{P}(ℝ^{n}) → ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞}\) with \(δ(ι)\) given by

  \[\mathbf{inf} \{r ∈ ℝ | ι \text{ is \(⟨r⟩^{n}\)-dense}\}\]

  if any such \(r\) exists, and \(∞\) otherwise. This is monotone and thus at least a morphism of preorders, but according to this definition, no \(ι\) could be dense which did not contain \(0\), since \(0\) is
  invariant under scaling. We can remedy this defect by introducing a slight variant of our definition of density: we say that \emph{\(ι\) is \(λ\)-dense up to
    translation} if there exists some translation, i.e. affine isomorphism \(θ\) such that \(ι\) is \((λ⨾ θ)\)-dense. So using lattices we do actually get a decently
  well-behaved density-function. We could also replace the points in \(λ\) with \(n\)-dimensional disks, cube or other shapes of some diameter, which would give us two density
  parameters that are, essentially, pixel size and pixel density — the denser the pixels, the fewer subobjects will look dense compared to them, and the larger the pixels, the
  more subobjects will look dense compared to them, since this increases the area that they can intersect with.

  Now, \(ι\) is \(λ\)-sated if and only if for each subset \(κ\) of \(R^{n}\) such that \(ι\) contains \(κ \cap λ\) it holds that \(ι\) also contains \(κ\). This is too general,
  however, to be of much interest: \(ι\) would in particular have to contain \((ι \cap λ) \cup \left(R^{n} ∖ (λ ∖ ι)\right)\). But if we restrict \(κ\) to a second set of tablets
  \(τ\) as we described in \cref{rmα_:28}, then we can exercise much finer control over satedness. In particular, let \(τ\) be given by the embedding of all convex subsets of
  \(R^{n}\). Then \(ι\) is sated with regard to \(λ\) and \(τ\) if and only if for each family \(F\) of points in \(λ\) it contains the convex closure \(\overline{F}\) of \(F\), so if it is convex relative to
  \(λ\): only on its intersection with\(λ\) need it be convex.

  But if we have a set of generators \(B\) of \(Λ\), then we can restrict the tablets still more and take \(τ'\) to be given by the embedding of all convex subsets formed by points \(q_{i}\)
  that are each adjacent to a point \(p\) in \(λ\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are adjacent if and only if there exists a \(b ∈ B\) such that \(bp = q\) (so if they are connected by an
  edge in their Ceyley graph). So for \(λ\) being the embedding of \(ℤ^{n}\) into \(ℝ^{n}\), \(τ'\) is given by all subsimplices with integral vertices that have a tip \(p\) and
  \(p\)-adjacent points \(q_{i}\), so that the triangle for each triple \(p, q_{i}, q_{j}\) with \(i ≠ j\) is rectangular in \(p\). So basically, \(ι\) is \((τ, τ')\)-dense if and only if
  it contains the triangulation of its intersection with \(λ\). For instance this shape is \((λ, τ')\)-sated with \(λ\) the unit cubic lattice and \(τ'\) the minimal rectangular subsimplices of \(λ\):

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzpicture}
      \fill (0, 0) -- (0, 1) -- (1, 1) -- (1, 0); \fill (0, 0) -- (0, -1) -- (-1, -1) -- (-1, 0);
    \end{tikzpicture}
    \caption{\label{fi♭_:23}}
  \end{figure}

  where all squares are unit squares whose vertices are on \(λ\), and it would remain so whatever we add around this ``core'' part as long as it does not intersect with any other
  vertices in \(λ\). But this part of the unit square is not:

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzpicture}
      \fill[black] (0, 0) -- (0, 1) -- (0.5, 0) -- cycle; \fill[black] (1, 0) -- (1, 1) -- (0.5, 0) -- cycle;
    \end{tikzpicture}
                             
  \end{figure}

  but it is \(\frac{λ}{4}\)-sated, i.e. sated if we quarter the grid size:

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \begin{tikzpicture}
    \fill[black] (0, 0) -- (0, 1) -- (0.5, 0) -- cycle; \fill[black] (1, 0) -- (1, 1) -- (0.5, 0) -- cycle; \draw[blue] (0, 0) rectangle (0.25, 0.5) -- cycle; \draw[red] (0, 0.5) -- (0, 1)
    -- (0.25, 0.5) -- cycle; \draw[yellow] (0.25, 0) -- (0.25, 0.5) -- (0.5, 0) -- cycle; \draw[blue] (0.75, 0) rectangle (1, 0.5) -- cycle; \draw[red] (1, 0.5) -- (1, 1) -- (0.75, 0.5) --
    cycle; \draw[yellow] (0.75, 0) -- (0.75, 0.5) -- (0.5, 0) -- cycle;
  \end{tikzpicture}
                           
\end{figure}

 By using a different discrete lattice, in particular a hexagonal one, we can
change the shape of these simplices, in particular to equilateral ones. So satedness says that a subobject \(ι\) actually contains its approximation
\(\overline{ι \cap λ}\), obtained by taking the convex closure of each of its minimal \(λ\)-sub-simplices, i.e. its ``support''
\(ι \cap λ\). In particular the minimal sub-simplices of \(ι \cap λ\) form a subdivision of \(\overline{ι \cap λ}\).\footnote{We will define subdivisions formally in future work, here we
  just mean a decomposition of \(ι\) into topological closed a irreducible subsets whose intersection factors through through their boundary.} 

So an element is sated if and only if it contains the simplices spanned by the vertices of its lattice squares. If each point of \(λ\) stands for a sensor, and an image is created by
flipping the color of a pixel at \((i, j)\) if and only if \((i, j)\) is in \(ι\), then the resulting image essentially corresponds to \(\overline{ι \cap λ}\), so \(ι\) being sated
states that it the image we can form of it through \(λ\) corresponds to \(ι\) at least on the parts of it we can see. Note also that for
\emph{any} discrete lattice \(λ{:} Λ → ℝ^{n}\), i.e. a lattice in \(ℝ^{n}\) consisting of nowhere dense vertices, any union of the subsimplices spanned by its vertices is locally
convex and piecewise linear and thus locally contractible. So if \(ι\) is \(λ\)-sated for any discrete \(λ\), \(ι\) is locally contractible up to some stuff outside its pixellated
support \(ι \cap λ\).

If we now add a scale \(σ{:} \mathbf{P}(ℝ^{n}) → S\) we can relax this condition up to some kind of neglibility. Note that, since we do not assume general additivity, we do not
need to restrict to the measurable subsets of \(ℝ^{n}\) but can instead take \(σ(S)\) as the volume measure of the closure of \(S\), which is Borel measurable since it is the
closure of a subset. Since each sub-simplex of \(ℝ^{n}\) is in particular closed, this reduces to the volume measure \(υ\) on the tablets we use to measure satedness, i.e.
minimal sub-simplices of \(λ\). Then \(ι\) is \((λ, σ)\)-sated if and only if each minimal sub-simplex on the vertices in \(ι \cap λ\) that \(ι\) does not fully contain is of volume
\(0\), i.e. lower-dimensional. But we can also take as \(σ\) the postcomposition \(υ_{h}\) of \(υ\) (on closures) with some rounding scale \(ρ{:} ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞} → ℕ_{∞}\) as in \cref{xmp_:12}
that maps everything under a certain threshold \(h\) to \(0\). Then \(ι\) is \((λ, υ_{h})\)-sated if and only if the sub-simplices on its \(λ\)-vertices that it does not contain
have volume \(< h\). We can also keep this \(σ\) fixed but allow the tablets to vary, and so say that \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow ℝ^{N}\) is \emph{\(h\)-lattice-sated} if there exists some discrete
sub-lattice \(λ\) of \(ℝ^{n}\) such that \(ι\) is \((λ, υ_{h})\)-sated, so if the volume of the sub-simplices on \(λ\)-vertices in \(ι\) that are not themselves in \(ι\) is
\(< h\). Again it makes sense to relativize this to translations of discrete lattices. We can call this \emph{equivariantly \(h\)-lattice-satedness}, where the equivariance is
understood as translation invariance.
<!-- end example-44 -->
<!-- example-45: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:23}
\index{Minkowski's theorem!via tablets}
On the other hand, we can we take as the tablets the embedding \(τ{:} \{λ, \{0\}\} \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}\supseteq \{0\}(ℝ^{n})\) where \(λ{:} Λ \hookrightarrow ℝ^{n}\) is a lattice embedding (i.e. an embedding of an
additive subgroup), \(\mathbf{P}_{\supseteq \{0\}}(ℝ^{n})\) is the set of subsets of \(ℝ^{n}\) that contain \(0\). Then \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow ℝ^{n}\) is \(τ\)-dense if and only if it contains a point in \(λ\) apart
  from \(0\). This kind of condition characterizes \emph{Minkowski's Theorem}, which states that each radially symmetric convex set around \(0\) in \(ℝ^{n}\) whose volume is larger than \(2^{n}\)
  times the determinant of \(λ\) is \(τ\)-dense.

  More generally, if we take as the tablets \(τ{:} T \hookrightarrow P\) for a bounded preorder only one tablet \(λ\) and a bottom tablet in the preimage of \(\bot_{P}\), then any element of \(P\)
  whose intersection with \(τ(λ)\) is not \(\bot_{P}\) is \(τ\)-dense.
<!-- end example-45 -->
<!-- definition-28: body_md -->
\label{dfn:3}\index{\(\mathbf{PrO}\)}\index{\(\mathbf{UBP}\)}\index{\(\mathbf{UBP}_{w}\)}
  The \emph{2-category of preorders} \(\mathbf{PrO}\) is the 2-category whose objects are preorders, whose morphisms are preorder morphisms and whose 2-morphisms are objectwise inequalities
  between morphisms.

  The 2-category \(\mathbf{UBP}\) of \emph{upward-bounded preorders and preorder morphisms} is the full sub-2-category of \(\mathbf{PrO}\) on upward-bounded preorders.

  The
  wide sub-2-category \(\mathbf{UBP}_{w}\) of \emph{upward-bounded preorders and top-preserving preorder morphisms} is the wide sub-2-category of \(\mathbf{UBP}\) whose objects are upward-bounded preorders and whose morphisms are
  top-preserving preorder morphisms.
<!-- end definition-28 -->
<!-- remark-23: body_md -->
\label{rmk:17}
  \index{ideal embedding!is principal}
  In particular, each ideal embedding \(ι{:} a \hookrightarrow P\) in \(\mathbf{UBP}\) is principal since  \(\top_{ι}\) represents \(ι\) as an ideal.
<!-- end remark-23 -->
<!-- remark-24: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:35}
  So visually, \(\mathbf{UBP}\) looks a bit like a saw: \(\top_{P}\) is the tip of a tooth, \(f{:} P → Q\) a tooth-diagonal downward and \(\top_{f} \leq \top_{Q}\) the blade going back up to the tip.
<!-- end remark-24 -->
<!-- definition-29: body_md -->
\label{defn_:9}
\index{contravariantly terminal}
\index{contravariantly initial}
  An object \(O\) of a 2-category \(\mathcal{B}\) is \emph{contravariantly initial} if for each object \(X\) of \(\mathcal{B}\) the category \(\mathcal{B}(O, X)\) has a terminal object. Dually, an object
  \(T{:} \mathcal{B}\) is \emph{contravariantly terminal} if for each object \(X\) of \(\mathcal{B}\) the category \(\mathcal{B}(X, T)\) has an initial object.
<!-- end definition-29 -->
<!-- remark-25: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:21}
  This definition has a global component and a local one, and in the name we track the variance between the two.
<!-- end remark-25 -->
<!-- counterexample-3: body_md -->
\label{cxmp:2}
\index{contravariantly terminal object!non-uniqueness}
  Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be the 2-category on two elements \(a, b\), generated by two morphisms \(f{:} a → b, g{:} b → a\) and two 2-morphisms
  \(α{:} \mathbf{id}_{a} \Rightarrow f⨾ g, β{:} \mathbf{id}_{b} \Rightarrow g⨾ f\). Then each of \(a\) and \(b\) are contravariantly terminal, but they are not equivalent. Moreover, if we introduce an inverse to
  \(β\), then \(a\) is (weakly) initial but \(b\) is still contravariantly initial.
<!-- end counterexample-3 -->
<!-- example-46: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:4}
  Actually, every object \(P\) of \(\mathbf{UBP}\) is contravariantly initial, with the terminal object in \(\mathbf{UBP}(P, Q)\) given by \(\top_{Q}\) for each \(Q{:} \mathbf{UBP}\), but \(*\)
  is uniquely described by being terminally contravariantly initial, since it is terminal. Moreover, \(*\) is the unique contravariantly
  initial object in the monic part \(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}\) of \(\mathbf{UBP}\).
<!-- end example-46 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:ofs}
  \index{orthogonal factorization system!on \(\mathbf{UBP}\)}
  \index{ideal-top factorization system@ideal-top factorization system}
  \index{top-preserving map!in factorization system}
  \index{ideal embedding!in factorization system}
  In the \(2\)-category \(\mathbf{UBP}\), the classes
  \[
    \mathcal{E} \;=\; \{\text{top-preserving maps}\}, \qquad \mathcal{M} \;=\; \{\text{ideal embeddings}\}
  \]
  constitute an orthogonal factorization system. Explicitly, every morphism \(f {:} P → Q\) factors uniquely up to unique isomorphism as
  \[
    P \;\xrightarrow{\;f'\;}\; (\top_{f}) \;\xhookrightarrow{\;\iota_{\top_{f}}\;}\; Q,
  \]
  where \((\top_{f}) = \{q ∈ Q \mid q \leq \top_{f}\}\) is the principal ideal of \(\top_{f}\) in \(Q\), the map \(f'\) is the corestriction \(f'(p) = f(p)\), and \(\iota_{\top_{f}}\) is the inclusion.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
We verify the defining properties of an orthogonal factorization system: existence of factorizations and the diagonal fill-in.

  \emph{Factorization.}
  Given \(f {:} P → Q\), set \(\top_{f} := f(\top_{P})\). Since \(f\) is monotone, \(f(p) \leq f(\top_{P}) = \top_{f}\) for every \(p ∈ P\), so \(f\) corestricts to \(f' {:} P → (\top_{f})\) with \(f'(p) = f(p)\). This map is top-preserving:
  \[
    f'(\top_{P}) \;=\; f(\top_{P}) \;=\; \top_{f} \;=\; \top_{(\top_{f})}.
  \]
  The inclusion \(\iota_{\top_{f}} {:} (\top_{f}) \hookrightarrow Q\) is an ideal embedding whose image is the principal ideal \((\top_{f})\), and \(f = f' ⨾ \iota_{\top_{f}}\).

  \emph{Diagonal fill-in.}
  Suppose given a strictly commuting square
  \[
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
      P \ar[r, "h"] \ar[d, "e"'] & R \ar[d, "m"] \\
      Q \ar[r, "k"'] & S
    \end{tikzcd}
    \qquad e ⨾ k \;=\; h ⨾ m,
  \]
  where \(e {:} P → Q\) is top-preserving and \(m {:} R \hookrightarrow S\) is an ideal embedding with image \((\top_{m})\). We construct a unique diagonal \(d {:} Q → R\).

  For each \(q ∈ Q\), monotonicity of \(k\) gives \(k(q) \leq k(\top_{Q})\). Since \(e\) is top-preserving, \(\top_{Q} = e(\top_{P})\), whence
  \[
    k(\top_{Q}) \;=\; k(e(\top_{P})) \;=\; m(h(\top_{P})) \;\leq\; m(\top_{R}) \;=\; \top_{m},
  \]
  so \(k(q) \leq \top_{m}\), i.e.\ \(k(q) ∈ (\top_{m}) = \mathbf{Im}(m)\). Because \(m\) is an order-embedding, it admits an order-theoretic inverse \(m^{-1} {:} (\top_{m}) \xrightarrow{\;\cong\;} R\). We may therefore define
  \[
    d(q) \;:=\; m^{-1}(k(q)),
  \]
  which is monotone as the composite \(Q \xrightarrow{k} (\top_{m}) \xrightarrow{m^{-1}} R\). The two triangles commute:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \(d ⨾ m = k\) since for all \(q ∈ Q\), \(m(d(q)) = m(m^{-1}(k(q))) = k(q)\).
  \item \(e ⨾ d = h\) since for all \(p ∈ P\), \(d(e(p)) = m^{-1}(k(e(p))) = m^{-1}(m(h(p))) = h(p)\).
  \end{itemize}
  Uniqueness is immediate: if \(d' {:} Q → R\) also satisfies \(d' ⨾ m = k\), then \(m(d'(q)) = m(d(q))\) for all \(q\), and injectivity of \(m\) forces \(d' = d\).

  \emph{Intersection.}
  If \(f {:} P → Q\) is both top-preserving and an ideal embedding, then \(f\) is an order-embedding with image \((\top_{f}) = (\top_{Q}) = Q\), hence an order-isomorphism. Thus
  \(\mathcal{E} \cap \mathcal{M}\) is the core groupoid \(\mathbf{Core}(\mathbf{UBP})\) of isomorphisms in \(\mathbf{UBP}\).
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-26: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:ofs}
  The diagonal fill-in admits a natural oplax \(2\)-categorical strengthening: if the square commutes only up to a \(2\)-cell \(e ⨾ k \leq h ⨾ m\), the same construction yields \(d\) with \(d ⨾ m = k\) strictly and a \(2\)-cell \(e ⨾ d \leq h\). This oplax lifting is unique, since \(\mathbf{UBP}\) is preorder-enriched and there is at most one \(2\)-cell between any pair of parallel morphisms.
<!-- end remark-26 -->
<!-- remark-27: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:22}
  Building on \cref{rmα_:35} we can understand the ``saw-toothedness'' of \(\mathbf{UBP}\) as a correspondence between horizontal and vertical distance for ideals in that for each \(a, b ∈ P\) the
  interval between \(a\) and \(b\) is in one-to-one correspondence with the principal ideals that \((a)\) factors through that factor through \((b)\).
<!-- end remark-27 -->
<!-- remark-28: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:34}
  Of course dual statements hold for the category \(\mathbf{DBP}\) of downward-bounded preorders, with filters instead of ideals.
<!-- end remark-28 -->
<!-- definition-30: body_md -->
\label{defn:elemwise-small-pres-reflect}\index{smallness-preserving morphism}\index{smallness-reflecting morphism}
  Let \(f {:} P → Q\) be a morphism in \(\mathbf{UBP}\):
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \(f\) \emph{preserves smallness at \(a\)} if \(a\) small in \(P\) implies \(f(a)\) small in \(Q\).

  \item \(f\) \emph{reflects smallness at \(a\)} if \(f(a)\) small in \(Q\) implies \(a\) small in \(P\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-30 -->
<!-- definition-31: body_md -->
\label{def:a-cover-lifting}
\index{top-join-lifting}
\index{join-lifting}
  Let \(f{:} P → Q\) in \(\mathbf{UBP}\) and \(a\in P\).
  We say that \(f\) is \emph{\(\top\)-join-lifting on \(a\)} if for every \(c ∈ Q\) with
  \[
    f(a)∨ c = \top_{Q}
  \]
  there exists a \(b ∈ P\) such that \(f(b) \leq c\) and \(a ∨ b = \top_P\).
<!-- end definition-31 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{prp:8}
  Given \(f {:} P → Q\) in \(\mathbf{UBP}\) and \(a ∈ P\), assume that \(f\) preserves joins of \(a\) to \(\top_{P}\) and lifts \(\top\)-joins on \(a\). Then \(f\) preserves smallness at \(a\).
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Let \(c ∈ Q\) satisfy \(f(a)∨c = \top_{Q}\). By the \(a\)-join-lifting property there exists a \(b ∈ P\) with \(f(b)\le c\) and \(a∨b=\top_P\). If \(a\) is small, then \(b = \top_{P}\), so that
  \(f(a) \leq f(a) ∨ f(b) = f(a) ∨ \top_{f} = \top_{f} \leq c\). So \(f(a) ∨ c = c = \top_{Q}\).
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- example-47: body_md -->
\label{xmp:105}
  Let \(f^{*}{:} \mathbf{C}([0, 1]) → \mathbf{C}([0, 2])\) from \cref{xmp:7} be induced through pullback along the continuous function \(f{:} [0, 2] \twoheadrightarrow [0, 1]\) that is the identity on
  \([0, 1] \subseteq [0, 2]\) and maps \([1, 2]\) to \(1\). Then \(f^{*}\) is not smallness-preserving because the fiber over \(1\) is not small:
  \([0, 1] ∨ f^{*}(\{1\}) = [0, 1] ∨ [1, 2] = [0, 2]\), so \(f^{*}(\{1\})\) is not small even though \(\{1\}\) is.
<!-- end example-47 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:2}
  Let \(f{:} P → Q\) be a top-join preserving morphism of preorders that is injective on \(\top_{f}\). If \(\top_{f}\) is reduced then \(f\) is smallness-reflecting.
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
\label{prf:3}
  Let \(a \in P\) be an element such that \(f(a)\) is small in \(Q\).
  Suppose \(b \in P\) is such that \(a ∨ b = \top_{P}\).
  Since \(f\) preserves top-joins, we have:
  \[
    f(a) ∨ f(b) \;=\; f(\top_{P}) \;=\; \top_{f}.
  \]
  By the hypothesis that \(f(a)\) is small in \(Q\) and \(\top_{f}\) is reduced in \(Q\), it follows from \cref{defn_:7} that:
  \[
    f(b) \;=\; \top_{f}.
  \]
  Using the assumption that \(f\) is injective on \(\top_{f}\), this implies \(b = \top_{P}\).
  Thus, the only element \(b\) in \(P\) that joins with \(a\) to give \(\top_{P}\) is \(\top_{P}\) itself.
  Therefore, \(a\) is small in \(P\).
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{crl:11}
  Let \(ι\) be an ideal embedding. If \(\top_{ι}\) is reduced then \(ι\) reflects smallness.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- definition-32: body_md -->
\label{def:rel-preserve-topjoin}
  With \(f = (h,g,k)\) as in \cref{fi♭_:9} and \(a ∈ P\), we say that \((h,g,k)\) \emph{preserves \((τ,a)\)-top-joins} or \emph{preserves \(τ\)-top-joins on \(a\)} if for every
  \(b ∈ T\) such that \(a ∨ τ(b) = \top_{P}\) one has
  \[
    g\!\bigl(a ∨ τ(b)\bigr) \;=\; g(a) ∨ g(τ(b)) = g(a) ∨ τ'(h(b)) \;=\; \top_{g}.
  \]

  On the other hand we say that \(f\) \emph{reflects \(τ'\)-top-joins on \(a\)} if for each \(b ∈ T\) with \(g(a) ∨ (τ⨾ g)(b) = \top_{g}\) it holds that \(a ∨ τ(b) = \top_{P}\).
<!-- end definition-32 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{prop:rel-reflect-small}
  Assume:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{item:71}  \((h,g,k)\) preserves \(τ\)-top-joins on \(a\);
  \item\label{item:72}  the top \(\top_{g}\) is reduced under \(τ'\) over \(σ'\),
  \item\label{item:66}  \(k\) reflects \(\top_{σ⨾ k}\),
  \end{enumerate}
  Under these hypotheses \((h,g,k)\) reflects relative smallness at \(a{:} P\).
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Suppose \(a' := g(a)\) is \((τ' \mid σ')\)-small. To show \(a\) is \((τ \mid σ)\)-small, take any \(b ∈ T\) such that
  \[
    a ∨ τ(b) = \top_{P}.
  \]
  Let now \(b'\) be given by \(h(b)\). Applying \(g\) and using preservation of \(τ\)-top-joins on \(a\)-joining families:

  \begin{equation}
    \label{qn_:1}
    \top_{g}
    \;=\;
    g(a ∨ τ(b))
    \;=\;
    g(a) ∨ (τ⨾ g)(b)
    \;=\;
    a' ∨ τ'(b').
  \end{equation}

  So \(b'\) joins with \(a'\) to contain \(\top_{g}\) under \(τ'\) in \(P'\), and since \(a'\) is \((τ' \mid σ')\)-small in \(P'\) and \(\top_{g}\) is \((τ' \mid σ')\)-reduced, it follows from
  \cref{defn_:21} that
\begin{equation}
    \label{qn_:3}
    (τ⨾ σ⨾ k)(b) = (τ'⨾ σ')(b') \geq σ'(\top_{g}) = (g⨾ σ')(\top_{P}) = (σ⨾ k)(\top_{P}) = \top_{σ⨾ k},
  \end{equation}

  and since \(τ(b) \leq \top_{P}\) and thus \(τ'(b') \leq g(\top_{P})\), the reverse inequality also holds and thus \((τ'⨾ σ')(b') = \top_{σ⨾ k}\).

  But since \(k\) reflects \(\top_{σ⨾ k}\) and \((τ⨾ σ⨾ k) (b) = \top_{σ⨾ k}\), it follows that \((τ⨾ σ)(b) = \top_{σ}\). Since this holds for every \(b ∈ T\), \(a\) is small.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- remark-29: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:14}
  It seems like not much (or nothing) can be gained from laxifying the squares of \cref{fi♭_:9}: for instance to apply \((τ' \mid σ')\)-reducedness in the proof of \cref{prop:rel-reflect-small}
  we would have to assume that the left square is lax so that the last equality in \cref{qn_:1} became \(g(a) ∨ (τ⨾ g)(b) \leq a' ∨ τ'(b')\). But then the first equality of \cref{qn_:3} would
  become an inequality in the wrong direction \((τ⨾ σ⨾ k)(b) \leq (τ'⨾ σ')(b')\), so that the proof would fall apart.
<!-- end remark-29 -->
<!-- definition-33: body_md -->
\label{defn_:8}
