  With \((h,g,k)\) as in \cref{fi♭_:9} and \(a {:} P\), \(g\) and \(h\) are \emph{\(\top\)-join-lifting on \(a\)} if for each \(b' ∈ T'\) such that \(g(a) ∨ τ'(b') = \top_{P'}\) there exists a
  \(b ∈ T\) such that \(h(b) \leq b'\) and \(a ∨ τ(b) = \top_{P}\).
<!-- end definition-33 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{prop:rel-preserve-small}
  Given a diagram of preorders as in \cref{fi♭_:9} and  \(a\) in \(P\). Suppose:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \((h,g,k)\) preserves \(τ\)-top-joins on \(a\)-joining families;
  \item \(g\) and \(h\) are \(\top\)-join-lifting on \(a\);
  \item\label{item:77} \(k\) maps \(\top_{σ}\) to \(\top_{σ'}\).
  \end{enumerate}
  Then \((h,g,k)\) preserves relative smallness at \(a\).
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Assume \(a\) is \((τ \mid σ)\)-small.  Let \(b'\) be such that
  \[
    g(a) ∨ τ'(b') = \top_{P'}.
  \]
  Using the \((τ,a)\)-join-lifting property, there exists a \(b ∈ T\) with
  \(h(b) \leq b'\) and
  \[
    a ∨ τ(b) = \top_{P}.
  \]
  By smallness of \(a\) in the unprimed context we have
  \[
    (τ⨾σ)(b) = \top_{σ}.
  \]
  Since \(k\) maps \(\top_{σ}\) to \(\top_{σ'}\) and \(h(b) \leq b'\), \((τ'⨾ σ')(b') \geq (τ⨾ σ⨾ k)(b) = \top_{σ'}\), hence \((τ'⨾ σ')(b') = \top_{σ'}\), so \(g(a)\) is \((τ' \mid σ')\)-small, hence \((h,g,k)\) preserves relative smallness at \(a\).
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- definition-34: body_md -->
\label{def:global-rel-pres-reflect}
  In the above diagram, we say that the triple \((h,g,k)\):
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{reflects \((τ'\mid σ')\)-smallness} if it reflects \((τ'\mid σ')\)-smallness at every \(a{:}P\);
  \item \emph{preserves \((τ\mid σ)\)-smallness} if it preserves \((τ\mid σ)\)-smallness at every \(a{:}P\).
  \end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-34 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{prop:global-rel-small}\index{global reflection/preservation of smallness}
  In the situation of \cref{fi♭_:9}:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{item:global-reflect}
    Assume that:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item\label{item:67}  \((h,g,k)\) preserves \(τ\)-top-joins,
    \item\label{item:69} \(\top_{g}\) is \((τ' \mid σ')\)-reduced in \(P'\) in the sense of \cref{defn_:21};
    \item\label{item:70} \(k\) reflects \(\top_{σ⨾ k}\).
    \end{enumerate}
    Then \((h,g,k)\) globally reflects \((τ'\mid σ')\)-smallness.

  \item\label{item:global-preserve}
    Assume that for every \(a{:}P\):
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item\label{item:12} \((h,g,k)\) preserves \(τ\)-top-joins;
    \item\label{item:11} \((h,g,k)\) are \(\top\)-join-lifting;
    \item\label{item:13} \(k\) maps \(\top_{σ}\) to \(\top_{σ'}\).
    \end{enumerate}
    Then \((h,g,k)\) globally preserves \((τ\mid σ)\)-smallness.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
The preservation and reflection statements follow directly from \cref{prop:rel-reflect-small} and  \cref{prop:rel-preserve-small}
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-30: body_md -->
\label{rmk:global-rel-small-intuition}
  Conceptually:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The \emph{reflection} part says that if the comparison triple \((h,g,k)\) preserves joins and reflects \(\top_{σ⨾ k}\), then smallness-reflection follows from the
    reducedness of \(\top_{g}\).
  \item The \emph{preservation} part says that, if the upstairs context \((τ,σ)\) sees \(a\) as negligible and \((h,g,k)\) can systematically lift downstairs joining situations back upstairs without changing
    the measurements, then the downstairs image \(g(a)\) remains small for \((τ',σ')\).
  \end{itemize}
<!-- end remark-30 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{crl:1}
  Let \(ι{:} P → Q\) be an ideal embedding. If \(ι\) reflects smallness, then \(\top_{ι}\) is reduced.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
\label{prf:16}
  Let \(\top_{ι} \leq a ∨ b\)  in \(Q\) be such that \(ι^{*}(b)\) is small in \(P\). Since ideals are downward-closed, \(ι\) both preserves and reflects joins in its image. Thus,
  \(ι^{-1}(a) ∨ ι^{-1}(b) = \top_{ι}\). Since \(ι\) reflects smallness, \(ι^{-1}(b)\) is small in \(P\), so that \(ι^{-1}(a) = \top_{P}\). So \(ι(ι^{*}(a)) = \top_{ι}\), so \(\top_{ι} \leq a\).
  Since this holds for each \(a, b{:} Q\), \(\top_{ι}\) is reduced in \(Q\).
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- remark-31: body_md -->
\label{rmk:dual-global-rel}
  Given a commutative diagram as above but in the  category of downward-bounded preorders, the following hold:

  \begin{enumerate}
    \item (Global reflection of \((τ'\mid σ')\)-density)
      Assume that:
      \begin{enumerate}
      \item \((h,g,k)\) preserves \(τ\)-bottom-meets;
      \item \(\bot_{g}\) is sated in \(P'\) relative to \((τ' \mid σ')\);
      \item \(k\) reflects \(\bot_{σ⨾ k}\).
      \end{enumerate}
      Then \((h,g,k)\) globally reflects \((τ'\mid σ')\)-density.

    \item (Global preservation of \((τ\mid σ)\)-density)
      Assume that:
      \begin{enumerate}
      \item \((h,g,k)\) lifts \(τ\)-bottom-meets;
      \item \((h,g,k)\) preserves \(τ\)-bottom-meets;
        \item \(k\) maps \(\bot_{σ}\) to \(\bot_{σ'}\).
      \end{enumerate}
      Then \((h,g,k)\) globally preserves \((τ\mid σ)\)-density.
  \end{enumerate}
  The proofs are obtained from those of \cref{prop:global-rel-small} by systematically reversing all orders, replacing joins by meets, \(\top\) by \(\bot\), smallness by density, and reducedness by satedness.
<!-- end remark-31 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{coR_:9}
  Let \(ι\) be a downward-closed embedding \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow P\) with \(P\) a downward-bounded preorder. Then \(ι\) is density-reflecting.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
\label{prf:15}
  Since \(ι\) is downward-closed it in particular contains \(\bot{:} P\) and thus by the dual of \cref{■pn_:2} density-reflection holds if and only if \(ι\) is injective on \(\bot\). But
  this holds because \(ι\) is an embedding.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{coR_:density-preserved}
\index{density!preservation by surjections}
  Let \(f{:} P → Q\) be a monotone map between downward-bounded preorders. Assume that:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{item:121} \(f\) reflects bottoms;
  \item\label{item:122} \(f\) is surjective on elements.
  \end{enumerate}

Then if \(d\in P\) is dense, then \(f(d)\) is dense in \(Q\).
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Let \(c\in Q\) with \(c∧f(d)=\bot_Q\). Since \(f\) is surjective, choose \(b\in P\) with \(f(b)=c\). Because \(f\) is monotone we have
  \[
    f(b∧d) \;\le\; f(b)∧f(d) \;=\; c∧f(d) \;=\; \bot_Q.
  \]
  Hence \(f(b∧d) = \bot_Q = f(\bot_P)\). Thus, since \(f\) reflects bottoms, \(b ∧ d = \bot_{P}\).
  Since \(d\) is dense in \(P\), this yields \(b=\bot_P\), hence \(c=f(b)=\bot_Q\), which is exactly the density of \(f(d)\) in \(Q\).
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:16}
  Given \(\leq{:} f \Rightarrow g{:} P → S\) then \(∀ a ∈ P\):

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:82} if \(g\) is smallness-preserving at \(a\), then \(f\) is smallness-preserving at \(a\),

  \item\label{item:83} if \(f\) is smallness-reflecting at \(a\), then \(g\) is smallness-reflecting at \(a\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
\label{prf_:11}
  For \cref{item:82} first assume that \(a\) is small. Since \(g\) is smallness-preserving at \(a\), \(g(a)\) is small. But since the small elements of \(S\) form an ideal and \(f(a) \leq g(a)\), so is
  \(f(a)\). If \(a\) is not small, then the statement is void.

  For \cref{item:83}, assume that \(g(a)\) is small, else the statement is void. Since \(f(a) \leq g(a)\), \(f(a)\) is small, so \(a\) is small.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- definition-35: body_md -->
\label{dfn:1}
\index{pseudocomplement}
Given an element \(a\) of a bounded preorder \(P\), an \emph{open pseudocomplement} \(\overset{\circ}{¬} a\) of \(a\) is a largest \(b\) such that \(a ∧ b = \bot_{P}\).

More
generally, given an embedding \(τ{:} T \hookrightarrow P\), a \emph{\((τ \mid σ)\)-relative open pseudocomplement} of \(a\) is a largest \(b ∈ T\) such that \(σ(a ∧ τ(b)) = \bot_{σ}\).

Dually, \(a\) has a \emph{closed
    pseudocomplement} \(\overline{¬}a\) if there exists a smallest \(b\) such that \(a ∨ b = \top_{P}\) and similar for a \emph{\((τ \mid σ)\)-relative closed pseudocomplement}.
<!-- end definition-35 -->
<!-- example-48: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:14}
  For the tablets \(τ{:} \mathbf{O}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(X)\) given by the opens of a topological space, a \(τ\)-open pseudocomplement \(\overset{\circ}{¬}ι\) is a largest open that does not intersect with a given subspace \(ι\), so the
  interior of the set-theoretic complement of \(ι\). Dually for closeds.
<!-- end example-48 -->
<!-- remark-32: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:15}
  We will generally refrain from studying closed pseudocomplements in this paper, as we will do that more in an upcoming paper anyway. So when we say ``pseudocomplement'' without a qualifier then we mean open
  pseudocomplements.
<!-- end remark-32 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{prop:pseudocomplement-density}
\index{density!pseudocomplement characterization}
Let \(T \xrightarrow{τ} P \xrightarrow{σ} S\) be morphisms of downward-bounded preorders with bottom \(\bot_P\), and let \(a\in P\) have a \(τ\)-relative pseudocomplement
  \(¬a\) . Then the following are equivalent:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \(a\) is \((τ \mid σ)\)-dense in the sense of \cref{rmk:dual-sigma-mu};
  \item \((τ⨾ σ)(¬a) = \bot_σ\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Assume \(a\) is dense. Since \(a∧ τ(¬a)=\bot_P\), the definition of \((τ \mid σ)\)-density forces \((τ⨾ σ)(¬a) = \bot_{σ}\).
  Conversely, if \((τ⨾ σ)(¬a) = \bot_{σ}\) then for any \(c \in T\) with \(a∧ τ(c) = \bot_P\) we have \(c\le ¬a\), hence \((τ⨾ σ)(c) = \bot_σ\). Thus \(a\) is \((τ \mid σ)\)-dense.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- remark-33: body_md -->
In a Heyting algebra, where the pseudocomplement is defined by the Heyting implication \(¬a' := a'→\bot\), the condition \(¬a'=\bot\) is exactly the usual definition of a dense element.
<!-- end remark-33 -->
<!-- definition-36: body_md -->
\label{dfn:5}
\index{pullback tablets}
  Let \(f{:} Q → P, T \xrightarrow{τ} P \xrightarrow{σ} S\) be preorder morphisms between upward-bounded preorders. We define the \emph{\(T\)-pullback tablets and scales} on \(Q\) as the sequence
  \(T_{f} \xrightarrow{τ_{f}} Q \xrightarrow{σ_{f}} S\) with \(τ_{f} := f^{*}(τ), σ_{f} := f⨾ σ\).

  We say that \emph{the pullback smallness} under \(f\) \emph{reflects \((τ \mid σ)\)-smallness} if
  \[
    \forall a∈Q,\quad f(a) \text{ is \((τ\mid σ)\)-small in \(P\)} \;\Rightarrow\; a \text{ \((τ_f \mid σ_f)\)-small in \(Q\)}
  \].

  We say that \emph{the pullback smallness} under \(f\) \emph{preserves \((τ \mid σ)\)-smallness} if
  \[
    \forall a∈Q,\quad a \text{ is \((τ_f \mid σ_f)\)-small in \(Q\)} \;\Rightarrow\; f(a) \text{ \((τ \mid σ)\)-small in \(P\)}.
  \]

  If \(f\) is an ideal embedding we call this the \emph{subobject tablets and scale}.
<!-- end definition-36 -->
<!-- remark-34: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:26}
  If the tablets \(τ{:} \mathbf{O}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(X)\) are the opens of a topological space and \(ι{:} U \hookrightarrow X\) is a subset of \(X\), then the pullback tablets \((ι_{*})^{*}(τ)\), where
  \(ι_{*}{:} \mathbf{P}(U) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(X)\) is the morphism induced by postcomposition, are the opens contained in \(ι\). If \(ι\) is open in \(X\) then this is the same as the
  subspace topology on \(U\) but if \(ι\) is not closed in \(X\), then the opens of the subspace topology of \(U\) are the \emph{intersections} of opens in \(X\) with \(U\) and
  thus \emph{not} the same as the opens contained in \(ι\), so the pullback tablets of do not describe the subspace topology of non-opens. In fact, there is not even a canonical morphism
  from the opens of the subspace topology of \(U\) to the opens of \(X\) if \(ι\) is not open. Dually for \(\mathbf{C}(X)\).
<!-- end remark-34 -->
<!-- proposition-25: body_md -->
\label{prp:7-re}
  In a situation as in \cref{dfn:5} assume that \(f\) preserves joins to \(\top_{Q}\). Then:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:156} if \(\top_{f}\) is reduced, then the pullback smallness under \(f\) reflects \((τ \mid σ)\)-smallness.

  \item \label{item:151} If \(f\) is a full epimorphism, \(f\) preserves \(f^{*}(τ)\)-top-joins and \(f\) reflects \(τ\)-top-joins, then the pullback smallness under \(f\) preserves \((τ \mid σ)\)-smallness.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-25 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
\cref{item:156} follows from \cref{crl:11}. For \cref{item:151} assume \(f\) is a full epimorphism and preserves joins with \(\top\). To show global preservation of smallness, we use
  \cref{prop:global-rel-small}(\cref{item:global-preserve}) in our setting, with \(h\) the pullback morphism, \(g=f\), \(k=\mathbf{id}_S\). The three conditions required there reduce to:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(f\) preserves top-joins on \(τ\)-joining families: this is our hypothesis that \(f\) is top-join-preserving.

  \item \((h,g,k)\) lift \(\top\)-joins: for any \(f(a) ∨ τ(b) = \top_P\) there exists a \(c ∈ f^{*}(T)\) with \(τ^{*}(f) (c) = b\). Then
    by \(τ\)-top-join-preservation
    \[f(a ∨ f^{*}(τ)(c)) = f(a) ∨ f(f^{*}(τ)(c)) = f(a) ∨ τ(b) = \top_P = \top_{f}.\]
    Because \(f\) reflects \(τ\)-top-joins, we must have \(a ∨ f^{*}(τ)(c) = \top_{P}\).

  \item \(k = \mathbf{id}_S\) maps \(\top_{σ_f}\) to \(\top_{σ}\), which is trivial
\end{enumerate}

Thus all hypotheses of \cref{prop:global-rel-small}(\cref{item:global-preserve}) are met, so \(f\) globally preserves \((τ \mid σ)\)-smallness. This proves \cref{item:151}.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- counterexample-4: body_md -->
\label{cxmp:1}
  Let \(P\) be the order given by elements \(v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}, l_{1|2}, l_{2|3}, l_{3|1}, v_{1} \cup v_{2}, \top, \bot\) such that \(v_{2} ∨ v_{3} = l_{2|3}\) and \( v_{3} ∨ v_{1} = l_{3 | 1}\) but
  \(v_{1} ∨ v_{2} = v_{1} \cup v_{2} < l_{1|2}\). Geometrically, this is a triangle simplex except that the two vertices \(v_{1}\) and \(v_{2}\) join to their set-theoretic union \(v_{1} \cup v_{2}\) while the
  other vertices join to their containing line. Let \(ι{:} (l_{1|2}) \hookrightarrow P\) be the principal ideal embedding of \(l_{1|2}\). Since \(v_{1} ∨ v_{2} = v_{1} \cup v_{2} < l_{1|2}\), \(v_{1}\) is small in
  \((l_{1|2})\), but \(v_{1} ∨ l_{2|3} = \top\), so \(v_{1}\) is not small in \(\mathbf{SOb}(\top)\). So not every ideal embedding preserves smallness.
<!-- end counterexample-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lmm:4}
\index{small element!preservation in modular lattices}
\index{modular lattice!smallness preservation}
  Let \(L\) be a modular lattice and \(ι{:} (a) \hookrightarrow L\) a principal ideal embedding. Then \(ι\) preserves smallness.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
\label{prf:8}
  Since principal ideal embeddings are in particular join-preserving, we can use \cref{prp:8}. So we just have to check that for each \(b \leq a\) and \(c\) such that \(b ∨ c = \top\) there is
  a \(d \leq c\) such that \(b ∨ d = a\). But it follows from modularity that
  \[b ∨ (c ∧ a) = (b ∨ c) ∧ a = \top ∧ a = a.\]
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- remark-35: body_md -->
\label{rmk:18}
  Geometrically the failure of general smallness-preservation can be understood through the tablets we introduced in \cref{sec:tablets}: the image of an element \(a\) of \((ι)\) under
  \(ι\) is still small according to the tablets from \((ι)\), but \(P\) can contain wholly new tablets that are fine enough to make \(a\) seem big.
  Modularity then says that the subobjects of \(Y\) restrict to \(X\) cleanly enough to guarantee fine tablets in each ideal.
<!-- end remark-35 -->
<!-- proposition-26: body_md -->
\label{prop:reducedness-under-morphisms}
  Consider a commuting diagram in \(\mathbf{UBP}\):

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
      \begin{tikzcd}
    T \ar[r,"τ"] \ar[d,"h"] & P \ar[r,"σ"] \ar[d,"g"] & S \ar[d,"k"] \\
    T'  \ar[r,"τ'"]            & P'  \ar[r,"σ'"]            & S'
  \end{tikzcd}
    \caption{\label{fi♭_:11}}
  \end{figure}

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{(Preservation)}
    Assume that:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item\label{item:refl-small} \((h,g,k)\) reflects \((τ'\mid σ')\)-smallness (as in \cref{prop:global-rel-small} \cref{item:global-reflect});
    \item\label{item:68} \(g\) and \(h\) are ideal embeddings.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then for any \(a ∈ P\) that is \((τ\mid σ)\)-reduced, \(g(a)\) is \((τ'\mid σ')\)-reduced in \(P'\).

  \item \textbf{(Reflection)}
    Assume that:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item\label{item:pres-small} \((h,g,k)\) preserves \((τ'\mid σ')\)-smallness;
      \item\label{item:79} \(g\) preserves binary joins;
    \item\label{item:pres-inj} \(k\) is order-reflecting.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then for any \(a ∈ P\), if \(g(a)\) is \((τ'\mid σ')\)-reduced in \(P'\), then \(a\) is \((τ\mid σ)\)-reduced in \(P\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-26 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
We treat the two parts separately.

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Preservation.}
    Let \(a\) be \((τ\mid σ)\)-reduced.
    Suppose \(g(a) \leq b' ∨ τ'(c')\) in \(P'\) with  \(b'\) being \((τ'\mid σ')\)-small.
    Since \(g\) and \(h\) are ideal embeddings and thus order-reflecting and bijective on its image,
    \[a = g^{*}(a) \leq g^{*}(b' ∨ c') = g^{*}(b') ∨ g^{*}(c') = g^{*}(b') ∨ g^{*}(c') = g^{*}(b') ∨ τ(h^{*}(c')).\]
thus there exist \(b ∈ P, c ∈ T\) with \(g(b) = b',\; h(c) = c'\) and \(a \leq b ∨ τ(c)\), so that \(σ(a) \leq σ(b ∨ τ(c))\).
    By \cref{item:refl-small} the condition that \(b'\) is \((τ'\mid σ')\)-small implies \(b\) is \((τ\mid σ)\)-small.
    Since \(a\) is \((τ\mid σ)\)-reduced, \(σ(a) = σ(τ(c))\), hence
    \[σ'(g(a)) = k(σ(τ(c))) = σ'(τ'(c')).\]
    Thus \(σ'(g(a)) \leq σ'(τ'(c'))\), showing that \(g(a)\) is \((τ'\mid σ')\)-reduced.

  \item \emph{Reflection.}
    Let \(g(a)\) be \((τ'\mid σ')\)-reduced in \(P'\).
    Suppose \(a \leq b ∨ τ(c)\) in \(P\) with \(b\) being \((τ\mid σ)\)-small. Then we have \(g(a) \leq g(b) ∨ g(τ(c))\).

    By \cref{item:pres-small} the fact that \(b\) is \((τ\mid σ)\)-small implies \(g(b)\) is \((τ'\mid σ')\)-small.
    Because \(g(a)\) is \((τ'\mid σ')\)-reduced, we obtain

    \[k(σ(a)) = σ'(g(a)) \leq σ'(g(τ(c))) = k(σ(τ(c))).\]
    Order-reflectivity of \(k\) then forces \(σ(a) \leq σ(τ(c))\), so \(a\) is \((τ\mid σ)\)-reduced.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- remark-36: body_md -->
\label{rmk:dual-completeness-under-morphisms}
  Consider the diagram in \cref{fi♭_:11} but in the category of downward-bounded preorders.

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{(Preservation of satedness)}
    Assume that:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item\label{item:dual-refl-small} \((h,g,k)\) reflects \((τ'\mid σ')\)-density;
    \item\label{item:dual-68} \(g\) and \(h\) are filter embeddings.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then for any \(a ∈ P\) that is \((τ\mid σ)\)-sated, \(g(a)\) is \((τ'\mid σ')\)-sated in \(P'\).

  \item \textbf{(Reflection of satedness)}
    Assume that:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item\label{item:pres-dense} \((h,g,k)\) preserves \((τ'\mid σ')\)-density;
    \item \(g\) preserves binary meets;
    \item\label{item:dual-pres-inj} \(k\) is order-reflecting.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then for any \(a ∈ P\), if \(g(a)\) is \((τ'\mid σ')\)-sated in \(P'\), then \(a\) is \((τ\mid σ)\)-sated in \(P\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-36 -->
<!-- proposition-27: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:11}
  Let \(a\) be an element of a downward-bounded preorder \(P\) and \(b \leq a\) such that \(b\) is sated in the ideal \((a)\) of \(a\). Then for each dense \(c\) and arbitrary \(d\) in
  \(P\) it holds that:

  \[\text{ if } b \geq c ∧ d, \text{ then } b \geq a ∧ d\].
<!-- end proposition-27 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
\label{prf_:13}
  Since \(b \leq a\) and meets commute and are idempotent,
  \[b \geq c ∧ d = a ∧ c ∧ d = (a ∧ c) ∧ (a ∧ d)\].

  These are all in \((a)\), so since \(b\) is sated in \((a)\) and \((a ∧ c)\) is dense in \((a)\),
  \[b \geq (a ∧ c) ∧ (a ∧ d) = a ∧ d\].
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{coℝ_:1}
  In the situation of \cref{■pn_:11}, if \(P\) is also upward-bounded, then it follows that if \(b\) contains any dense subobject of \(P\), then \(b = a\). Thus, no subobject
  containing a dense subobject can be sated in anything but itself.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
\label{prf_:1}
  Apply \cref{■pn_:11} for \(d = \top\).
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- counterexample-5: body_md -->
\label{cxmp:8}
  We present a counterexample in a meet-semilattice (with bottom) that is not a Heyting algebra.  The example shows that the conditions

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \(a\) is sated in \(P\),
  \item \(b\le a\) and \(b\) is sated in the ideal \((a)\),
  \end{enumerate}

  do not force \(b\) to be sated in \(P\).

Let \(P\) be the partially ordered set consisting of the eight elements
\[
\{0,\; a,\; b,\; c,\; d,\; e,\; f,\; 1\}
\]
with the order generated by the following covering relations (reflexive closure is understood):

\[
\begin{tikzcd}
& 1 \ar[dl,-] \ar[dr,-] & \\
d \ar[dd,-] & {} & c \ar[dl,-] \ar[dd,-] \\
& a \ar[dl,-] \ar[d,-] & \\
b \ar[dr,-] & f \ar[d,-] & e \ar[dl,-] \\
& 0  &
\end{tikzcd}
\]

More explicitly:
\[
0 < b, f < a < c < 1,\quad 0 < e < c,\quad b < d < 1,
\]
Only \(c\) and \(1\) are dense:
\begin{itemize}
\item \(c\) meets every nonzero element nontrivially;
\item \(1\) is trivially dense;
\item \(a\) is not dense because \(a∧ e = 0\) with \(e\neq0\);
\item \(d\) is not dense because \(d∧ f = 0\) with \(f\neq0\);
\item \(b,e,f\) are not dense for similar reasons.
\end{itemize}

\(a\) is sated:
\begin{itemize}
\item  \(a = 1∧ y\text{ if and only if }a = y\) is trivially true.
\item For \(c\), the equation \(a = c∧ y\) forces \(y\ge a\).
  Among the elements \(\ge a\) we have \(a,c,1\).  Only \(y=a\) gives \(c∧ a = a\);
  \(y=c\) gives \(c∧ c = c\neq a\); \(y=1\) gives \(c\neq a\).
  Hence the condition that \(a = c∧ y \Rightarrow a = y\) holds vacuously except for the valid
  instance \(y=a\).
\end{itemize}

In \((a)\) the only dense element is \(a\). Thus, every element is sated in \((a)\), so in particular \(b\) is.

Take the dense element \(c\) and the element \(d\).  We have
\[
b = c∧ d \qquad\text{(by construction)},
\]
but \(d > b\) (so \(d \neq b\)).  A sated element would force \(b = d\); hence \(b\) is not
sated in \(P\).

So our counterexample evades \cref{prop:completeness-reflection-dense-envelope} because \(P\) is not distributive.
<!-- end counterexample-5 -->
<!-- proposition-28: body_md -->
\label{prop:completeness-reflection-dense-envelope}
  \index{sated element!reflection} Consider a commuting diagram in \(\mathbf{DBP}\):

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \begin{tikzcd}
    T \ar[r,"τ"] \ar[d,"h"] & P \ar[r,"σ"] \ar[d,"g"] & S \ar[d,"k"] \\
    T' \ar[r,"τ'"] & P' \ar[r,"σ'"] & S'
  \end{tikzcd}
                 
\end{figure}

Assume the following:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \label{item:155} \(g\) is an ideal embedding;
\item\label{item:16} \(P'\) is distributive;
\item \label{item:1} There exists a \((τ', σ')\)-pseudocomplement for each element of \(P'\) in \(T'\) and pseudocomplements distribute over joins;
\item\label{item:8} \(k\) is order- and bottom-reflecting;

  \end{enumerate}
  Then \((h, g, k)\) is satedness-reflecting.
<!-- end proposition-28 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Let \(a ∈ P\) and assume that \(g(a)\) is \((τ' \mid σ')\)-sated in \(P'\); we show that \(a\) is \((τ \mid σ)\)-sated in \(P\). Unfolding \cref{rmk:dual-sigma-mu}, this amounts to the following: whenever \(d ∈ P\) is \((τ \mid σ)\)-dense and \(t ∈ T\) satisfies \(d ∧ τ(t) \leq a\), then \((τ⨾ σ)(t) \leq σ(a)\). So fix such a pair \(d, t\).

The strategy is to transplant the situation upstairs to \(P'\): we enlarge \(g(d)\) by the pseudocomplement of \(\top_{g}\), obtaining an element
\[d' \;:=\; g(d) ∨ τ'\bigl(¬\top_{g}\bigr) \;\in\; P'\]
that is still \((τ' \mid σ')\)-dense and whose meet with \(τ'(h(t))\) remains below \(g(a)\); the satedness of \(g(a)\) then delivers the desired inequality, which we pull back along \(k\).

\emph{Step 1: \(d' ∧ τ'(h(t)) \leq g(a)\).} Since the left square commutes, \(τ'(h(t)) = g(τ(t))\), so distributivity of \(P'\) (\cref{item:16}) gives
\[d' ∧ τ'(h(t)) \;=\; \bigl(g(d) ∨ τ'\bigl(¬\top_{g}\bigr)\bigr) ∧ g\bigl(τ(t)\bigr) \;=\; \bigl(g(d) ∧ g\bigl(τ(t)\bigr)\bigr) ∨ \bigl(τ'\bigl(¬\top_{g}\bigr) ∧ g\bigl(τ(t)\bigr)\bigr).\]
The ideal embedding \(g\) preserves binary meets, so the first summand equals \(g(d ∧ τ(t)) \leq g(a)\). For the second summand, note that \(τ(t) \leq \top_{P}\) implies \(g(τ(t)) \leq \top_{g}\), whence by \cref{dfn:1}
\[τ'\bigl(¬\top_{g}\bigr) ∧ g\bigl(τ(t)\bigr) \;\leq\; τ'\bigl(¬\top_{g}\bigr) ∧ \top_{g} \;=\; \bot_{P'}.\]
Thus the second summand vanishes and \(d' ∧ τ'(h(t)) = g(d ∧ τ(t)) \leq g(a)\).

\emph{Step 2: \(d'\) is \((τ' \mid σ')\)-dense.} By \cref{prop:pseudocomplement-density} it suffices to verify \((τ'⨾ σ')(¬d') = \bot_{σ'}\). Pseudocomplements of elements of \(P'\) exist in \(T'\) and distribute over joins by \cref{item:1}, so
\[¬d' \;=\; ¬\bigl(g(d) ∨ τ'\bigl(¬\top_{g}\bigr)\bigr) \;=\; ¬g(d) ∧ ¬τ'\bigl(¬\top_{g}\bigr).\]
The density of \(d\) translates, again via \cref{prop:pseudocomplement-density}, into \((τ⨾ σ)(¬d) = \bot_{σ}\). Since \(g(d) \leq \top_{g}\), every element of \(T'\) that meets \(\top_{g}\)
trivially also meets \(g(d)\) trivially, whence \(¬\top_{g} \leq ¬g(d)\). Moreover, for each \(e ∈ P'\) it holds that if \(ε ∧ g(d)\) is not \(\bot_{P'}\), then \(g^{*}(ε)\) is not
\(\bot_{P}\) since \(g\) is an ideal embedding, so that \(¬\top_{g} = ¬g(d)\)
. Evaluating the scale on the complement therefore yields
\[(τ'⨾ σ')(¬d') \;=\; σ'\Bigl(τ'\bigl(¬g(d)\bigr) ∧ τ'\bigl(¬τ'\bigl(¬\top_{g}\bigr)\bigr)\Bigr) = σ'\Bigl(τ'\bigl(¬\top_{g}\bigr) ∧ τ'\bigl(¬τ'\bigl(¬\top_{g}\bigr)\bigr)\Bigr) \;=\; σ'(\bot_{P'}) \;=\; \bot_{σ'},\]
where the penultimate identity holds because \(τ'(¬\top_{g}) ∧ τ'(¬τ'(¬\top_{g})) = \bot_{P'}\) by the defining property of the pseudocomplement \(¬τ'(¬\top_{g})\). Hence \(d'\) is \((τ' \mid σ')\)-dense.

\emph{Step 3: apply the satedness of \(g(a)\).} Combining Steps 1 and 2, the element \(d'\) is \((τ' \mid σ')\)-dense and satisfies \(d' ∧ τ'(h(t)) \leq g(a)\). Since \(g(a)\) is \((τ' \mid σ')\)-sated, \cref{rmk:dual-sigma-mu} yields
\[(τ'⨾ σ')\bigl(h(t)\bigr) \;\leq\; σ'\bigl(g(a)\bigr).\]
By commutativity of the diagram, \(h⨾ τ'⨾ σ' = τ⨾ g⨾ σ'\) and \(g⨾ σ' = σ⨾ k\), so
\[(τ⨾ σ⨾ k)(t) \;=\; (τ'⨾ σ')\bigl(h(t)\bigr) \;\leq\; σ'\bigl(g(a)\bigr) \;=\; (σ⨾ k)(a) \;=\; k\bigl(σ(a)\bigr).\]
Since \(k\) is order-reflecting by \cref{item:8}, this forces \((τ⨾ σ)(t) \leq σ(a)\).

As \(d\) and \(t\) were arbitrary, \(a\) is \((τ \mid σ)\)-sated in \(P\); hence \((h, g, k)\) is satedness-reflecting.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{coR_:7}
\index{sated element!reflection by monomorphisms}
  If \(P\) is a Heyting algebra, then the ideal embedding \((a)\) of an element \(a ∈ P\) is satedness-reflecting.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
\label{prf_:15}
  \cref{item:8} is trivial if we don't use a non-trivial scale, \cref{item:155} is true by assumption and \cref{item:16} and \cref{item:1} are true because \(P\) is a Heyting algebra.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- definition-37: body_md -->
\label{defn_:31}
  (See, e.g. Section 0.6 of \cite{adamekLocallyPresentableAccessible1994})A category \(\mathcal{C}\) is \emph{well-powered} if for each object \(X{:} \mathcal{C}\) the subobject preorder \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) is essentially small, i.e. a set (up to equivalence).
<!-- end definition-37 -->
<!-- example-49: body_md -->
\label{xmp:103}
  \(\mathbf{Set}\) is well-powered but not small.
<!-- end example-49 -->
<!-- counterexample-6: body_md -->
\label{cxmp:3}
  If \(\mathcal{C}\) is the delooping of a group, then all monics into
  its point \(*\) are isomorphisms and thus isomorphic to the identity in \(\mathcal{C}_{/*}\). So \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(*)\) is the one-element preorder, and thus the representation
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathbf{UBP}\) is trivial.
<!-- end counterexample-6 -->
<!-- definition-38: body_md -->
\label{dfn:2}\index{subobject-separated category}
  A category \(\mathcal{C}\) is \emph{subobject-separated} if for each pair of morphisms \(f, g{:} X \rightrightarrows Y\) there exists a subobject \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) such that for each \(σ{:} \mathbf{Aut}(A)\):

  \begin{equation}
    \label{qn_:2}
    \text{if } ι⨾ f = σ⨾ ι⨾ g \text{ then } f = g.
  \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-38 -->
<!-- example-50: body_md -->
\label{xmp:101}
  Suppose \(\mathcal{C}\) has a separating family of subterminal objects \(\mathcal{S}\). Remember that an object \(S\) is subterminal if and only if for every \(Y\), the hom-category \(\mathcal{C}(Y,S)\) has at most one element
  and a family of morphisms \(\mathcal{S}\) is separating if and only if for any two distinct parallel morphisms \(f,g {:} X \rightrightarrows Y\) there exists \(S \in \mathcal{S}\) and a morphism \(h {:} S \to X\) with \(h⨾ f \neq h⨾ g\).

  Given such \(f, g\), pick an \(h {:} S \to X\) such that \(h⨾ f \neq h⨾ g\). Because \(S\) is subterminal, any morphism out of \(S\) is trivially monic.
  Therefore \(h\) is a monomorphism. Is it proper? If \(h\) is an isomorphism, then \(X \cong S\) is subterminal, so both \(h\) and \(σ\) in \cref{qn_:2}  necessarily equal
  \(\mathbf{id}_{X}\), so \(\mathbf{id}_{X}\) is a suitable \(ι\). If \(h\) is a proper monomorphism, then, \(σ\) in \cref{qn_:2} still has to be an identity, so that \(ι\) subobject-separates \(f\) and \(g\) by the
  separativeness of \(\mathcal{S}\).

  This applies in particular to all localic topoi (see C1.4.7. of \cite{johnstoneSketchesElephantTopos2002}).
<!-- end example-50 -->
<!-- proposition-29: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:1}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a monic well-powered category and let \(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathcal{C}}\) be its wide subcategory of monomorphisms.
  If \(\mathcal{C}\) is subobject-separated (in the sense of \cref{dfn:2}), then the subobject functor
  \[
    \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}} {:} \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathcal{C}} \longrightarrow \mathbf{UBP}
  \]
  is faithful.
<!-- end proposition-29 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Let \(f,g {:} X  
  \mathrel{\vcenter{\offinterlineskip
    \ialign{##\cr
       \hfil$\hookrightarrow$\hfil\cr
       \noalign{\vskip -0.3ex}
       \hfil$ 
  \scalebox{1}[-1]{\(\hookrightarrow\)}
$\hfil\cr
    }}} 
 Y\) be two monomorphisms and assume \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(f) = \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(g)\).
  Concretely, this means that for every subobject \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow X\), the two monomorphisms \(ι⨾ f\) and \(ι⨾ g\) become equal in the subobject preorder of \(Y\); i.e. there exists an isomorphism \(σ {:} A \to A\) (depending on \(ι\)) such that
  \[
    ι⨾ f \;=\; σ ⨾ ι⨾ g .
   \]

   Now apply the hypothesis that \(\mathcal{C}\) is subobject-separated: then for the pair \((f,g)\) there exists a subobject \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow X\) with the property that if there exists such an isomorphism \(σ {:} A \to A\) for \(ι\), then \(f = g\).  Hence \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}\) is faithful.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- remark-37: body_md -->
\label{rmk:14}
  Note that this means that \(\mathbf{SOb}\) induces an equivalence relation on \( \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}}\), given by \(\mathcal{C} \sim D\) if and only if the image of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}\) is isomorphic to that of
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}}\), which is like Morita-equivalence for \(\mathbf{UBP}\). We can call \(\mathcal{C}\) \emph{subobject-equivalent} to \(\mathcal{D}\) in this case.
<!-- end remark-37 -->
<!-- example-51: body_md -->
\label{xmp:32}
  The delooping of every group is subobject-equivalent to the terminal category.
<!-- end example-51 -->
<!-- definition-39: body_md -->
\label{defn_:32}
\index{monomorphism-preserving functor}
  A functor \(F{:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) is \emph{monomorphism-preserving} if for each monomorphism \(ι{:} X \hookrightarrow Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\), \(F(ι)\) is a monomorphism.
<!-- end definition-39 -->
<!-- example-52: body_md -->
\label{xmp:109}
  Every pullback-preserving functor is monomorphism-preserving because every monomorphism is a pullback along itself. In particular, every right adjoint \(R\) is monomorphism-preserving since it preserves limits.
<!-- end example-52 -->
<!-- example-53: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:6}
  Let \(\widehat{(-)}{:} \mathcal{S} \hookrightarrow \widehat{\mathcal{S}}\) be the Yoneda embedding of a site with a subcanonical coverage and a strict initial object \(∅\) such
  that \(∅_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}} \cong \widehat{∅_{\mathcal{S}}}\)
  (i.e. the empty sheaf is representable) and consider the induced map on subobject preorders \(\top_{\widehat{(-)}, X}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{S}}(X) → \mathbf{SOb}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}}(\widehat{X}){:} ι ↦ \hat{ι}\).
  Since \(\mathcal{S}\) is subcanonical, \(\widehat{(-)}\) preserves finite limits and by assumption it preserves the initial object \(∅\). Since \(\top_{\widehat{(-)}, X}\)  is also fully faithful (by the
  Yoneda lemma and subcanonicity), it reflects \(∅\). Thus, \(\widehat{(-)}\) reflects density.
<!-- end example-53 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{le↘_:3}
  Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a thin site with a subcanonical coverage. Then every nonzero sheaf \(F\) on \(\mathcal{S}\) receives a monomorphism from some representable.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
\label{prf_:12}
  Consider presheaves \(F {:} \mathcal{S}^{op} → \mathbf{Set}\). Recall that a natural transformation \(\widehat{x}{:} \widehat{X} ⇒ F\) from a representable corresponds, by Yoneda, to a choice of element \(x ∈ F(X)\). Its component at \(Y\) is
  \[
  \overline{x}_Y {:} \mathcal{S}(Y,X) → F(Y),\quad f \mapsto F(f)(x).
\]
In a presheaf category, \(\widehat{x}\) is monic if and only if every component \(\widehat{x}_Y\) is injective, and since \(\mathcal{S}\) is subcanonical, finite limits in \(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}\) reduce to those in the surrounding presheaf
topos \(\mathbf{PSh}(\mathcal{S})\). So we have to find a componentwise monic into \(F\). If \(F\) is non-trivial, then there exists some  \(x ∈ F(X)\) for some object \(X\). But since for each object \(Y\), the hom-set \(\mathcal{S}(Y,X)\) has size \(0\) or \(1\) and any function with domain of size ≤ 1 is trivially
injective. Thus, \(\widehat{x}\) is componentwise injective. So any element of any sheaf in \(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}\) is monic.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- proposition-30: body_md -->
\label{prp:6}
  Given a thin site \(\mathcal{S}\) with a subcanonical coverage and an initial object, the natural transformation \(\top_{\widehat{(-)}}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{S}} \hookrightarrow \widehat{(-)}⨾ \mathbf{SOb}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}}\) induced by the Yoneda embedding \(\widehat{(-)}{:} \mathcal{S} \hookrightarrow \mathbf{Set}^{\mathcal{S}^{op}}\) is density-preserving.
<!-- end proposition-30 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
\label{prf:9}
  We need to show that if \(ι\) is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{S}}(X)\), then \(\widehat{ι}\) is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}}(\widehat{X})\). Let
  \(κ{:} K \hookrightarrow \widehat{X}\) be any subsheaf such that
  \[
    κ ∧ \widehat{ι} = \bot
  \]
  in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}}(\widehat{X})\). We must show \(κ = \bot\). Since \(\mathcal{S}\) is subcanonical, the sheafification functor preserves meets, so we can take the meet of
  \(κ ∧ \widehat{ι}\) as sub-presheaves, which is given by objectwise pullback. If \(κ\) is not initial, then by \cref{le↘_:3} there is some \(X{:} \mathcal{S}\) such that \(K(X)\) contains an element
  \(y\), so that \(κ ∧ \widehat{ι} \geq \widehat{y}⨾ κ\), where \(\widehat{y}\) is the morphism \(\widehat{X} → K\) induced by the Yoneda lemma. But since each cover of \(\mathcal{S}\) is
  jointly epimorphic and thus in particular non-empty, the empty presheaf on \(\mathcal{S}\) is a sheaf and thus initial. So in particular \(\widehat{y}⨾ κ > \bot\).
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- remark-38: body_md -->
\label{rmk:1}
\index{density-equivalence}
  So the embedding of a thin subcanonical site with an initial object into its sheaf topos is both density-preserving and density-reflecting, so a \emph{density-equivalence}.
<!-- end remark-38 -->
<!-- definition-40: body_md -->
Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category with an initial object \(∅\). A coproduct \(X + Y\) with coprojections
\[
τ_X {:} X → X+Y,\qquad τ_Y {:} Y → X+Y
\]
is called a \emph{disjoint coproduct with monic coprojections} if \(τ_{X}\) and \(τ_{Y}\) are monic and the pullback of \(τ_X\) and \(τ_Y\) is initial.

Equivalently, the images of \(τ_X\) and \(τ_Y\) are subobjects of \(X+Y\) with intersection equal to the initial subobject.
<!-- end definition-40 -->
<!-- proposition-31: body_md -->
\label{prop:density-coproduct}
\index{density!in coproducts}
\index{disjoint coproduct!density}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category with an initial object \(∅\) and disjoint coproducts with monic coprojections. Then the following equivalent statements hold:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{item:146} If for some monomorphism \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow X\) the composite
    \[
      ι⨾τ_X {:} A \longrightarrow X+Y
    \]
    is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}(X+Y)\), then \(Y \simeq ∅\).

  \item\label{item:147} The coprojection \(τ_X\) itself is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}(X+Y)\) if and only if \(Y \simeq ∅\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-31 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
For \cref{item:146} assume \(ι⨾τ_X\) is dense.  Consider the subobject \(τ_Y {:} Y \hookrightarrow X+Y\).
  Because the coproduct is disjoint, the pullback of \(τ_X\) and \(τ_Y\) is initial.  Since \(ι⨾τ_X\) factors through \(τ_X\), the pullback of \(τ_Y\) and \(ι⨾τ_X\) is also initial; in symbols,
  \[
    τ_Y ∧ (ι⨾τ_X) = \bot .
  \]
  By definition of density, this forces \(τ_Y = \bot\), i.e. the monomorphism \(τ_Y\) is isomorphic to the initial subobject.  Hence \(Y \simeq ∅\).

  The first direction of \cref{item:147} follows from \cref{item:146} by taking \(ι = \mathbf{id}_X\).  For the converse, note that if \(Y \simeq ∅\),
  then the coproduct \(X+∅\) is isomorphic to \(X\) via \(τ_X\).
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{crl:2}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category such that each subobject preorder of objects in \(\mathcal{C}\) is a modular lattice. Then each monomorphism in \(\mathcal{C}\) is smallness-preserving.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- example-54: body_md -->
\label{xmp:13}
  In the internal language of any topos \(\mathcal{T}\), for any \(f{:} X → Y, ι{:} A \hookrightarrow Y\), \(f^{*}(ι) = \{x ∈ X| ∃ a ∈ A{:} f(x) ∈ ι\}\), so that it holds that \(x ∈ f^{*}(ι) \Leftrightarrow f(x) ∈ ι\), so if for all \(ι\) in \(Y\)
  \(f^{*}(ι) = g^{*}(ι)\), then \(∀ x ∈ X{:} f(x) = g(x)\). Since elements in the internal language of a topos correspond to \(κ{:} B \hookrightarrow X\) such that \(B\) is subterminal, it follows that \(f = g\) if \(\mathcal{T}\) is
  separated by its subterminal objects. So again \(\mathbf{SOb}^{*}\) is faithful on all topoi that are separated by subterminal objects.
<!-- end example-54 -->
<!-- proposition-32: body_md -->
\label{prp:1-restated}
\index{extensive category!subobjects}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be an extensive category.
  For any coproduct \(X + Y\) with coprojections
  \[
    τ_X {:} X → X+Y,\qquad τ_Y {:} Y → X+Y,
  \]
  the canonical map
  \[
    (τ_X^*, τ_Y^*) {:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X+Y) \longrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) × \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)
  \]
  is an isomorphism of preorders.
<!-- end proposition-32 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Let \(m {:} A \hookrightarrow X+Y\) be a subobject. By extensivity, the pullbacks \(m_X {:} A_X \hookrightarrow X\) and \(m_Y {:} A_Y \hookrightarrow Y\) along the coprojections form a coproduct \(A ≅ A_X + A_Y\). This establishes a bijection between subobjects of \(X+Y\) and pairs of subobjects of \(X\) and \(Y\).
  Conversely, given a pair \((a {:} A \hookrightarrow X, b {:} B \hookrightarrow Y)\), the universal property of the coproduct induces a monomorphism \(a + b {:} A + B \hookrightarrow X + Y\) (the coproduct of monomorphisms in an extensive category is monic). These constructions are clearly order-preserving and mutually inverse, yielding the isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- remark-39: body_md -->
\label{rmk:10}
  Thus, in an extensive category, the subobject functor converts coproducts into products, behaving much like a powerset. This preservation of limits allows us to analyze smallness and density component-wise.
<!-- end remark-39 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{coR_:5}
\index{small element!in coproducts}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be extensive. For a monomorphism \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow X+Y\) with associated decomposition \(A ≅ A_X + A_Y\) under \cref{prp:1-restated}, the following are equivalent:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \(ι\) is small in \(\mathbf{SOb}(X+Y)\);
  \item Both pullbacks \(ι_X {:} A_X \hookrightarrow X\) and \(ι_Y {:} A_Y \hookrightarrow Y\) are small in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) and \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\) respectively.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Under the isomorphism \(\mathbf{SOb}(X+Y) \cong \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) × \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\), joins are computed componentwise. Thus, \(ι ∨ κ = \top_{X+Y}\) holds if and only if \(ι_X ∨ κ_X = \top_X\) and \(ι_Y ∨ κ_Y = \top_Y\).
  \(ι\) is small precisely when the only pair \((κ_X, κ_Y)\) satisfying this condition is \((\top_X, \top_Y)\). This is equivalent to the requirement that there is no proper \(κ_X\) in \(X\) joining with \(ι_X\) to \(\top_X\) (and similarly for \(Y\)); otherwise, taking \((κ_X, \top_Y)\) would contradict the smallness of \(ι\). Hence, both components must be small.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{crl:6}
\index{density!in coproducts}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be an extensive category. Then each subobject \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X + Y\) of a coproduct \(X + Y\) is dense if and only if both pullbacks \(τ_{X}^{*}(ι)\) and \(τ_{Y}^{*}(ι)\) are dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) and \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\) respectively.
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
By \cref{prp:1-restated}, we identify \(\mathbf{SOb}(X+Y)\) with the product \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) × \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\), where the bottom element is \((\bot_X, \bot_Y)\) and meets are computed pointwise. An element \((d_X, d_Y)\) in a product of downward-bounded preorders is dense if and only if for any \((a, b)\), the condition \((a ∧ d_X, b ∧ d_Y) = (\bot_X, \bot_Y)\) implies \((a, b) = (\bot_X, \bot_Y)\).

  This condition holds precisely when \(d_X\) is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) and \(d_Y\) is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\): testing with \(b = \bot_Y\) shows that \(a ∧ d_X = \bot_X\) forces \(a = \bot_X\), and symmetrically for \(b\). The claim follows by transporting this characterization back along the isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{coR_:6}
\index{small element!in coproducts}
  If \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) is small in \(X\) and \(\mathcal{C}\) is extensive, then \(ι⨾ τ_{X}{:} A \hookrightarrow X + Y\) is small for each \(Y\).
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label{crl:5}
\index{density!reflection by regular epimorphisms}
  In a category \(\mathcal{C}\) with a strict initial object, let \(\mathfrak{f}\) be a factorization system whose right orthogonal part includes all initial morphisms. Then for each morphism \(f\) in
  the left part of \(\mathfrak{f}\)  the induced pullback morphism \(f^{*}\) is density-reflecting.
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- definition-41: body_md -->
A category \(\mathcal{C}\) is \emph{regular} if:

  \begin{enumerate}
\index{regular category}
  \item \(\mathcal{C}\) has all finite limits.

  \item Every morphism \(f {:} X → Y\) admits a factorization
    \[
      X \xrightarrow{e_f} I_f \xrightarrow{\mathbf{Im}(f)} Y
    \]
    where
    \begin{itemize}
    \item \(e_f\) is a \emph{regular epimorphism} (i.e. a coequalizer of some parallel pair),
    \item the \emph{image} \(\mathbf{Im}(f)\) of \(f\) is a monomorphism,
    \end{itemize}
    and this factorization is \emph{stable under pullback}: for any morphism \(g {:} Z → Y\), if we form the pullback
    \[
      \begin{tikzcd}
        X' \ar[r] \ar[d] & X \ar[d,"f"] \\
        Z \ar[r,"g"'] & Y
      \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    then the induced map \(X' → Z\) again factors as a regular epi followed by a mono, and this factorization is the pullback of \(e_f\) and \(\mathbf{Im}(f)\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-41 -->
<!-- corollary-15: body_md -->
\label{crl:4}
\index{density!preservation by pullbacks}
  Given a morphism \(f{:} X → Y\) in a regular category \(\mathcal{C}\) with a strict initial object, the induced morphism \(f^{*}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}^{*}(Y) → \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}^{*}(X)\) is
  density-preserving. In particular, if \(g\) has a dense image \(m\), then since the regular-epi/mono factorization \(g = e⨾ m\) is functorial, the pullback \(f^{*}(g)\) of \(g\) has a dense
  image \(\mathbf{Im}(f^{*}(g)) = f^{*}(m)\).

  Thus, and by \cref{crl:5}, the contravariant subobject morphism \(e^{*}\) of a regular epimorphism \(e\) is a density-equivalence.
<!-- end corollary-15 -->
<!-- remark-40: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:11}
  When \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) is a monomorphism in a regular category with a strict initial object then the density-reflection along \(ι\) is a special case of \cref{crl:4} but it is important to note that although \(f^{*}\) is density-preserving, \(f_{*}\) is not always density-reflecting.
<!-- end remark-40 -->
<!-- definition-42: body_md -->
\label{dfn:6}\index{density coverage}
  Given a regular category \(\mathcal{C}\) with  a strict initial object, the \emph{density coverage} is given by the morphisms in \(\mathcal{C}\) whose image is dense.
<!-- end definition-42 -->
<!-- example-55: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:7}
\index{density coverage}
\index{rational map}
Let \(k\) be a field, \(\mathbf{Var}_{k}\) the category of varieties over \(k\) and for each \(V{:} \mathbf{Var}_{k}\) let \(\mathbf{O}(V)\) be given by the preorder of open
subvarieties of \(V\). Fix some variety \(Y\) over \(k\) and let \(\mathbf{Var}_{k, V}(-, Y){:} \mathbf{O}(V)^{op} → \mathbf{Set}\) be the composition of the forgetful functor
\(\mathbf{s}{:} \mathbf{O}(V) → \mathbf{Var}_{k}\) with the Yoneda functor
  of \(Y\), which assigns to each \(V\) the set of algebraic maps from \(V\) to \(Y\). The sheafification \(\widehat{\mathbf{Var}_{k}(-, Y)}\) of \(\mathbf{Var}_{k}(-, Y)\) with
  respect to the density coverage on \(\mathbf{O}(V)\) freely
  adds for each open dense \(d{:} V' \hookrightarrow V\) and algebraic map \(f{:} V' → Y\) an element \(\hat{f}\) to \(\widehat{\mathbf{Var}_{k}(V, Y)}\) such that if \(e{:} V'' \hookrightarrow V'\) is dense in \(V'\), then
  \(\widehat{e⨾ f} = \hat{f}\). It follows that \(\hat{f}\) represents a rational map from \(V\) to \(Y\).
<!-- end example-55 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:SOb-epi}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a regular category and \(ε {:} X \twoheadrightarrow Y\) a regular epimorphism. Then the induced monotone map
  \[
    \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(ε) {:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) \to \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y),\qquad
    ι \mapsto \,\mathbf{Im}(ι⨾ε)\,
  \]
  is surjective on elements.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
To see this, take any subobject \(κ{:} B \hookrightarrow Y\) and form its pullback along \(ε\), yielding a subobject \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) and a pullback square where \(ε'{:} A \to B\) is a regular epimorphism. Since \(ε'⨾ κ = ι⨾ ε\), the image of \(ι⨾ ε\) is isomorphic to \(κ\). Thus, \(\mathbf{SOb}(ε)(ι) = κ\), proving surjectivity.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proposition-33: body_md -->
\label{prop:density-regular-epi}
\index{density!preservation by regular epimorphisms}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a regular category with strict initial object, and \(ε{:}X\twoheadrightarrow Y\) a regular epimorphism. If \(ι{:}A\hookrightarrow X\) is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\), then its image \(\mathbf{Im}(ι⨾ε)\hookrightarrow Y\) is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\).
<!-- end proposition-33 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Let \(ι\in\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) be dense. Then \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(ε)(ι) = \mathbf{Im}(ι⨾ε)\) is dense in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\) by \cref{coR_:density-preserved}, specialized to \(f=\mathbf{SOb}_{*}(ε)\),
  using the regular-epi properties noted above and the fact that regular epimorphisms in a strict initial regular category reflect bottoms, as we saw at the section beginning.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- remark-41: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:12}
  So density is stable under composition with regular epimorphisms and thus \(e^{*}\) is a density-equivalence and \(e_{*}\) preserves density. The only thing \(e\) does not do is induce a density-reflecting \(e_{*}\).
<!-- end remark-41 -->
<!-- corollary-16: body_md -->
\label{crl:8}
  Let \(e{:} X → Y\) be a regular epimorphism in a regular category. Then the pullback morphism \(e^{*}(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)) → \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) reflects satedness.
<!-- end corollary-16 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
\label{prf:10}
  By \cref{rmk:dual-completeness-under-morphisms} we have to show that \(e^{*}\) preserves meets, preserves density and is injective. Meet-preservation is clear because limits
  commute with each other. Density-preservation follows from \cref{crl:4}. Finally, order-reflection is proved below.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:pb-reg-epi-reflect}
\index{regular epimorphism!subobject reflection}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a regular category and \(e {:} X \twoheadrightarrow Y\) a regular epimorphism. Then the pullback functor
  \[
    e^{*} {:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y) \longrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)
  \]
  is order-reflecting: for subobjects \(ι, ι'\) of \(Y\), if \(e^{*}(ι) \leq e^{*}(ι')\) in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\), then \(ι \leq ι'\) in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\).
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
Let \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow Y\) and \(ι' {:} A' \hookrightarrow Y\) be subobjects of \(Y\), and form the pullbacks of \(e\) along each:
  \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
      P \ar[r, "e^{*}(ι)"] \ar[d, "ι^{*}(e)"'] & X \ar[d, "e"] \\
      A \ar[r, "ι"'] & Y
    \end{tikzcd}
    \qquad
    \begin{tikzcd}
      P' \ar[r, "e^{*}(ι')"] \ar[d, "ι'^{*}(e)"'] & X \ar[d, "e"] \\
      A' \ar[r, "ι'"'] & Y
    \end{tikzcd}
  \]
  Since pullbacks of monomorphisms are monomorphisms, \(e^{*}(ι)\) and \(e^{*}(ι')\) are monic; and since regular epimorphisms are stable under pullback in a regular category,
  \(ι^{*}(e) {:} P \to A\) and \(ι'^{*}(e) {:} P' \to A'\) are regular epimorphisms. The pullback squares give
  \[
    ι^{*}(e) ⨾ ι \;=\; e^{*}(ι) ⨾ e, \qquad ι'^{*}(e) ⨾ ι' \;=\; e^{*}(ι') ⨾ e.
  \]

  Suppose \(e^{*}(ι) \leq e^{*}(ι')\), so there exists \(h {:} P \to P'\) with \(h ⨾ e^{*}(ι') = e^{*}(ι)\). Then:
  \[
    ι^{*}(e) ⨾ ι \;=\; e^{*}(ι) ⨾ e \;=\; (h ⨾ e^{*}(ι')) ⨾ e \;=\; h ⨾ (e^{*}(ι') ⨾ e) \;=\; h ⨾ (ι'^{*}(e) ⨾ ι') \;=\; (h ⨾ ι'^{*}(e)) ⨾ ι'. \tag{\(\star\)}
  \]

  Since \(ι^{*}(e)\) is a regular epimorphism, it is the coequalizer of some pair \(r, s {:} R \rightrightarrows P\). By definition, \(r ⨾ ι^{*}(e) = s ⨾ ι^{*}(e)\), hence
  \(r ⨾ ι^{*}(e) ⨾ ι = s ⨾ ι^{*}(e) ⨾ ι\). Applying \((\star)\) to both sides:
  \[
    r ⨾ (h ⨾ ι'^{*}(e)) ⨾ ι' \;=\; s ⨾ (h ⨾ ι'^{*}(e)) ⨾ ι'.
  \]
  Since \(ι'\) is monic, we may cancel it on the right to obtain \(r ⨾ (h ⨾ ι'^{*}(e)) = s ⨾ (h ⨾ ι'^{*}(e))\). By the universal property of the coequalizer, there exists a unique
  \(g {:} A \to A'\) with \(ι^{*}(e) ⨾ g = h ⨾ ι'^{*}(e)\). Composing both sides with \(ι'\) and using \((\star)\):
  \[
    ι^{*}(e) ⨾ (g ⨾ ι') \;=\; (h ⨾ ι'^{*}(e)) ⨾ ι' \;=\; ι^{*}(e) ⨾ ι.
  \]
  Since \(ι^{*}(e)\) is an epimorphism, we conclude \(g ⨾ ι' = ι\), which is precisely \(ι \leq ι'\).

  The equality-reflection statement follows by applying the argument in both directions.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- definition-43: body_md -->
\label{dfn:9}
\index{regular quotient}
  A \emph{regular quotient} (or effective quotient) in a regular category \(\mathcal{C}\) is the coequalizer \(e{:} X \twoheadrightarrow Y\) of its kernel pair \((ι, κ){:} R \rightrightarrows X\).
<!-- end definition-43 -->
<!-- proposition-34: body_md -->
\label{prop:exact-square}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a regular category, and let
  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
      \begin{tikzcd}
    R \ar[r,"ι"] \ar[d,"κ"'] & X \ar[d,two heads,"e"] \\
    X \ar[r,two heads,"e"']          & Y
  \end{tikzcd}
                                 
  \end{figure}
  be the commutative square formed by a regular epimorphism \(e\) and its kernel pair \((ι, κ)\). Then this square is both a pullback and a pushout.
<!-- end proposition-34 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
This is a standard fact in regular categories: every regular epimorphism is the coequalizer of its kernel pair. By definition, a kernel pair is a pullback of \(e\) along itself, so the square is a pullback. Because \(e\) is the coequalizer of \(ι\) and \(κ\), the square is also a pushout.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- proposition-35: body_md -->
\label{prop:subobject-quotient}
  If \(\mathcal{C}\) is a regular category, then the subobject functor \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}\) preserves regular quotients. Specifically, in the situation of \cref{prop:exact-square}, the induced diagram
  \[
    \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(R) \;\; 
  \ext@arrow 0359 
  \arrowfill@ 
  \mathrel{ 
    \mathpalette 
  \raise3\hbox to 0pt{$\m@th.\relbar$\hss} 
  \lower3\hbox{$\m@th.\relbar$} 
86ex
  } 
 
  \mathrel{ 
    \mathpalette 
  \raise3\hbox to 0pt{$\m@th.\relbar$\hss} 
  \lower3\hbox{$\m@th.\relbar$} 
86ex
  } 
\rightrightarrows
{\kappa_{*}}{ι_{*}} 
\;\; \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) \; 
  \ext@arrow 0579 
  \arrowfill@\relbar\relbar\twoheadrightarrow
{}{e_{*}} 
\; \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)
  \]
  is a coequalizer diagram in \(\mathbf{UBP}\).
<!-- end proposition-35 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Since \(ι ⨾ e = κ ⨾ e\), we have \(ι_{*} ⨾ e_{*} = κ_{*} ⨾ e_{*}\).

  Suppose \(h {:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) \to P\) is a monotone map satisfying \(ι_{*} ⨾ h = κ_{*} ⨾ h\). By \cref{lem:SOb-epi}, \(e_{*}\) is surjective on elements, so every \(y \in \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\) admits some preimage \(x\) with \(e_{*}(x) = y\). We set \(k(y) := h(x)\) and must verify independence of the chosen preimage.

  \emph{Well-definedness.} Suppose \(x {:} A \hookrightarrow X\) and \(x' {:} A' \hookrightarrow X\) satisfy \(e_{*}(x) = e_{*}(x') = y {:} B \hookrightarrow Y\). Factor \(x ⨾ e\) and \(x' ⨾ e\) through their common image \(y\):
  \[
    A \xrightarrow{\bar{x}} B \xrightarrow{y} Y, \qquad A' \xrightarrow{\bar{x}'} B \xrightarrow{y} Y,
  \]
  where \(\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{x}'\) are regular epimorphisms. Form the pullback \(P = A \times_{B} A'\) with projections \(p_{1} {:} P \to A\) and \(p_{2} {:} P \to A'\); by stability of regular epimorphisms under pullback in a regular category, both \(p_{1}\) and \(p_{2}\) are regular epimorphisms. The two composites \(p_{1} ⨾ x\) and \(p_{2} ⨾ x'\) from \(P\) to \(X\) become equal after postcomposition with \(e\), since both factor as \(P \to B \xrightarrow{y} Y\). Hence they induce a map \(u {:} P \to X \times_{Y} X = R\). Let \(\bar{r} {:} \bar{P} \hookrightarrow R\) be the monomorphism in the image factorization of \(u\). Then
  \[
    ι_{*}(\bar{r}) \;=\; \mathbf{Im}(\bar{P} \hookrightarrow R \xrightarrow{ι} X) \;=\; \mathbf{Im}(P \xrightarrow{p_{1} ⨾ x} X) \;=\; x,
  \]
  where the last equality holds because \(P \xrightarrow{p_{1}} A \xrightarrow{x} X\) is already a regular-epi/mono factorization: \(p_{1}\) is a regular epimorphism and \(x\) is monic. By the same token \(κ_{*}(\bar{r}) = x'\). The hypothesis \(ι_{*} ⨾ h = κ_{*} ⨾ h\) now gives \(h(x) = h(x')\).

  \emph{Monotonicity.} Let \(y \leq y'\) in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\), and choose preimages \(x, x'\) with \(e_{*}(x) = y\) and \(e_{*}(x') = y'\). Set \(z = e^{*}(y)\) and \(z' = e^{*}(y')\), the pullbacks along \(e\). Since \(e\) is a regular epimorphism, the map \(e^{*}(y) \to y\) is a regular epimorphism (stability under pullback), so \(e_{*}(z) = y\) and similarly \(e_{*}(z') = y'\). By well-definedness, \(h(x) = h(z)\) and \(h(x') = h(z')\). Now \(y \leq y'\) implies \(z = e^{*}(y) \leq e^{*}(y') = z'\), so monotonicity of \(h\) yields \(h(x) = h(z) \leq h(z') = h(x')\).

  By construction \(h = e_{*} ⨾ k\), and uniqueness of \(k\) follows from the surjectivity of \(e_{*}\) (\cref{lem:SOb-epi}). Thus \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\) satisfies the universal property of the coequalizer in \(\mathbf{UBP}\).
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- definition-44: body_md -->
\index{coherent category}
  A category \(\mathcal{C}\) is \emph{coherent} if:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \(\mathcal{C}\) is regular;

  \item for every object \(X\), the subobject poset \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) has finite joins and for every arrow \(f {:} Y → X\), the pullback map
    \[
      f^{*} {:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) → \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)
    \]
    preserves finite joins.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-44 -->
<!-- remark-42: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:30}
  Since \(f^{*}\) commutes with other pullbacks, it also preserves finite meets, which exist since \(\mathcal{C}\) is regular, so that \(f^{*}\) is a lattice-morphism.
<!-- end remark-42 -->
<!-- corollary-17: body_md -->
\label{coR_:11}
\index{small element!preservation by monomorphisms}
  Smallness is covariantly preserved and reducedness reflected under monomorphisms in a coherent category.
<!-- end corollary-17 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lmm:1}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a regular category and \(f {:} X → Y\) a morphism. Then the following are equivalent:
  \begin{enumerate}
\index{coherent functor}
  \item \(f\) is a regular epimorphism;
  \item the pullback functor on subobjects
    \[
      f^* {:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y) → \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)
    \]
    \emph{reflects tops}, i.e. if \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow Y\) satisfies \(f^*(ι) = \top_X\) in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\), then \(ι = \top_Y\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
\(\Rightarrow\): If \(f^*(ι) = \top_X\), then \(f\) factors through the subobject \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow Y\). Since \(f\) is a regular epimorphism and \(ι\) is a monomorphism, the orthogonality property of the (regular epi, mono) factorization system supplies a morphism \(d{:}Y\to A\) with \(d⨾ι=\mathbf{id}_Y\), so \(ι\) is a split epimorphism and hence an isomorphism, so \(ι = \top_Y\).

  \(\Leftarrow\): Factor \(f\) into a regular epimorphism followed by a monomorphism, \(f = e⨾ m\). By the universal property of pullbacks, pulling back the subobject \(m\) along \(f\) yields \(f^*(m) = \top_X\). Because \(f^*\) reflects tops by hypothesis, we must have \(m = \top_Y\), meaning \(m\) is an isomorphism. Thus, \(f\) is a regular epimorphism.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- corollary-18: body_md -->
\label{crl:7}
\index{small element!reflection by pullbacks}
  For each regular epimorphism \(e{:} X → Y\) in a coherent category \(\mathcal{C}\) the pullback morphism \(e^{*}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y) → \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) is smallness-reflecting.
<!-- end corollary-18 -->
<!-- definition-45: body_md -->
Let \(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}\) be coherent categories. A functor \(F{:}\mathcal{C}→\mathcal{D}\) is \emph{coherent} if:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item It preserves finite limits.
  \item for every object \(X{:}\mathcal{C}\), the induced map on subobjects
    \[
      \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) \xrightarrow{\,\mathbf{SOb}(F)_X\,} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}}(F(X)),\quad ι \mapsto F(ι)
    \]
    preserves finite joins (including the initial subobject).
  \end{enumerate}

  A functor \(F{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathcal{D}\) \emph{preserves pure monics} if for each non-isomorphic monomorphism \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) the image \(F(ι)\) is a non-isomorphic monomorphism. \(F\) is \emph{purely
    monomorphism-preserving} if it preserves monomorphisms and pure monics.
<!-- end definition-45 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:pure-monic-fiber}
  Let \(F{:}\mathcal{C}→\mathcal{D}\) be a functor that
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item preserves monomorphisms;
  \item preserves pure monics.
  \end{enumerate}
  Fix \(X{:}\mathcal{C}\). Then the fiber
  \[
    (\mathbf{SOb}(F)_X)^{-1}(\top_{F(X)}) \;\subseteq\; \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)
  \]
  consists only of \(\top_X\); i.e. the only subobject \(ι{:}A\hookrightarrow X\) with \(F(ι) = \top_{F(X)}\) is \(ι = \top_X = \mathbf{id}_X\).
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Let \(ι{:}A\hookrightarrow X\) be a subobject such that \(F(ι) = \top_{F(X)}\). This means that \(F(ι){:}F(A)\hookrightarrow F(X)\) is an isomorphism. But since \(F\) preserves pure monics, \(ι\) must itself be an
  isomorphism in \(\mathcal{C}\) and thus \(ι=\top_X\) in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) (up to univalence).
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- proposition-36: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:3}
\index{small element!reflection by coherent functors}
  Let \(F{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathcal{D}\) be a coherent functor that is purely monomorphism-preserving. Then for each \(X{:} \mathcal{C}\) the induced morphism \(F_{*, X}\) is smallness-reflecting.
<!-- end proposition-36 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
\label{prf_:9}
  By \cref{lem:pure-monic-fiber}, \(F_{*, X}\) reflects \(\top_{F(X)}\) and by coherence it preserves joins, so smallness-reflection follows from \cref{prop:rel-reflect-small}.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
  \item All density statements assume a strict initial object so that \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) is downward-bounded.
  \item The decomposition in co-Heyting categories is mentioned in the text as an upcoming result.
  \item Behavior on disjoint coproducts with monic coprojections is induced by the isomorphism \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X+Y)\cong\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)×\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y)\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- definition-46: body_md -->
\label{dfn:11}\index{submonic hyperdoctrine}
  A \emph{submonic hyperdoctrine} \(η{:} \mathcal{H} \hookrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}^{*}_{\mathcal{C}}{:} \mathcal{C}^{op} → \mathbf{UBP}\) on a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is a monic natural transformation of functors into \(\mathbf{UBP}\) such
  that for each \(X{:} \mathcal{C}\) the top \(\top_{\mathbf{SOb}(X)} = \mathbf{id}_{X}\) is in the image of \(η_{X}\).
<!-- end definition-46 -->
<!-- example-56: body_md -->
\label{xmp:20}
  Since regular monomorphisms are stable under pullback (since for a regular \(ι\) the pullback \(f^{*}(ι)\) equalizes the composite of \(f\) and the cokernel pair of \(ι\)),
  the functor \(ι_{reg}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{reg}^{*} \hookrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}^{*}{:} \mathcal{C}^{op} → \mathbf{UBP}\) is a submonic hyperdoctrine.
<!-- end example-56 -->
<!-- definition-47: body_md -->
\label{defn_:13}\index{Heyting space}
  A \emph{Heyting space} \(X\) is an embedding of bounded lattices \(ω{:} \mathbf{O}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{B}(X)\) where \(\mathbf{O}(X)\) is a bounded Heyting algebra of \emph{opens} and
  \(\mathbf{B}(X)\) is a bounded Boolean algebra.
<!-- end definition-47 -->
<!-- example-57: body_md -->
\label{xmp:102}
  Every topological space \(X\) is a concrete Heyting space.
<!-- end example-57 -->
<!-- example-58: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:11}
  For each real closed field \(R\) and finite-dimensional \(R^{n}\), the embedding \(ω_{salg}{:} \mathbf{OSSAlg}(R^{n}) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{B}(R^{n})\) of the open real semialgebraic subsets of
  \(R^{n}\) from \cref{xmp:14} into the powerset lattice of \(R^{n}\) is a concrete Heyting space.
<!-- end example-58 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
\label{prf_:17}
  We saw in \cref{xmp:14} already that the category of semialgebraic subsets of \(R^n\) has a distinguished
  collection \(\mathbf{O}(V)\) of \emph{open semialgebraic} subsets of \(V\), closed under finite unions and finite intersections; Thus, almost all requirements of
  \cref{dfn:12} are already known. Note that \(U \subseteq R^{n}\) is semialgebraic open if and only if it is semialgebraic and open. For this assume otherwise, i.e. that \(ι\) is
  semialgebraic and open but not semialgebraic open. Since \(U\) is semialgebraic there exists a family of polynomial strict inequalities \(p_{i} > q_{i}\) and \(p'_{j} = q'_{j}\)
  such that \(U\) is the union of intersections of the sets defined by these relations. Since \(U\) is not open semialgebraic, there exist some \(j\) such that the equality \(p'_{j} = q'_{j}\) cannot
  be removed from the defining relations of \(U\), i.e. there exists a point \(x ∈ R^{n}\) such that \(p'_{j}(x) = q'_{j}(x)\) but the same does not hold for any \(p_{i}\) and
  \(q_{i}\). But then \(U\) does not contain any open disk around \(x\) and is thus not open. The implication in the other direction is trivial.

  We must still show that \(\mathbf{O}(V)\) is in fact a Heyting algebra; equivalently, that it is closed under \emph{Heyting implication}. But
  for this we can just use the Heyting implication in the normal opens
  \[
    U \Rightarrow W \;:=\; \bigl( (V \setminus U) \cup W \bigr)°.
  \]
  First, we verify that this is indeed an element of \(\mathbf{O}(V)\):

  \begin{itemize}
  \item \((V \setminus U) \cup W\) is a semialgebraic subset of \(V\), being a Boolean combination of semialgebraic sets.

  \item A classical result about semialgebraic sets is that they satisfy the Tarski-Seidenberg projection property, from which it follows that the closure, interior, and convex
    hull of a semialgebraic set are again semialgebraic (see the beginning of \cite{driesTameTopologyOminimal1998} for details). Since \(U\) is open, by definition of the topological
    interior, and semialgebraic, it is open semialgebraic, so that \(U° ∈ \mathbf{O}(V)\).
  \end{itemize}

  The argument that this has the required universal property proceeds as with the Heyting implication in a locale.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- example-59: body_md -->
\label{xmp:25}
  Let \(X\) be a scheme, \(\mathbf{O}(X)\) and \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) the open and closed immersions into \(X\) and \(\mathbf{R}(X)\) the preorder of all immersions into \(X\). As per
  \cite{Section261001IM} an open immersion \(ι_{\mathbf{O}}\) of schemes is given by an open subspace
  \(\mathopen{∣}ι_{\mathbf{O}}\mathclose{∣}{:} \mathopen{∣}A\mathclose{∣} \hookrightarrow \mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣}\) of the underlying topological space
  \(\mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣}\) of \(X\) with the structure sheaf induced by restriction. A closed immersion is locally in each affine neighborhood given by an embedding of an
  affine neighborhood, so dual to a ring quotient. An immersion is a closed immersion into an open immersion. By the Zariski topology, for each open immersion \(ι_{\mathbf{O}}\)
  the complement \(\mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣} ∖ \mathopen{∣}ι_{\mathbf{O}}\mathclose{∣}\) in the underlying topological space of \(X\) is the underlying subset of some reduced closed
  subscheme \(ι_{\mathbf{C}}\). Then \(ι_{\mathbf{O}}\) is the pseudocomplement
  of \(ι_{\mathbf{C}}\): since the two don't share any points and every non-trivial scheme has a point (since every non-trivial ring has a maximal ideal by the axiom of choice), no
  non-trivial subscheme factors through their intersection. On the other hand, every other subscheme \(κ\) that does not factor through \(ι_{\mathbf{O}}\) shares some point \(p\)
  with \(\mathopen{∣}ι_{\mathbf{C}}\mathclose{∣}\) and thus there exists a subscheme of \(X\) under \(ι\) and \(κ\) (the maximal subscheme corresponding to \(p\)), so that
  \(ι_{\mathbf{O}}\) is in fact maximal with respect to being disjoint with \(ι_{\mathbf{C}}\).
<!-- end example-59 -->
<!-- definition-48: body_md -->
\label{dfn:10}\index{open-closed duality}
  An \emph{open-closed duality} \(\mathcal{D}\) on a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is a triple \(\mathbf{o} \xhookrightarrow{ω} \mathbf{d} \xhookleftarrow{χ} \mathbf{c}\) of submonic hyperdoctrines such
  that for each \(X{:} \mathcal{C}\)  and element \(o ∈ \mathbf{O}(X)\) of the underlying preorder of \(\mathbf{o}(X){:} \mathbf{O}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}(X)\) there exists an element
  \(c ∈  \mathbf{C}(X)\) for which \(ω(o)\) is the pseudocomplement of  \(χ(c)\) in the source \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) of \(\mathbf{d}(X)\).

  An open-closed duality \(\mathcal{D}\) is \emph{regular} if \(\mathbf{d}\) is \(ι_{reg}\).

  
  \(\mathcal{D}\) is \emph{reduced} if also for each \(c\) in each \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) there exists an \(o\) such that \(χ(c)\) is the pseudocomplement of \(ω(o)\).

  \(\mathcal{D}\) is \emph{Heyting} if

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:75} for each \(X\) it holds that \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) is a Boolean lattice, \(\mathbf{O}(X)\) a Heyting algebra and \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) a co-Heyting algebra and
    \(ω\) and \(χ\) are morphisms of bounded lattices,

  \item\label{item:76} and for \(f{:} X → Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) the morphisms \(\mathbf{O}(f){:} \mathbf{O}(Y) → \mathbf{O}(X)\) and \(\mathbf{C}(f){:} \mathbf{C}(Y) → \mathbf{C}(X)\) are
    lattice morphisms and \(\mathbf{D}(f){:} \mathbf{D}(Y) → \mathbf{D}(X)\) is a Boolean algebra morphism.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-48 -->
<!-- remark-43: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:37}
  We take the direction of pseudocomplementation in \cref{dfn:10} such that it aligns with the case of subschemes of a scheme.
<!-- end remark-43 -->
<!-- definition-49: body_md -->
\label{dfn:open-closed-space}\index{open-closed space}
  An \emph{open-closed space} \(X\) is an open-closed duality whose middle submonic preorder \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) is also its underlying category. Thus the data are preorder
  embeddings
  \[
    \mathbf{O}(X) \xhookrightarrow{ω} \mathbf{D}(X) \xhookleftarrow{χ} \mathbf{C}(X)
  \]
  satisfying the same pseudocomplement condition as in \cref{dfn:10}, but with \(\mathbf{D}\) itself playing the role of the ambient category of subobjects.

  A \emph{morphism of open-closed spaces} \(f{:} X → Y\) is the dual of a morphism of diagrams

  \[f^{*}_{\mathbf{O}}{:} \mathbf{O}(Y) → \mathbf{O}(X), f^{*}_{\mathbf{D}}{:} \mathbf{D}(Y) → \mathbf{D}(X), f^{*}_{\mathbf{C}}{:} \mathbf{C}(Y) → \mathbf{C}(X)\]

  from \(Y\) to \(X\) which preserves tops in \(\mathbf{O}, \mathbf{D}\) and \(\mathbf{C}\).
<!-- end definition-49 -->
<!-- example-60: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:2}
  Every object \(X {:} \mathcal{C}\) in the base category of an open-closed duality \(\mathbf{o} \xhookrightarrow{ω} \mathbf{d} \xhookleftarrow{χ} \mathbf{c}\) gives rise to an open-closed space
  \[
    \mathbf{O}(X) \xhookrightarrow{ω_X} \mathbf{D}(X) \xhookleftarrow{χ_X} \mathbf{C}(X),
  \]
  whose underlying category is the middle preorder \(\mathbf{D}(X)\). Thus, open-closed spaces are the fibrewise form of an open-closed duality.
  Properties such as regularity and Heytingness are inherited fibrewise whenever they are present in the ambient open-closed duality; reducedness is fulfilled by definition.
<!-- end example-60 -->
<!-- example-61: body_md -->
\label{xmp:24}
  Let \(\mathbf{O}, \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{D}{:} \mathbf{Top}^{op} → \mathbf{UBP}\) be given by mapping each topological space \(X\) to its lattices of opens and closeds and subsets. Then
  \(\mathbf{O}\), \(\mathbf{C}\) and \(\mathbf{D}\) with their embeddings into \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathbf{Top}}\) form the components of a regular Heyting open-closed duality.
<!-- end example-61 -->
<!-- example-62: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:19}
  Open and closed immersions of schemes are also stable under pullbacks. For open immersions this follows from the pullback-stability of the opens of a topological space, for
  closed ones this is Exercise II.3.11.a of \cite{Hartshorne_engl}, see \cite{babaiAnswerClosedImmersions2014} for a proof. Now let \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) be a general immersion of
  schemes. Since \(ι\) is a composite of a closed and an open immersion, the pullback of \(ι\) along any morphism \(f{:} Y → X\) is also an immersion.
  But note that the pullback morphism \(f^{*}{:} \mathbf{R}(X) → \mathbf{R}(Y)\) of a morphism of schemes does not generally have a right adjoint, since the set-theoretic image of
  a scheme need not be a scheme.

  Concretely, let \(f\) be the projection \(π_{1}{:} ℝ^{3} → ℝ^{2}\) and \(H\) be the hyperbola in \(ℝ^{3}\) given by the  \(xy = 1\). Then the
  set-theoretic image \(f(H)\) is \(\{(u, v)\mid u ≠ 0\} \cup \{0, 0\}\). This is not a sub-scheme of \(ℝ^{2}\) since it is not closed within any open (since each open that contains \(f(H)\)
  also contains some disk around \(0\)). Now, if the
  preimage morphism \(f^{*}\) had a right adjoint \(f_{*}\), then there would have to exist an \(f_{*}(H)\) such that \((f^{*}⨾ f_{*})(A) \leq H\) and
  \(f_{*}⨾ f^{*}⨾ f_{*}(H) = f_{*}\). If \(f_{*}(H)\) did not contain a point \(p\) in \(f(H)\), then \(p\) would not be in the image of the preimage of \(f_{*}(H)\), so
  \(f_{*}(H)\) has to contain \(f(H)\). There is a smallest sub-scheme of \(ℝ^{2}\) that contains \(f(H)\), which is its closure \(\overline{f(H)}\) of \(f(H)\) in \(ℝ^{2}\), which is
  \(ℝ^{2}\). But \(H\) is not larger than \(f^{*}(ℝ^{2}) = ℝ^{3}\), so \(f^{*}\) cannot have a right adjoint.

  There is a smallest \emph{closed} subscheme containing the image for each subscheme under a morphism, which \cite{Section29601R5} uses as an image, but the failure of this to be
  adjoint to the pullback functor on all subschemes is one of the primary reasons for the prominence of constructible closures in algebraic geometry. We will use the existence
  of such a right adjoint as a defining condition in \cref{dfn:12}.
<!-- end example-62 -->
<!-- definition-50: body_md -->
\label{dfn:12}\index{abstract Heyting space}\index{concrete Heyting space}
  An \emph{abstract Heyting space} is a Heyting open-closed space
  \[
    \mathbf{O}(X) \xhookrightarrow{ω_X} \mathbf{D}(X) \xhookleftarrow{χ_X} \mathbf{C}(X)
  \]
  in the sense of \cref{dfn:open-closed-space}: thus \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) is a bounded Boolean lattice, \(\mathbf{O}(X)\) is a bounded Heyting algebra, \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) is a bounded co-Heyting algebra, and
  the open and closed parts are concrete duals under the complementation inside \(\mathbf{D}(X)\).

  A \emph{morphism of abstract Heyting spaces} \(f{:} X → Y\) is a morphism of open-closed spaces such that

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:15} each component map of \(f\) is a bounded lattice morphism,

  \item\label{item:80} \(f^{*}_{\mathbf{D}}{:} \mathbf{D}(Y) → \mathbf{D}(X)\) preserves Boolean negations and has a right adjoint \(f_{\mathbf{D}, *}\).
  \end{enumerate}

  A \emph{concrete Heyting space} is a set \(\mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣}\) with an abstract Heyting space \(X\) for which the middle Boolean lattice \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) is the subset
  preorder \(\mathbf{P}(X) := \mathbf{P}(\mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣})\) of \(\mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣}\), with \(ω_X\) and \(χ_X\) given by subset embeddings. Equivalently, it is a set \(\mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣}\)
  equipped with a lattice embedding \(ι_{\mathbf{O}}{:} \mathbf{O}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(X)\), where \(\mathbf{O}(X)\) is a Heyting algebra; so that the \emph{closed subsets} are the set-theoretic
  complements of opens, with embedding \(ι_{\mathbf{C}}{:} \mathbf{C}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{P}(X)\).

  A \emph{morphism of concrete Heyting spaces} \(f {:} X → Y\) is a function \(\mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣} → \mathopen{∣}Y\mathclose{∣}\) such that the pullback along \(f\) induces a
  morphism of abstract Heyting algebras.
<!-- end definition-50 -->
<!-- remark-44: body_md -->
\label{rmk:12}
  Note that we do \emph{not} assume that \(\mathbf{O}(f)\) and \(\mathbf{C}(f)\) preserve the Heyting and co-Heyting implications, which is in line with the topological case, but we \emph{do} assume that \(\mathbf{D}(f)\) preserves
  complements, as it does in the case of pullbacks of sets (and thus regular subobjects of a topological space).
<!-- end remark-44 -->
<!-- remark-45: body_md -->
\label{rmk:11}
  In pointless topology, originally developed in \cite{johnstoneStoneSpaces}, the assumption is frequently made that what is important about a topological space is its locale of
  opens. Here we challenge this assumption: not just is it that the closeds matter as well, but in particular also that these two are jointly embedded into some larger algebra,
  which allows us to extend the notions we derive from opens and closeds to other elements.
<!-- end remark-45 -->
<!-- remark-46: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:36}
  So according to \cref{dfn:12} a concrete Heyting space is an abstract Heyting space whose middle is maximal. We could abstract this setup a little further and say that a
  \emph{concretification} of an abstract Heyting space is a morphism of Heyting spaces that is the identity on opens and closeds and an embedding of the middle Boolean algebra.
<!-- end remark-46 -->
<!-- example-63: body_md -->
\label{xmp:27}
  It follows almost immediately from \cref{dfn:12} that both the category of concrete Heyting spaces \(\mathbf{CHS}\) and that of abstract Heyting spaces \(\mathbf{AHS}\) house a Heyting
  open-closed duality.
<!-- end example-63 -->
<!-- definition-51: body_md -->
\label{defn_:10}
  Given an abstract Heyting space \(X\) and \(ι{:} \mathbf{O}(X)\), the \emph{induced Heyting space} \(X|_{ι}\) on \(ι\) is the Heyting space:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item such that \(\mathbf{D}(X)|_{ι}\) is given by the ideal \((ι)\) in \(\mathbf{D}(X)\),

  \item \(ω|_{ι} := ω_{X|_ι}\) is given by the embedding into \((ι)\) of the image of \(ω_{X}\) under the morphism \((- ∧ ι)\) given by taking meets with \(ι\).

  \item \(χ|_{ι}\) is  also given like that and that opens and closeds are complementary follows from the fact that if \(χ_{X}(C) = ¬ ω_{X}(O)\) then for each
    \(κ{:} \mathbf{D}(X)\) it holds that \(κ ∧ χ_{X}(C) = κ ∧ ¬ω_{X}(O)\) since \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) is Boolean.
  \end{itemize}

  This space comes with a morphism of Heyting spaces \(ι_{*}{:} X|_{ι} \hookrightarrow X\) where

  \begin{itemize}
  \item \((ι_{*})^{*}_{\mathbf{D}}\), \((ι_{*})^{*}_{\mathbf{O}}\) and \((ι_{*})^{*}_{\mathbf{C}}\) are given by \((- ∧ ι)\),

    \item \((ι_{*})_{*, \mathbf{D}}\) (which we'll just denote \(ι_{*}\)) is given by the ideal embedding \((ι) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{D}(X)\).
  \end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-51 -->
<!-- proposition-37: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:10}\index{satedness restricts to heyting subspaces}
  Given a concrete Heyting space \(X\), \(κ{:} \mathbf{O}(X)\) and \(ι \leq ω_{X}(κ)\), if \(ι\) is \(ω_{X}\)-sated in \(X\), then \(ι\) is \(ω|_{ι}\)-sated in \(X|_{\iota}\).
<!-- end proposition-37 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
\label{prf_:18}
  It follows from \cref{defn_:10} and the closedness opens under meets that \(ω|_{ι}⨾ ι_{*}\) factors through \(ω_{X}\), so that there exists a diagram

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzcd}
