      \mathbf{O}(X|_{ι}) \ar[r, "ω|_{ι}"] \ar[d, "ι_{*}|_{\mathbf{O}(X|_{ι})}"] & \mathbf{B}(X) \ar[d, "ι_{*}"] \\
      \mathbf{O}(X) \ar[r, "ω_{X}"] & X
    \end{tikzcd}
                                 
  \end{figure}
  that fulfills the preconditions of \cref{prop:completeness-reflection-dense-envelope} for a trivial scale.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- definition-52: body_md -->
\label{defn_:27}\index{constructible closure}
  Given an open-closed space \(X\) such that \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) is a lattice with (open) pseudocomplements, the \emph{constructible closure} in \(\underline{X}\) is the open-closed space with the same opens
  and closeds such that the middle \(\underline{\mathbf{D}}(X)\) of \(\underline{X}\) is the joint closure of \(ω\) and \(χ\) in \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) under joins, meets and pseudocomplements.
<!-- end definition-52 -->
<!-- remark-47: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:5}
  If \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) does not have joins, meets or pseudocomplements, then it does still make sense to close \(ω\) and \(χ\) under whatever \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) does have and refer
  to that as the constructible closure.
<!-- end remark-47 -->
<!-- remark-48: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:39}
  In infinite-dimensional topology, the definition of constructibility is often restricted to those being generated by \emph{retrocompact} opens, i.e. opens that are compact on
  each compact open. We use the more naïve definition of constructibility here, since the intuitive meaning of retrocompactness in our setting is not yet clear.
<!-- end remark-48 -->
<!-- example-64: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:13}
  The constructible closure \(\underline{ω}_{salg}\) of \(ω_{salg}\) from \cref{xmp_:11} is the embedding \(\mathbf{OSSAlg}(R^{n}) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{SAlg}(R^{n})\) of
  \(\mathbf{OSSAlg}(R^{n})\) into the preorder of all semialgebraic subsets of \(R^{n}\).
<!-- end example-64 -->
<!-- proposition-38: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:10-restated}
  Let \(f{:} X → Y\) be a morphism in \(\mathbf{CHS}\).

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:104} \(f\) is a monomorphism in \(\mathbf{CHS}\) if and only if the underlying function \(\mathopen{∣}X\mathclose{∣} → \mathopen{∣}Y\mathclose{∣}\) is injective.

  \item \label{item:105} \(f\) is a regular monomorphism in \(\mathbf{CHS}\) if and only if the Heyting structure on \(X\) is the pullback structure induced from \(Y\), i.e.
    \[
      \mathbf{O}(X) \;\cong\; \{\, f^{*}(U) \mid U ∈ \mathbf{O}(Y)\,\}
    \]
    via the lattice embedding \(ι_{\mathbf{O},X}\), and similarly for closed sets.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-38 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
We establish the two claims in turn.

  \textbf{Monomorphisms.}
  If \(f\) is monic, distinct points \(x_{1} \neq x_{2}\) in \(X\) cannot map to the same point in \(Y\); otherwise, the two maps from the terminal object \(1\) (a single point) picking \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) would compose with \(f\) to give the same morphism, violating monicity. Thus, \(f\) is injective.
  Conversely, if \(\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}\) is injective and \(f⨾g = f⨾h\), then for every \(z\) we have \(\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}(g(z)) = \mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}(h(z))\), which forces \(g(z) = h(z)\). Since the underlying functions agree, their inverse images of opens must also agree, so \(g = h\) as morphisms of \(\mathbf{CHS}\).

  \textbf{Regular monomorphisms.}
  Recall that regular monomorphisms in concrete categories are equalizers.
  Suppose \(f\) is regular. As equalizers in \(\mathbf{CHS}\) are computed pointwise (set-theoretically), \(f\) represents an inclusion of a subset \(X \subseteq Y\).
  The equalizer carries the coarsest Heyting structure making the inclusion continuous; consequently, every open of \(X\) is the pullback of an
  open from \(Y\), establishing the isomorphism.

  For the converse, assume \(\mathbf{O}(X) \cong f^{*}(\mathbf{O}(Y))\).
  Let \(Z\) be the codiscrete space on the disjoint union \(Y + \{*\}_{1} + \{*\}_{2}\).
  Define two morphisms \(g, h {:} Y \to Z\) which are equal on \(X\) but map the complement of \(X\) to the two distinct points \(\{*\}_{1}\) and \(\{*\}_{2}\) respectively.
  (Continuity is guaranteed because \(Z\) is codiscrete.)
  One verifies immediately that \(X\) is the set of points where \(g\) and \(h\) agree and that \(f\) is the equalizer of \(g\) and \(h\).
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- definition-53: body_md -->
\label{defn_:26}
  \index{adjoint open-closed duality}
  An \emph{adjoint open-closed duality} is an open-closed duality such that

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:125} \(ω\) has an \emph{interior} right adjoint \((-)^{\circ}{:} \mathbf{D} → \mathbf{O}\),

  \item\label{item:126} \(χ\) has a \emph{closure} left adjoint \(\overline{(-)}{:} \mathbf{D} → \mathbf{C}\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-53 -->
<!-- remark-49: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:2}
  In the Heyting case it follows from duality that if either adjoint to the embeddings of an open-closed duality exists then the other exists. For instance, if \((-)^{\circ}\) is given then for
  \(r ∈ \mathbf{D}(X)\) of some \(X\) the closure \(\overline{ℝ}\) is just the complement of \((¬ r)^{\circ}\). For non-Heyting open-closed dualities it makes sense to consider variants of \cref{defn_:26} for
  which only one adjoint is given.
<!-- end remark-49 -->
<!-- proposition-39: body_md -->
\label{prop:constructible-closure-adjoint}
  Let \(X\) be a Heyting space with constructible closure \(\underline{X}\) with middle \(\underline{\mathbf{D}}(X)\). Then the restricted embeddings form an adjoint open-closed duality.
<!-- end proposition-39 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
Since \(\underline{\mathbf{D}}(X)\) is the Boolean subalgebra of \(\mathbf{D}(X)\) generated by the image of \(\omega\), every element \(k \in \underline{\mathbf{D}}(X)\) decomposes as a finite join of locally closed elements \(L = \omega(o) \wedge \neg_{\mathbf{D}} \omega(v)\) with \(o, v \in \mathbf{O}(X)\). (Here \(\neg_{\mathbf{D}}\) denotes Boolean complementation in \(\mathbf{D}(X)\), so that \(\neg_{\mathbf{D}} \omega(v) = \chi(c_{v})\) for the closed element \(c_{v}\) complementary to the open \(v\).)

  \emph{Closure on locally closed elements.}
  For \(L = \omega(o) \wedge \neg_{\mathbf{D}} \omega(v)\), define
  \[
    \overline{L} \;:=\; \neg_{\mathbf{D}}\, \omega(o \Rightarrow v),
  \]
  where \(\Rightarrow\) is the Heyting implication in \(\mathbf{O}(X)\). This is a closed element, and we claim it is the least closed element above \(L\).

  First, \(L \leq \overline{L}\): the identity \(o \wedge (o \Rightarrow v) \leq v\) gives \(\omega\bigl(o \wedge (o \Rightarrow v)\bigr) \leq \omega(v)\), hence
  \[
    L \wedge \omega(o \Rightarrow v) \;=\; \omega(o) \wedge \omega(o \Rightarrow v) \wedge \neg_{\mathbf{D}} \omega(v) \;\leq\; \omega(v) \wedge \neg_{\mathbf{D}} \omega(v) \;=\; \bot,
  \]
  so \(L \leq \neg_{\mathbf{D}} \omega(o \Rightarrow v) = \overline{L}\).

  For minimality, write any closed element as \(\chi(c) = \neg_{\mathbf{D}} \omega(w)\) for some \(w \in \mathbf{O}(X)\). Then the following are equivalent:
  \begin{align*}
    L \leq \chi(c)
    &\;\Longleftrightarrow\; L \wedge \omega(w) = \bot \\
      &\;\Longleftrightarrow\; \omega(o \wedge w) \wedge \neg_{\mathbf{D}} \omega(v) = \bot \\
      &\;\Longleftrightarrow\; \omega(o \wedge w) \leq \omega(v) \\
      &\;\Longleftrightarrow\; o \wedge w \leq v \\
      &\;\Longleftrightarrow\; w \leq o \Rightarrow v \\
      &\;\Longleftrightarrow\; \neg_{\mathbf{D}}\, \omega(o \Rightarrow v) \leq \neg_{\mathbf{D}}\, \omega(w) \\
      &\;\Longleftrightarrow\; \overline{L} \leq \chi(c).
  \end{align*}
  Thus \(L \leq \chi(c)\) holds if and only if \(\overline{L} \leq \chi(c)\). This universal property characterizes \(\overline{L}\) as the least closed element containing \(L\), so the definition is independent of the chosen presentation of \(L\) as \(\omega(o) \wedge \neg_{\mathbf{D}} \omega(v)\).

  \emph{Extension over finite joins.}
  For a general element \(k = \bigvee_{i} L_{i}\), set \(\overline{k} := \bigvee_{i} \overline{L_{i}}\). This is the least closed element above \(k\): for any \(c \in \mathbf{C}(X)\),
  \[
    k \leq \chi(c)
    \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
    L_{i} \leq \chi(c) \text{ for every } i
    \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
    \overline{L_{i}} \leq c \text{ for every } i
    \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
    \overline{k} \leq c,
  \]
  where the middle equivalence uses the locally closed case. Hence \(\overline{k}\) depends only on \(k\) and not on the decomposition, and the assignment \(k \mapsto \overline{k}\) is a left adjoint to \(\chi {:} \mathbf{C}(X) \hookrightarrow \underline{\mathbf{D}}(X)\).

  \emph{Interior by duality.}
  Define \(k^{\circ} := \neg_{\mathbf{D}}\, \overline{\neg_{\mathbf{D}} k}\). This is an open element (the Boolean complement of a closed). For every \(o \in \mathbf{O}(X)\), writing \(c_{o}\) for the closed complement of \(o\) so that \(\chi(c_{o}) = \neg_{\mathbf{D}} \omega(o)\), we have
  \[
    \omega(o) \leq k
    \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
    \neg_{\mathbf{D}} k \leq \chi(c_{o})
    \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
    \overline{\neg_{\mathbf{D}} k} \leq c_{o}
    \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
    \omega(o) \leq \neg_{\mathbf{D}}\, \overline{\neg_{\mathbf{D}} k} = k^{\circ},
  \]
  where the second equivalence applies the left-adjoint property of \(\overline{(-)}\). Thus \(k^{\circ}\) is the right adjoint to \(\omega\).
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- definition-54: body_md -->
\label{dfn:13}\index{R-ringed Heyting space}
  Given a ring \(R\), an \emph{\(R\)-ringed abstract Heyting space} \(X\) is an abstract Heyting space \([X]\) equipped with a \emph{structure sheaf} \(\mathcal{S}_{X}{:} \mathbf{O}(X)^{op} → R-\mathbf{Alg}\) into the category of \(R\)-algebras
  \(R-\mathbf{Alg}\) that is a sheaf with respect to the finite union coverage.

  A \emph{morphism of \(R\)-ringed abstract Heyting spaces} \(f{:} X → Y\) is a tuple \(([f], f_{\mathcal{S}})\) where \([f]\) is a
   morphism of abstract Heyting spaces \([X] → [Y]\) and \(f_{\mathcal{S}}{:} \mathcal{S}(Y) → [f]_{*}\left(\mathcal{S}(X)\right)\) is a natural transformation from  \(\mathcal{S}(Y)\) to the pushforward of \(\mathcal{S}(X)\) as a
   sheaf of \(R\)-algebras.

   Similar for concrete Heyting spaces.
<!-- end definition-54 -->
<!-- remark-50: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:27}
  Note that we do not assume that our space is \emph{locally ringed}, i.e. that the stalks of the structure sheaf are local rings. This is in line with \cite{delfsSemialgebraicTopologyReal1981}.
<!-- end remark-50 -->
<!-- proposition-40: body_md -->
\label{prp:4}
  Let \(ι{:} V \hookrightarrow R^{n}\) be a semialgebraic subset of \(R^{n}\). Then \(V\) is an \(R\)-ringed concrete Heyting space.
<!-- end proposition-40 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
\label{prf:13}
  We fix a real closed field \(R\), an integer \(n ≥ 0\), and a semialgebraic subset \(V \subseteq R^n\). We saw in \cref{xmp_:11} that \(V\) under its usual semialgebraic topology carries the structure of a
  concrete Heyting space in the sense of \cref{dfn:12,dfn:13}. We can endow this with the structure of the usual semialgebraic function sheaf \(\mathcal{S}_V{:} \mathbf{O}(V)^{op} → R\text{-}\mathbf{Alg}\)
  of \(R\)-algebras, which assigns to each open semialgebraic \(U \subseteq V\) the \(R\)-algebra of semialgebraic maps \(U → R\), and restriction maps along inclusions. Delfs-Knebusch show that
  this is a sheaf for the finite-union coverage and that the resulting ringed space structure matches the ``usual'' semialgebraic geometry.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- example-65: body_md -->
\label{xmp:112}
\index{semialgebraic space}
Let \(R\) be a real closed field. We define the category \(\mathbf{CSAS}_{R}\) of concrete semialgebraic spaces over \(R\) as the category whose objects \(S\) are \(R\)-ringed
  concrete Heyting spaces such that there exists an open cover of \(\mathopen{∣}S\mathclose{∣}\) by affine semivarieties. Then it follows from the definition of concrete Heyting spaces that
  \(\mathbf{CSAS}_{R}\) features a Heyting open-closed duality. Passing fibrewise to the Boolean algebra generated by opens and closeds gives the corresponding abstract constructible
  closures.
<!-- end example-65 -->
<!-- definition-55: body_md -->
\label{dfn:14}\index{scale on a hyperdoctrine}
  Given a preorder \(P\) and a submonic hyperdoctrine \(\mathcal{H}\), a \emph{weak \(P\)-scale } on \(\mathcal{H}\) is a weak natural transformation \(σ{:} \mathcal{H} \Rightarrow \mathbf{K}(P)\) to the constant functor \(\mathbf{K}(P)\) on \(P\).
<!-- end definition-55 -->
<!-- definition-56: body_md -->
\label{defn_:28}
\index{regular scale}
\index{prescale}
  Given a preorder \(P\) and a submonic hyperdoctrine \(\mathcal{H}{:} \mathcal{C}^{op} → \mathbf{PrO}\), a \emph{\(P\)-prescale} is a natural transformation \(σ{:} \mathbf{Core}_{\mathcal{C}}⨾ \mathcal{H} \Rightarrow \mathbf{K}(P)\), where
  \(\mathbf{Core}_{\mathcal{C}}\) is the embedding of the core groupoid on the objects of \(\mathcal{C}\) into \(\mathcal{C}\) (so that naturality reduces to isomorphism-invariance).

  \(σ\) is a \emph{lax \(P\)-scale} if it descends
  to a lax natural transformation of hyperdoctrines \(\mathcal{H} \Rightarrow \mathbf{K}(P)\) and dually an \emph{oplax \(P\)-scale}.

  \(σ\) is a \emph{regular \(P\)-scale} if it is a lax scale on the monic part of \(\mathcal{C}\) and an
  oplax scale on the regular epimorphisms in \(\mathcal{C}\).
<!-- end definition-56 -->
<!-- example-66: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:8}
  Cardinality is a regular scale on each concrete category whose monomorphisms are injections and whose regular epimorphisms are surjections, e.g. in \(\mathbf{Top}\), valued in
  the category of cardinals.
<!-- end example-66 -->
<!-- example-67: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:24}
  Let \(\mathbf{M}(X)\) be the \(σ\)-algebra of measurable subsets of a measure space and \(μ{:} X → ℝ_{\geq 0}\) be its measure. Then the family \(μ|_{M}{:}(M) → ℝ_{\geq 0}\) with
  \(M{:} \mathbf{M}(X)\) a measurable subset of \(X\) and \((M)\) its principal ideal in \(\mathbf{M}(X)\) is a scale on \(\mathbf{M}(X)\).
<!-- end example-67 -->
<!-- definition-57: body_md -->
\label{dfn:15}\index{Borel-Heyting measure}
  Given an ordered monoid \(M\) and an open-closed duality \(\mathcal{D} = (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{c})\) on a category \(\mathcal{C}\), an \emph{open Borel-Heyting measure} \(μ\) on \(\mathcal{D}\) is
  an \(M\)-scale on the underlying functor \(\mathbf{O}\) of \(\mathbf{o}\) such that if
  \(ι ∨_{\mathbf{O}} κ\) and \(ι ∧_{\mathbf{O}} κ\) exist and \(ι ∧_{\mathbf{O}} κ = \bot_{\mathbf{O}}\), then \(μ(ι ∨_{\mathbf{O}} κ) = μ(ι) + μ(κ)\).

  A \emph{closed Borel-Heyting measure} is the same but defined on \(\mathbf{C}\).
<!-- end definition-57 -->
<!-- definition-58: body_md -->
\label{dfn:modular-measure}\index{modular measure}
  An open (resp. closed) Borel-Heyting measure \(μ\) on \(\mathcal{D} = (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{c})\) with values in a commutative monoid \(M\) is \emph{modular} if for all subobjects \(ι, κ\),
  \[
    μ(ι ∨ κ) + μ(ι ∧ κ) = μ(ι) + μ(κ).
  \]

  \(μ\) is \emph{standard} if \(\mathcal{D}\) is defined on a category \(\mathcal{C}\) with an initial object \(∅\), \(\mathbf{O}\) resp. \(\mathbf{C}\) contains each initial morphism \(0_{X}{:} ∅ → X\) and \(μ\)
  maps each \(0_{X}\) to the neutral element \(0 ∈ M\).
<!-- end definition-58 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:2}
\index{Smiley-Horn-Tarski theorem}
\cite{gierzContinuousLatticesDomains}(IV-9.3., IV-9.4.) A modular standard measure \(μ{:} L → ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞}\) from a sub-lattice \(L\) of a Boolean algebra \(B\) to a left-cancellative monoid
  extends to a finitely additive measure on the Boolean closure \(\overline{L}\) of \(L\) in \(B\). Moreover, if \(μ\) is finitely valued, then this extension is unique.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-41: body_md -->
\label{prop:borel-heyting-extension}
\index{Borel-Heyting measure!extension}
Let \(\mathcal{D} = (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{c})\) be an abstract Heyting open-closed duality.
  Then any standard modular open Borel-Heyting measure \(μ{:} \mathbf{O} \Rightarrow \mathbf{K}(ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞})\) extends to a finitely additive measure \(\hat{μ}\) on the constructible closure
  \(\underline{\mathbf{D}}\) of \(\mathbf{D}\).
  The same holds for any standard modular closed Borel-Heyting measure \(ν{:} \mathbf{C} \Rightarrow \mathbf{K}(ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞})\). Moreover, if \(μ\) is finitely valued, then \(\hat{μ}\) is unique.
  Consequently, there is a natural bijection between finite open and closed modular Borel-Heyting measures.
<!-- end proposition-41 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
\label{prf:borel-heyting-extension}
  Fix an object \(X {:} \mathcal{C}\). By the definition of a Heyting open-closed duality, \(\mathbf{O}(X)\) is a distributive sublattice of the Boolean algebra \(\mathbf{D}(X)\), and
  \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) consists precisely of the Boolean complements of elements of \(\mathbf{O}(X)\).

  Let \(\underline{\mathbf{D}}(X)\) be the constructible closure. By the Smiley-Horn-Tarski extension theorem \(μ_{X}\) uniquely
  extends to an additive measure \(\hat{μ}_{X} {:} \underline{\mathbf{D}}(X) → ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞}\), which is unique if \(μ\) is finite. Because the closed subobjects \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) are the Boolean complements of the opens, the Boolean algebra generated by \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) is precisely
  \(\underline{\mathbf{D}}(X)\). Restricting \(\hat{μ}_{X}\) to \(\mathbf{C}(X)\) yields a function \(ν_{X} {:} \mathbf{C}(X) → ℝ_{\geq 0, ∞}\) which is trivially modular, hence a closed
  Borel-Heyting measure.

  For any open \(U ∈ \mathbf{O}(X)\) with closed complement \(¬U ∈ \mathbf{C}(X)\), finite additivity on \(\underline{\mathbf{D}}(X)\) implies:
  \[
    μ_{X}(U) + ν_{X}(¬U) = \hat{μ}_{X}(U) + \hat{μ}_{X}(¬U) = \hat{μ}_{X}(\top_X) = μ_{X}(\top_X).
  \]
  Conversely, starting with a finite modular closed Borel-Heyting measure \(ν\), it uniquely extends to \(\underline{\mathbf{D}}(X)\), and restricting this extension to \(\mathbf{O}(X)\)
  recovers an open measure. These two extension-restriction procedures are mutually inverse.

  Finally, we must check that the extension is natural (i.e. it acts as a hyperdoctrine scale). For any morphism of Heyting spaces \(f {:} Y → X\), the pullback \(f^{*}\) on
  \(\mathbf{D}\) is a Boolean homomorphism that restricts to the given pullbacks on \(\mathbf{O}\) and \(\mathbf{C}\). Because \(f^{*}\) preserves the Boolean operations and
  \(\hat{μ}_{X}\) is the unique additive extension of \(μ_{X}\), it follows that \(f^{*} ⨾ \hat{μ}_{Y} = \hat{μ}_{X}\) on \(\underline{\mathbf{D}}(X)\). Thus, naturality holds for the
  extensions, and the bijection is complete.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- remark-51: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:16}
  As mentioned in \cref{sec:size-assumptions} we take everything strict (up to contractible homotopy). This might seem evil but a weak framework would further complicate the
  already strained exposition for little gain: the material is orthogonal to questions of weakness, the only significant adaptation would be to have to consider the naturality
  2-cells of weak natural transformations in 2-categories other than \(\mathbf{UBP}\) (which is locally thin up to homotopy) in the latter part of \cref{sec:univ-char-mathbf}.
<!-- end remark-51 -->
<!-- definition-59: body_md -->
\label{def:2-category}
\index{2-category}
  A \emph{(strict) 2-category} \(\mathcal{C}\) consists of:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item A class of \emph{objects} (or \emph{0-cells}) \(X, Y, Z, \dots\)
  \item For each pair of objects \(X, Y\), a category \(\mathcal{C}(X,Y)\) whose
    \begin{itemize}
    \item objects are called \emph{1-cells} (or \emph{morphisms}) \(f, g {:} X \to Y\),
    \item morphisms are called \emph{2-cells} (or \emph{2-morphisms}) \(α {:} f \Rightarrow g {:} X \to Y\).
    \end{itemize}
  \item A \emph{horizontal composition} functor
    \[
      ⨾_{X,Y,Z} {:} \mathcal{C}(X,Y) \times \mathcal{C}(Y,Z) \to \mathcal{C}(X,Z)
    \]
    for each triple of objects, written simply as \(f⨾ g\) on 1-cells and \(β⨾ α\) on 2-cells.
  \item For each object \(X\), a distinguished 1-cell \(\mathbf{id}_X {:} X \to X\) serving as the identity for horizontal composition.
  \end{enumerate}
  Subject to the \emph{strict} associativity and unit axioms:
  \begin{align*}
    f ⨾ (g ⨾ h) &= (f ⨾ g) ⨾ h, & f ⨾ \mathbf{id}_Y &= f = \mathbf{id}_X ⨾ f
  \end{align*}
  for all composable 1-cells (and similarly for 2-cells). Thus horizontal composition is strictly associative and unital.

  Vertical composition of 2-cells (i.e. composition within each hom-category) is written with a semicolon: given \(α {:} f \Rightarrow g\) and \(β {:} g \Rightarrow h\), the composite is \(α; β {:} f \Rightarrow h\). The \emph{interchange law}
  \[
    (α; β)⨾ (α'; β') = (α⨾ α'); (β⨾ β')
  \]
  holds automatically from the functoriality of \(⨾\).
<!-- end definition-59 -->
<!-- definition-60: body_md -->
\label{def:2-functor}
\index{2-functor}
  Let \(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{D}\) be strict 2-categories. A \emph{(strict) 2-functor} \(F {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) consists of:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item A function on objects: \(X \mapsto F(X)\).
  \item For each pair \(X, Y\), a functor \(F_{X,Y} {:} \mathcal{C}(X,Y) \to \mathcal{D}(F(X), F(Y))\) on hom-categories, mapping 1-cells \(f \mapsto F(f)\) and 2-cells \(α \mapsto F(α)\).
  \end{enumerate}
  Subject to \emph{strict} preservation of identities and horizontal composition:
  \begin{align*}
    F(\mathbf{id}_X) &= \mathbf{id}_{F(X)}, & F(f ⨾ g) &= F(f) ⨾ F(g), & F(α; β) &= F(α); F(β).
  \end{align*}
<!-- end definition-60 -->
<!-- definition-61: body_md -->
\label{def:2-nat-trans}
\index{2-natural transformation}
  Let \(F, G {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) be strict 2-functors. A \emph{(strict) 2-natural transformation} \(θ {:} F \Rightarrow G\) consists of:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item For each object \(X {:} \mathcal{C}\), a 1-cell \(θ_X {:} F(X) \to G(X)\) in \(\mathcal{D}\) (the \emph{component} at \(X\)),
  \end{enumerate}
  such that for every 1-cell \(f {:} X \to Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) the following square of 1-cells in \(\mathcal{D}\) \emph{commutes strictly}:
  \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
      F(X) \ar[r, "F(f)"] \ar[d, "θ_X"'] & F(Y) \ar[d, "θ_Y"] \\
      G(X) \ar[r, "G(f)"'] & G(Y)
    \end{tikzcd}
  \]
  i.e. \(θ_X ⨾ G(f) = F(f) ⨾ θ_Y\), and for every 2-cell \(α {:} f \Rightarrow g {:} X \to Y\):
  \[
    F(α) ⨾ θ_Y = θ_X ⨾ G(α) \qquad \text{(equality of 2-cells).}
  \]
  If only the 1-cell condition holds and the 2-cell condition is replaced by a morphism \(θ(f){:} θ_{X}⨾ G(f) → F(f)⨾ θ_{Y}\) satisfying coherence conditions that make it behave
  sensibly with respect to composition and identities,\footnote{The coherence conditions are the same as for a pseudonatural transformation, see e.g. p.5 of
    \cite{leinsterBasicBicategories1998} for details.} the transformation is called \emph{lax}; if the
  inequality is reversed, \emph{oplax}.
<!-- end definition-61 -->
<!-- definition-62: body_md -->
\label{def:2-adjunction}
\index{2-adjunction}
  Let \(F {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) and \(U {:} \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{C}\) be strict 2-functors. A \emph{(strict) 2-adjunction} \(F \dashv U\) consists of strict 2-natural transformations
  \[
    η {:} \mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}} \Rightarrow F ⨾ U \qquad \text{(the \emph{unit})}, \qquad \varepsilon {:} U ⨾ F \Rightarrow \mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{D}} \qquad \text{(the \emph{counit})},
  \]
  satisfying the \emph{triangle identities} strictly:
  \[
    F \xrightarrow{η ⨾ F} F ⨾ U ⨾ F \xrightarrow{F ⨾ \varepsilon} F \;=\; \mathbf{id}_F, \qquad U \xrightarrow{U ⨾ η} U ⨾ F ⨾ U \xrightarrow{\varepsilon ⨾ U} U \;=\; \mathbf{id}_U.
  \]
  Equivalently, for each \(X {:} \mathcal{C}\) and \(Y {:} \mathcal{D}\) there is an isomorphism of hom-categories
  \[
    \mathcal{D}(F(X), Y) \cong \mathcal{C}(X, U(Y))
  \]
  that is strictly natural in \(X\) and \(Y\) and strictly 2-natural in the 2-cells.
<!-- end definition-62 -->
<!-- remark-52: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:18}
  So \(\mathbf{\overset{\hookrightarrow}{Cat}}_{◆ \mathbf{UBP}}\) is a particular variant of a slice-2-category with morphisms and 2-morphisms given by two lax kinds of triangles. We pronounce this construction
  as ``diamond-over''.
<!-- end remark-52 -->
<!-- remark-53: body_md -->
\label{rmk:9}
  We can describe the image of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{(-)}\) more precisely: since each \(ι ∈ \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) corresponds to a monomorphism \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) and every principal ideal of
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) corresponds to an element \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) by definition, every principal ideal embedding \(κ{:} (a) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) with \(a\) an element of
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) is in the image of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}\). Thus, \(\mathbf{Im}(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}})\) is closed under precomposition and thus an ideal\footnote{Note that we mean ideal in the category-theoretic sense, i.e. closed under precomposition but without binary upward bounds.} in
  \(\mathopen{↓}\mathbf{UBP}\mathclose{↓}\), and, conversely, every 1-categorical ideal in \(\mathopen{↓}\mathbf{UBP}\mathclose{↓}\) is a subcategory of
  \(\mathopen{↓}\mathbf{UBP}\mathclose{↓}\) that maps to itself.

  It is important that the ideal that is the image of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}\) is not generally a principal ideal as a subcategory of \(\mathbf{UBP}\), i.e. not upward-bounded: each object in \(\mathcal{C}\) is composed
  of its parts, but \(\mathcal{C}\) itself is generally only a context in which these objects interact, they don't assemble into one whole.
<!-- end remark-53 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lmm:3}
  Given a functor of monic categories \(F{:} \mathcal{C} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{D}\), \(F_{*}\) is the only top-preserving natural transformation \(ε{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}} \Rightarrow  F⨾ \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}}{:} \mathcal{C} → \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}\).
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
\label{prf:6}
  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
      \begin{tikzcd}
        \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(A) \ar[r, hook, "ε_A"] \ar[d, hook, "ι_{*}"'] & \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}}(F(A)) \ar[d, hook, "F(ι)_{*}"] \\
    \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) \ar[r, hook, "ε_X"'] & \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}}(F(X))
  \end{tikzcd}
                                
  \end{figure}

  Evaluate at \(\mathbf{id}_A\). The left-down leg gives \(\mathbf{id}_A⨾ ι = ι\); the top-right leg gives \(ε_A(\mathbf{id}_A) = \mathbf{id}_{F(A)}\) (by top-preservation) and then \(\mathbf{id}_{F(A)}⨾ F(ι) = F(ι)\).
  Thus, naturality forces \(ε_X(ι) = F(ι)\). Since every element of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) is some monomorphism in \(\mathcal{C}\) we have \(ε_X = F_{*, X}\) for all \(X\); hence \(ε = F_{*}\).
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lmm:2}
  For each functor \(F{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathbf{UBP}\) and morphism \(f {:} X \hookrightarrow Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\) it holds that \(f_{*}⨾ F_{★, Y}  = F_{★, X}⨾ F(f)\). Thus \(F_{★}\) is a natural transformation
  \[
    F_{★} {:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}} ⇒ F.
  \]
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
\label{prf:lmm2}
  Consider the diagram:

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzcd}
      \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) \ar[r, "f_{*}"] \ar[d, "F_{★, X}"'] & \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y) \ar[d, "F_{★, Y}"] \\
      F(X) \ar[r, "F(f)"'] & F(Y)
    \end{tikzcd}
                                 
  \end{figure}
  Given \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow X\),  we have:
  \[f_{*}⨾ F_{★, Y}(ι⨾ f) = \top_{F(ι⨾ f)} = \top_{F(ι)⨾ F(f)} = F(f)(\top_{F(ι)}) =  F_{★, X}⨾ F(f).\]

  Since this holds for all \(ι ∈ \mathbf{SOb}(X)\) for all \(X{:} \mathcal{C}\) we have that \(F_{★}\) is natural.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:1}
\index{subobject functor!representability}
\index{subobject functor!adjoint}
  The 2-functor \(\mathbf{SOb}_{(-)}{:} \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}} → {\mathbf{\overset{\hookrightarrow}{Cat}}_{◆ \mathbf{UBP}}}\) is left adjoint to the 2-functor
  \(\mathbf{s}{:} {\mathbf{\overset{\hookrightarrow}{Cat}}_{◆ \mathbf{UBP}}} → \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}}{:} (F{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathbf{UBP}) ↦ \mathcal{C}\).
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
We establish the adjunction by explicitly constructing the unit and counit. First, we verify that \(\mathbf{SOb}_{(-)}\) is a well-defined 2-functor. For the unit of the
  adjunction \(\mathbf{SOb}_{(-)} ⊣ \mathbf{s}\), since \(\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}) = \mathcal{C}\), we may simply take the identity functor:
  \[
    \mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}}{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathbf{s}(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}).
  \]

  For the counit, given an object \(E{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathbf{UBP}\) in \(\mathbf{\overset{\hookrightarrow}{Cat}}_{◆ \mathbf{UBP}}\), we need a 1-cell
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}} → E\) over \(\mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}}\). This 1-cell \((\mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}}, E_{★})\) consists of \(\mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}}\) with the natural transformation
  \(E_{★}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}} ⇒ E\), defined componentwise for each \(X ∈ \mathcal{C}\) by
  \[
    E_{★, X}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X) → E(X), \qquad ι ↦ \top_{E(ι)}:
  \]

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large]
    \mathcal{C} \ar[d, "\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}"{name=S}, bend left=50] \ar[d, "\mathbf{E}"'{name=E}, bend right=50] \\
    \mathbf{UBP} \ar[from=S, to=E, Rightarrow, shift left=6pt, shorten <= 6pt, xshift=3pt]
  \end{tikzcd}
\end{figure}

This is order-preserving since \(E(ι)\) is a monotone map and naturality follows from \cref{lmm:2}.

It remains to verify the triangle identities. The first identity requires
\((\mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}})_{*}⨾ (\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}})_{★} = \mathbf{id}_{\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}}\). Indeed, for any \(X{:} \mathcal{C}\) this evaluates to

\[\mathbf{id}_{\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}}(X)⨾ \mathbf{id}_{\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}}(X) = \mathbf{id}_{\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}}(X).\]

The second identity requires \(\mathbf{s}(E_{★}) ⨾ \mathbf{id}_{\mathbf{s}(E)} = \mathbf{id}_{\mathbf{s}(E)}\). Since the underlying functor of the counit \(E_{★}\) is
\(\mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}}\) and \(ε_{\mathcal{C}} = \mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}}\), this identity holds trivially.

Having verified the triangle identities, we conclude that \(\mathbf{SOb}_{(-)} ⊣ \mathbf{s}\).
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- remark-54: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:8}
  So the basic distinguishing feature of \(\mathbf{UBP}\) that we use in this proof and the entire section is that each preorder in it has a top, which ensures that each
  monic \(ι: A \hookrightarrow X\) in a category \(\mathcal{C}\) is mapped to an ideal embedding \(ι_{*}\) under \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}\), gives us shadows of morphisms in categories and functors and natural
  transformations between categories ensures that many problematic functors from \(\mathcal{C}\) into the category of all preorders \(\mathbf{PrO}\) don't factor through \(\mathbf{UBP}\).
<!-- end remark-54 -->
<!-- remark-55: body_md -->
\label{rmk:6}
  If we don't assume that the natural transformations of  the 1-cells in \(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}}_{◆ \mathbf{UPB}}\) are top-preserving, then we still get a kind of laxification
  of an adjunction, where, given a category \(\mathcal{C}\) and functor \(F: \mathcal{C} → \mathbf{UBP}\), the morphisms from \((\mathcal{C}, \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}})\) to \((\mathcal{C}, F)\) are bounded by \(F_{★}\) but no
  longer (weakly) unique.
<!-- end remark-55 -->
<!-- remark-56: body_md -->
\label{rmk:4}
  There is a variant of this diamond-over category for the contravariant subobject-functor \(\mathbf{SOb}^{*}\). Take some finite-limit-preserving functor \(F{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathcal{D}\). This induces for each
  \(X{:} \mathcal{C}\) a morphism \(F_{*}{:} \mathbf{SOb}(X) → \mathbf{SOb}(F(X))\), which preserves \(\top\) and meets if they exist in \(\mathcal{C}\). Given now a natural transformation
  \(η{:} F \Rightarrow G{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathcal{D}\), we get a natural transformation \(η^{*}_{X}{:} G⨾ \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}} → F(X)⨾ \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}}\) and for each \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) a diagram

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
    & G(A) \ar[r, hook, "G(ι)"] & G(X) \\
    & η^{*}(G(ι)) \ar[u, "G(ι)^{*}(η_{X})"'] \ar[r, hook, "η_{X}^{*}(G(ι))"] & F(X) \ar[u, "η_{X}"'] \\
    F(A) \ar[uur, "η_{A}"] \ar[ur, hook, "{(η_{A}, F(ι))}"'{yshift=14pt, xshift=20pt}] \ar[urr, hook, "F(ι)"'] &&
  \end{tikzcd}
\caption{\label{fi♭_:7}}
\end{figure}
where \(\leq\) is the morphism to \(η^{*}(G(ι))\) induced by the universal property of the pullback, which is a monomorphism since \(F(ι)\) and \(η_{X}^{*}(G(ι))\) are.
Thus, we have for each such \(ι\) a triangle

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \begin{tikzcd}
    & \mathbf{SOb}(G(X)) \ar[ddr, "\mathbf{SOb}(η^{*}_{X})"] & \\
    & \rotatebox[origin=c]{90}{\(\leq\)} & \\
    \mathbf{SOb}(X) \ar[uur, "G_{*, X}"] \ar[rr, "F_{*, X}"'] && \mathbf{SOb}(F(X))
  \end{tikzcd}
  \caption{\label{fig:1}}
\end{figure}
so the inequality goes precisely in the other direction as before. Moreover, if \(η\) is Cartesian, then by definition each square as in \cref{fi♭_:7} is a pullback square, so that this inequality is an
equivalence. Thus, we can lift \(\mathbf{SOb}^{*}_{\mathcal{C}}\) to a 2-functor

\[\mathbf{SOb}^{*}_{(-)}{:} \mathbf{Cat}_{pb} → (\mathbf{Cat}_{pb})_{◆^{op} \mathbf{UBP}}\]

from the 2-category \(\mathbf{Cat}_{pb}\) of well-powered categories with pullbacks along monomorphisms, pullback-preserving functors and natural transformations to the 2-category \((\mathbf{Cat}_{pb})_{◆^{op} \mathbf{UBP}}\) which is defined as in \cref{def:diamond-over} but with the 2-cell modifications as in \cref{fig:1} instead of as in \cref{item:88}.

Note however that the contravariant \(\mathbf{SOb}^{*}\)-functor does not have the same universal property as the covariant one in the contravariant diamond category over
\(\mathbf{UBP}\): since for some \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) the morphism \(ι^{*}{:} \mathbf{SOb}(X) → \mathbf{SOb}(A)\) preserves tops, the entire calculus we're developing cannot be
applied and we're left without a way to compare \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}\) to some other functor \(F{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathbf{UBP}\).
<!-- end remark-56 -->
<!-- remark-57: body_md -->
\label{rmk:13}
  Note that there exists a 2-functor \(\mathbf{Cat}_{\hookrightarrow-prv} → \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}}\) from the 2-category of small categories, monomorphism-preserving functors and natural
  transformations between them, which we can postcompose with \(\mathbf{SOb}\). This is what we are implicitly using when we extend smallness from monic categories to all
  categories. Since every monic category is a category, \(\mathbf{Cat}_{\hookrightarrow-prv} → \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}}\) has a section. Moreover, for each category
  \(\mathcal{C}\) there exists a functor \( \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathcal{C}} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{C}\) embedding the monic part of a category. All in all this sure looks like a coreflective embedding — but it is very far from
  that. The universal property of an adjunction would force that for each category \(\mathcal{D}\) and functor \(F{:} \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathcal{C}} → \mathcal{D}\) there would exist a unique functor
  \(\mathcal{C} → \mathcal{D}\) over \(F\), we have nothing to determine how to map the non-monomorphisms in \(\mathcal{C}\). If we restrict to regular categories we have a decomposition
  \(f = e⨾ m\) for each \(f\) with \(m\) monic and \(e\) regular epi, and \(F\) fixes objects and monomorphisms, so in this case we would only have to determine how to map \(e\).
  Now, \(e\) is a coequalizer of its kernel pair \(k_{1}, k_{2}\) which is monic and \(F\) thus mapped by \(F\), so might try to map \(e\) to the coequalizer
  \(\mathbf{CEq}(F(k_{1}), F(k_{2}))\), but there is no reason to even assume that \((F(k_{1}), F(k_{2}))\) is a kernel pair in \(\mathcal{D}\), it can be a monic pair without a
  co-equalizer. And even if we assume \(\mathbf{CEq}(F(k_{1}), F(k_{2}))\) exists, there is no reason to assume that its codomain is \(\mathbf{s}(F(m))\), and one can construct
  counterexamples.
<!-- end remark-57 -->
<!-- definition-63: body_md -->
\label{defn_:2}\index{faithful 2-cell}\index{fully faithful 2-cell}
  \cite{FaithfulMorphismNLab} Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be a 2-category. A 1-cell \(ι {:} A → X\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) is called \emph{faithful} if for every object \(C\) of \(\mathcal{B}\), the induced functor of
  hom-categories
  \[
    ι_{*, \mathcal{C}} \;:=\; (- ⨾ ι) \;{:}\; \mathcal{B}(C,A) → \mathcal{B}(C,X)
  \]
  is faithful.

  Similarly, \(ι\) is \emph{fully faithful} if each \(ι_{*, \mathcal{C}}\) is fully faithful.
<!-- end definition-63 -->
<!-- definition-64: body_md -->
\label{defn_:3}\index{pseudomonic morphism}\index{pseudomonic 2-category}
  \cite{PseudomonicMorphismNLab} A morphism \(ι: X → Y\) in a 2-category \(\mathcal{B}\) is \emph{pseudomonic} if \(ι\) is faithful and for each pair \(f, g\) and 2-isomorphism
  \(σ: f⨾ ι \overset{\simeq}{\Rightarrow} g⨾ ι\) there exists a 2-isomorphism \(\overline{σ}: f \Rightarrow g\) such that \(σ = \overline{σ}⨾ ι\).

  \(\mathcal{B}\) itself is \emph{pseudomonic} if all its morphisms
  are pseudomonics.

  \(\mathcal{B}\) is \emph{2-pseudomonic} if it is pseudomonic and all its 2-cells are monic in their hom-categories.

  A morphism \(f{:} X → Y\)  is \emph{monomorphism-preserving} if for every \(A{:} B\) the functor \(f_{*}{:} \mathcal{B}(A, X) → \mathcal{B}(A, Y)\) is monomorphism-preserving.

  A 2-functor \(F{:} \mathcal{B} → \mathcal{B}'\) is \emph{2-pseudomonic} if

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:53} for each \(X, Y{:} \mathcal{B}\) the induced functor \(F_{X, Y}{:} \mathcal{B}(X, Y) → \mathcal{B}'(F(X), F(Y))\) is pseudomonic,
  \item\label{item:54} \(F\) preserves pseudomonics and reflects equivalences.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-64 -->
<!-- example-68: body_md -->
\label{xmp:10}
  Every monic category is a 2-pseudomonic 2-category. This follows because 2-cell preservation and isomorphism-reflection are trivially true for morphisms in a category.
<!-- end example-68 -->
<!-- definition-65: body_md -->
\label{defn_:11}
  A 2-category is \emph{monically left-ideal} if for each monic 2-cell \(φ{:} f \Rightarrow g{:} X → Y\)  and \(h{:} A → X\) it holds that the left whiskering \(h⨾ φ\) is monic.
<!-- end definition-65 -->
<!-- example-69: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:16}
  Each 2-pseudomonic 2-category is monically left-ideal, since all its 2-cells are monic.
<!-- end example-69 -->
<!-- definition-66: body_md -->
\label{defn_:6}
  \index{pseudomonic subobject preorder}
  Given an object \(X\) of a monically left-ideal 2-category \(\mathcal{B}\), the \emph{(2-covariant) pseudomonic subobject preorder} \(\mathbf{SOb}_{f, \mathcal{B}}(X)\) is the preorder:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{item:97} whose objects are pseudomonics \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) into \(X\) in \(\mathcal{B}\),
  \item\label{item:98} such that \(ι \leq κ{:} B \hookrightarrow X\) if and only if there exists a morphism \(μ{:} A → B\) and a monic 2-cell \(φ{:} ι \Rightarrow μ⨾ κ\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-66 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{le↘_:4}
  In a monically left-ideal 2-category \(\mathcal{B}\), \(\mathbf{SOb}_{f, \mathcal{B}}(X)\) is in fact a preorder.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
We must show that the relation \(\le\) on the class of pseudomonic 1-cells \(ι {:} A → X\) into a fixed object \(X {:} \mathcal{B}\) is reflexive and transitive.

  Let \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow X\) be a pseudomonic. The identity 2-cell is monic in any 2-category, so this witnesses
  \(ι \le ι\). For transitivity, suppose we have pseudomonics \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow X\), \(κ {:} B \hookrightarrow X\), and \(λ {:} C \hookrightarrow X\) with \(ι \le κ\) and \(κ \le λ\). By definition, there
  exists an \(f{:} A → B\) and a monic 2-cell \(α {:} ι ⇒ f ⨾ κ\) in \(\mathcal{B}(A,X)\) and a monomorphism-preserving \(g{:} B → C\) and a monic 2-cell
  \(β {:} κ ⇒ g ⨾ λ\) in \(\mathcal{B}(B,X)\). Define \(h := f ⨾ g {:} A → C\) and set
  \[
    \gamma \;:=\; α ; (f ⨾ β) {:} ι \Rightarrow h ⨾ λ .
  \]

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
  A \ar[r, "f"]
    \ar[dr, hook', bend right=35, "ι"', ""{name=I}]
  & B \ar[d, hook, "κ"', ""{name=K}]
  \ar[r, "g"]
  & C \ar[dl, hook, bend left=35, "λ"]
  \\
  & X
  \arrow[Rightarrow, from=I, to=1-2, "α"', shorten <=3pt, shorten >=5pt]
  \arrow[Rightarrow, from=K, to=1-3, "β"', shorten <=3pt, shorten >=5pt]
\end{tikzcd}
                             
  \end{figure}

  Since \(\mathcal{B}\) is monically left-ideal, whiskering preserves monics. Moreover, vertical composition of monics is monic and \(\gamma\) is monic, so \(ι \le λ\). Thus \(\le\) is reflexive and transitive.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- remark-58: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:23}
  The slice category of an object in a category is constructed as a comma category, i.e. a special kind of 2-limit. In 2-categories, this definition trifurcates into a lax, an
  oplax and a weak variant. Accordingly, \cref{defn_:6} has a 2-contravariant variant \(\mathbf{SOb}_{f^{op}, \mathcal{B}}(X)\) with inverse 2-cells, and a weak variant \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathopen{∣}f\mathclose{∣}, \mathcal{B}}(X)\), where the 2-cells have to be
  2-isomorphisms. But since we don't use these other functors in this subsection, we will write \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(X)\) for \(\mathbf{SOb}_{f, \mathcal{B}}(X)\) to simplify notation.
<!-- end remark-58 -->
<!-- remark-59: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:25}
  For \(ι{:} X \hookrightarrow Y\) faithful in a 2-category \(\mathcal{B}\) whose morphisms are faithful but not isomorphism-reflecting, we \emph{do} get for each
  \(κ{:} A \hookrightarrow X, κ'{:} B \hookrightarrow X\) and pair \((f, α){:} (A \hookrightarrow B, κ \hookrightarrow f⨾ κ')\) displaying \(κ \leq κ'\) a pair
  \((f, α⨾ ι){:} (A \hookrightarrow B, κ⨾ ι \hookrightarrow f⨾ κ⨾ ι)\), so that \(κ⨾ ι \leq κ' ⨾ ι\). Thus, we get an order-preserving morphism
  \(ι_{*}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(X) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(Y)\), which is essentially injective since \(ι\) is faithful. But, given
  \(f{:} A \hookrightarrow B\) and \(β{:} f⨾ κ⨾ ι \hookrightarrow κ'⨾ ι\) there is no reason to assume that \(β\) is in the image of \(ι_{*}{:} \mathcal{B}(A, X) → \mathcal{B}(A, Y)\), which means that
  \(ι_{*}\) is \emph{not} generally a monomorphism because \(β\) might be an isomorphism. So we need to at least assume that \(ι\) is isomorphism-reflecting i.e. each induced
  functor \(ι_{*}\) is isomorphism-reflecting. So we can understand isomorphism-reflectivity as a weakening of injectivity. This is why it excludes pathologies as in \cref{xmp:5},
  which go against our intuition on what a subcategory should be and why we have to use pseudomonics, not just faithful morphisms.
<!-- end remark-59 -->
<!-- proposition-42: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:6}
  Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be a 2-pseudomonic 2-category. Then the assignment \(X ↦ \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(X)\) from \cref{defn_:6} defines a 2-functor \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}{:} \mathcal{B} → \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}\).
<!-- end proposition-42 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
For a 1-cell \(f {:} X → Y\) in \(\mathcal{B}\), define the action of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}\) on \(f\) by postcomposition:
  \[
    \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(f) {:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(X) \longrightarrow \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(Y), \qquad ι \mapsto ι⨾ f.
  \]
  Since \(\mathcal{B}\) is 2-pseudomonic, the composite \(ι⨾ f\) is pseudomonic, hence an object of \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(Y)\). To verify monotonicity, let
  \(ι \leq \kappa\) in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(X)\). Then there exist a pseudomonic \(g {:} A \hookrightarrow B\) and a monic 2-cell
  \(α {:} ι \Rightarrow g⨾ \kappa\). Whiskering with \(f\) yields a monic 2-cell \(α⨾ f {:} ι⨾ f \Rightarrow g⨾ (\kappa⨾ f)\), which witnesses \(ι⨾ f \leq \kappa⨾ f\).

  For a 2-cell \(θ {:} f \Rightarrow g {:} X → Y\), define
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(θ) {:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(f) \Rightarrow \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(g)\) pointwise. For each \(ι {:} A \hookrightarrow X\), whiskering yields
  \(ι⨾ θ {:} ι⨾ f \Rightarrow ι⨾ g\). Because \(\mathcal{B}\) is 2-pseudomonic, \(ι⨾ θ\) is a monic 2-cell, corresponding to the relation
  \(ι⨾ f \leq ι⨾ g\) in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(Y)\). The interchange law in \(\mathcal{B}\) ensures that this assignment is natural.

  The 2-functor axioms follow directly from the unitality and associativity of composition in \(\mathcal{B}\). Specifically, \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathbf{id}_X)\) is the identity on
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(X)\) since \(ι⨾ \mathbf{id}_X = ι\), and \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}\) preserves composition of 1-cells since
  \(ι⨾ (f⨾ g) = (ι⨾ f)⨾ g\). Preservation of vertical and horizontal composition of 2-cells follows analogously from the functoriality of whiskering.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- remark-60: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:9}
  Let us take a look at the action of \(\mathbf{SOb}\) on \(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}\) itself, which will become crucial in a moment: it sends a preorder \(P\) to the preorder
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}}(P)\) we discussed in \cref{xmp:3} and acts on morphisms by postcomposition. Thus there exist morphisms

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{item:21} \(\{-\}{:} P → \mathbf{SOb}_{\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}}(P)\) which maps \(a ∈ P\) to the one-element sub-preorder \(\{a\}\),
  \item \label{item:9} \((-){:} P → \mathbf{SOb}_{\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}}(P)\) whose image is the ideal \((a)\),
  \end{enumerate}

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzcd}
  P && \mathbf{SOb}_{\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}}(P)
	\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, shift left=3, from=1-1, to=1-3, hook]
	\arrow[""{name=1, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, shift right=3, from=1-1, to=1-3, hook']
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-1, two heads]
	\arrow[phantom, from=1, to=0, "\rotatebox{90}{\leq}"{description, fill=white, inner sep=2pt}]
 \end{tikzcd} \\
\[
\{-\}⨾\top_{(-)}=\mathbf{id}=(-)⨾\top_{(-)}.
\]

                             
  \end{figure}

  It follows almost immediately from the definitions that \(\{-\}\) forms a strict natural 2-transformation and from \cref{■pn_:ofs} that \((-)\) forms an oplax one. But because each preorder in \(\mathbf{UBP}\) has a top, we can define a morphism
  \(\top_{(-)}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}}(P) \twoheadrightarrow P{:} ι ↦ \top_{ι}\) such that both \(\{-\}\) and \((-)\) are sections of
  \(\top_{(-)}\). Moreover, it also follows almost immediately from the definitions that \(\{-\}\) is a minimal section of \(\top_{(-)}\) and \((-)\) a maximal one, so that the three form a
  unity of opposites in the sense of \cite{lawvereUnityIdentityOpposites1996}. Note that the same does not hold for filters since we would need downward-boundedness.
<!-- end remark-60 -->
<!-- definition-67: body_md -->
\label{dfn:4}
  An \emph{oplaxly pointed 2-category} \((\mathcal{B}, ★_{\mathcal{B}}) := \mathcal{B}_{★}\) is a 2-category with terminal object \(*\) and an oplax natural transformation
  \(★_{\mathcal{B}}{:} \mathbf{K}(*) → \mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{B}}\) from the constant functor \(\mathbf{K}(*)\) on the terminal object \(*\).

  We call a morphism
  \(f{:} X → Y\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) \emph{point-preserving} if \(★_{\mathcal{B}, X}⨾ f = ★_{\mathcal{B}, Y}\) and a natural transformation \emph{point-preserving} if each of its component-morphisms is.
<!-- end definition-67 -->
<!-- definition-68: body_md -->
\label{def:diamond-over}
\index{diamond-over 2-category}
  Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a sub-2-category of \(\mathbf{Cat}\), and let \(\mathcal{B}_{★}\) be an oplaxly pointed 2-category.
                                         
      
                                                    
      
  The \emph{diamond-over 2-category} \(\mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}}\) \emph{of} \(\mathcal{A}\) \emph{over} \(\mathcal{B}_{★}\) is defined as follows.

  An object of \(\mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}}\) is a pair \((\mathcal{C},E)\) where:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \(\mathcal{C}\) is an object of \(\mathcal{A}\);
  \item \(E {:} \mathcal{C} → \mathcal{B}\) is a 2-functor (necessarily trivial on 2-cells since \(\mathcal{C}\) is a category).
  \end{itemize}

  A 1-cell
  \[
    (F,ε) {:} (\mathcal{C},E) \longrightarrow (\mathcal{C}',E')
  \]
  in \(\mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}}\) is an oplaxly (or, less confusingly, covariantly) commuting triangle, so:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item a functor \(F {:} \mathcal{C} → \mathcal{C}'\) in \(\mathcal{A}\);
  \item a point-preserving 2-natural transformation
    \[
      ε {:} E \Rightarrow F⨾ E'
    \]
    in \(\mathcal{B}_{★}\),
  \end{itemize}

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzcd}
      \mathcal{C} \ar[rr,"F"] \ar[dr,"E"', ""{name=E}] && \mathcal{C}' \ar[dl,"E'"] \\
      & \mathcal{B} \ar[Rightarrow, from=E, to=1-3, "ε"{below} description]
    \end{tikzcd}
                                
  \end{figure}

  A 2-cell
  \[
    (α,Φ) {:} (F,ε) \Rightarrow (F',ε')
  \]
  between 1-cells \((F,ε),(F',ε') {:} (\mathcal{C},E) → (\mathcal{C}',E')\) consists of:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item a natural transformation \(α {:} F \Rightarrow F'\) in \(\mathcal{A}\);
  \item a modification \(Φ{:} ε; (α⨾ E') \Rrightarrow ε'\).
  \end{itemize}

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzcd}
      F⨾ E' \ar[rr, Rightarrow, "α⨾ E'"] && F'⨾ E' \\
      & E \ar[ul, Rightarrow, "ε"] \ar[ur, Rightarrow, "ε'"{below, yshift=-2pt, xshift=3pt}, ""{name=E'}] \ar[triple, to=E', from= 1-1, "Φ", shorten >=6pt, shorten <=6pt]
    \end{tikzcd}
                                 
  \end{figure}

  Composition in \(\mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}}\) is defined by horizontal/vertical composition in \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) in the obvious way. Identities are given by
  \((\mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}},\mathbf{id}_E)\) on objects, and \((\mathbf{id}_F,\mathbf{id}_ε)\) on 1-cells. The 2-category axioms follow from those of \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\).
<!-- end definition-68 -->
<!-- remark-61: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:19}
  This reduces to our previous definition: for \(\mathcal{A} = \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}}\) and \(\mathcal{B} = \mathbf{UBP}\), the objects of \(\mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}}\) are representations \(F {:} \mathcal{C} → \mathbf{UBP}\); 1-cells are triangles \((H,ε)\) as in
  \cref{item:88}; 2-cells are natural transformations between the 1-cell functors over \(\mathbf{UBP}\) with a corresponding modifier (which has to be unique since \(\mathbf{UBP}\)
  consists of preorders). Thus, \(\mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}}\) is exactly \( \mathbf{\overset{\hookrightarrow}{Cat}}_{◆ \mathbf{UBP}}\).
<!-- end remark-61 -->
<!-- proposition-43: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:7}
  Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a sub-2‑category of \(\mathbf{Cat}\), \(\mathcal{B}_{★}, \mathcal{B}'_{★'}\) be oplaxly pointed 2‑categories, and \(F {:} \mathcal{B} → \mathcal{B}'\) a 2‑functor preserving the oplax point. Then \(F\) induces a 2‑functor \((-⨾ F) {:} \mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}} \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}'}\).
<!-- end proposition-43 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
We define \((-⨾ F)\) by postcomposition with \(F\). On objects, we set
  \[
    (-⨾ F)(\mathcal{C}, H) := (\mathcal{C}, H⨾F).
  \]
  On a 1-cell \((G, ε) {:} (\mathcal{C}, H) \to (\mathcal{D}, K)\), where \(G {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) and \(ε {:} H \Rightarrow G⨾K\), we define
  \[
    (-⨾ F)(G, ε) := (G, F(ε)) {:} (\mathcal{C}, H⨾F) \to (\mathcal{D}, K⨾F),
  \]
  where \(F(ε)\) denotes the whiskering of the 2-natural transformation \(ε\) with \(F\), which is point-preserving since \(ε\) and \(F\) are.
  On a 2-cell \((α, Φ) {:} (G, ε) \Rightarrow (G', \delta)\), consisting of a 2-natural transformation
  \(α {:} G \Rightarrow G'\) and a modification \(Φ {:} ε; (α⨾K) \Rightarrow \delta\), we set
  \[
    (-⨾ F)(α, Φ) := (α, Φ⨾ F),
  \]
  where \(Φ⨾ F\) is the whiskering of \(Φ\) with \(F\).

  To verify that \((-⨾ F)\) is a 2-functor, consider composable 1-cells \((G, ε) {:} (\mathcal{C}, H) \to (\mathcal{D}, K)\) and
  \((L, η) {:} (\mathcal{D}, K) \to (\mathcal{E}, J)\). Their composite in \(\mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}}\) is given by \((G⨾L, \gamma)\), where \(\gamma\) is the horizontal composite
  \[
    \gamma {:} H \xRightarrow{ε} G⨾K \xRightarrow{G⨾η} G⨾L⨾J.
  \]
  Applying \(F\), we obtain
  \[
    \gamma⨾ F {:} H⨾F \xRightarrow{ε⨾ F} G⨾K⨾F \xRightarrow{G⨾ η⨾ F} G⨾L⨾J⨾F.
  \]
  Because \(F\) is a 2-functor, this \(F(\gamma)\) is exactly the structure map of the composite \((G, F(ε))⨾ (L, F(η))\) in \(\mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}'}\). The preservation of identity 1-cells follows
  identically from \(F(\mathbf{id}) = \mathbf{id}\).

  Finally, vertical and horizontal composition of 2-cells in \(\mathcal{A}_{◆\mathcal{B}_{★}}\) are computed componentwise in \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\). Since \(F\) strictly preserves all compositions and
  identities of 2-cells, the assignment \((α, Φ) \mapsto (α, Φ⨾ F)\) is strictly functorial with respect to both vertical and horizontal composition. Thus, \((-⨾ F)\) is a strict 2-functor.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{le↘_:5}
  For each \(\mathcal{C}{:} \mathcal{A}\) and \(F{:} \mathcal{C} → \mathcal{B}_{★}\) with \(\mathcal{B}_{★}\) 2-pseudomonic and oplaxly pointed, \(F_{*}\) is a point-preserving 2-natural transformation \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}} \Rightarrow (F⨾ \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}){:} \mathcal{C} → \mathbf{UBP}\).
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
Since \(\mathcal{C}\) is a 1-category, 2-naturality holds trivially. It suffices to verify that each \(F_{*, X}\) is monotone and natural in 1-cells.

  For monotonicity, let \(ι \leq \kappa\) in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\), with representatives \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) and \(\kappa{:} B \hookrightarrow X\). By definition, there exists a (necessarily monic) 1-cell
  \(f{:} A \to B\) such that \(ι = f ⨾ \kappa\). Applying \(F\), we obtain a 1-cell \(F(f){:} F(A) \to F(B)\) in \(\mathcal{B}\). Since \(\mathcal{B}\) is pseudomonic, \(F(f)\) is pseudomonic, and thus
  \(F(ι) \leq F(\kappa)\) in \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(F(X))\). Hence \(F_{*, X}\) is order-preserving. Point-preservation holds since \(\top_{F(ι)} = \mathbf{id}_{F(ι)}\).

  For naturality, let \(g{:} X \to Y\) be a 1-cell in \(\mathcal{C}\). We must show that the maps \(F_{*, X} ⨾ F(g)_{*}\) and
  \(g_{*} ⨾ F_{*, Y}\) from \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)\) to \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(F(Y))\) are equal. Evaluating both on an element \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\), the left-hand side yields
  \[
    (F_{*, X} ⨾ F(g)_{*})(ι) = F_{*}(g)(F(ι)) = F(ι) ⨾ F(g),
  \]
  while the right-hand side yields
  \[
    (g_{*} ⨾ F_{*, Y})(ι) = F(ι ⨾ g).
  \]
  By the functoriality of \(F\), we have \(F(ι) ⨾ F(g) = F(ι ⨾ g)\), so the two composites agree pointwise. Thus, \(F_{*}\) is a natural transformation
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}} \Rightarrow F ⨾ \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}\).
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- definition-69: body_md -->
\label{defn_:4}
  \index{diamond}
  Given an oplaxly pointed 2-category \(\mathcal{B}_{★}\) and a sub-2-category \(\mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathbf{Cat}\), \emph{an \(\mathcal{A}\)-diamond in \(\mathcal{B}_{★}\)} is a section
  \(\mathcal{A} → \mathcal{A}_{◆ \mathcal{B}_{★}}\) of \(\mathbf{s}_{\mathcal{A}_{◆ \mathcal{B}_{★}}}\). We denote the 2-category of sections of \(\mathbf{s}_{\mathcal{A}_{◆ \mathcal{B}_{★}}}\) by \(\mathcal{A} ◆ \mathcal{B}_{★}\).
<!-- end definition-69 -->
<!-- remark-62: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:7}
  Thus, a diamond is a particular kind of reflection of \(\mathcal{A}\) in \(\mathcal{B}_{★}\), which assigns to each \(\mathcal{C}{:} \mathcal{A}\) a representation of \(\mathcal{A}\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) and to each functor and natural transformation in \(\mathcal{A}\)
  parameterized diagrams in \(\mathcal{B}\). So we have \(\mathcal{A}\) as a 2-category, so an object of \(2-\mathbf{Cat}\), but in a diamond we ``untangle'' \(\mathcal{A}\) into a diagram from which
  we define a coherent system out of. We can draw this like this:

  \begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzpicture}
    \draw[name=e] (0,0) ellipse (1cm and 0.5cm);
    \draw[black] (-1, 0) -- (0, -2);
    \draw[black] (1, 0) -- (0, -2);
    \node at (0, -2.25){\(\mathcal{A}_{★}\)};
    \node at (4, -2.25){\(\mathcal{B}\)};
    \draw[black] ({1/8 * (1 - sqrt(31))}, {1/16 * (-1 - sqrt(31))}) -- (4, -2);
    \draw[black] ({1/8 * (1 + sqrt(31))}, {1/16 * (sqrt(31) - 1)}) -- (4, -2);
  \end{tikzpicture}
                             
\end{figure}

Where the ellipse contains \(\mathcal{A}\) as a diagram in \(\mathbf{2-Cat}\) and the cone from that ellipse to \(\mathcal{B}\) is actually a special kind of 2-cocone consisting of a 2-functor
\(D(\mathcal{C}){:} \mathcal{C} → \mathcal{B}\) for each category \(\mathcal{C}\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) and lax higher cells as described in \cref{def:diamond-over}. But in the following we will denote such diamonds in diagrams like
this:

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \begin{tikzcd}
   \mathcal{A} \ar[r, -{Triangle[length=9mm, width=3mm]}] & \mathcal{B}_{★}.
 \end{tikzcd}
                           
\end{figure}
<!-- end remark-62 -->
<!-- remark-63: body_md -->
\label{rmk:3}
  By \cref{■pn_:7} we can postcompose a diamond with a 2-functor as if it was a functor. Since we use the \((-)_{*}\) notation quite a lot, we will just denote this as \(D⨾ F\).
<!-- end remark-63 -->
<!-- example-70: body_md -->
\label{xmp_:17}
  Let \(\mathbf{Cat}_{term}\) be the full sub-2-category of \(\mathbf{Cat}\) whose objects are small categories with a terminal object. Then slicing constitutes a
  \(\mathbf{Cat}_{term}\)-valued diamond (we spell out a proof below, but the procedure is the same as for \(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}}_{◆ \mathbf{UBP}}\)). Moreover, it seems like
  the proof of \cref{thm:1} can be straightforwardly adapted to \(\mathbf{Cat}_{◆ \mathbf{Cat}_{term}}\). Whether the currently going-on proof of \cref{thm:3} can also be adapted
  is less clear, but an analogue of it for non-monics should be true.
<!-- end example-70 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
We construct a 2-functor \(D: \mathbf{Cat}_{term} \to (\mathbf{Cat}_{term})_{◆ \mathbf{Cat}_{term}}\) that is a section of the source 2-functor \(\mathbf{s}\). Let \(\mathcal{A} = \mathbf{Cat}_{term}\).

  \emph{Action on objects.}
  For each category \(\mathcal{C} {:} \mathcal{A}\), we assign \(D(\mathcal{C}) = (\mathcal{C}, E_{\mathcal{C}})\), where \(E_{\mathcal{C}}{:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Cat}_{term}\) is the strict 2-functor given by taking slice categories:
  \[
    E_{\mathcal{C}}(X) \;=\; \mathcal{C}_{/X}.
  \]
  For a morphism \(f {:} X \to Y\) in \(\mathcal{C}\), the functor \(E_{\mathcal{C}}(f) = f_{*}{:} \mathcal{C}_{/X} \to \mathcal{C}_{/Y}\) acts by postcomposition, sending an object \(a {:} A \to X\) to \(a ⨾ f {:} A \to Y\). Because \(\mathcal{C}_{/X}\) has a terminal object \(\mathbf{id}_X\), it belongs to \(\mathbf{Cat}_{term}\). The oplax point \(\star_{\mathcal{C}_{/X}}{:} \mathbf{1} \to \mathcal{C}_{/X}\) selects this terminal object.

  \emph{Action on 1-cells.}
  For a functor \(F {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), we define \(D(F) = (F, \varepsilon_F)\), where \(\varepsilon_F{:} E_{\mathcal{C}} \Rightarrow F ⨾ E_{\mathcal{D}}\) is a point-preserving 2-natural transformation.
  For each \(X {:} \mathcal{C}\), the component \((\varepsilon_F)_X {:} \mathcal{C}_{/X} \to \mathcal{D}_{/F(X)}\) is the functor \(F_{/X}\) induced by postcomposition with \(F\):
  \[
    (A \xrightarrow{a} X) \quad \mapsto \quad (F(A) \xrightarrow{F(a)} F(X)).
  \]
  To see that \(\varepsilon_F\) is point-preserving, evaluate it on the point of \(\mathcal{C}_{/X}\), which is \(\mathbf{id}_X\):
  \[
    (\varepsilon_F)_X(\mathbf{id}_X) \;=\; F(\mathbf{id}_X) \;=\; \mathbf{id}_{F(X)},
  \]
  which is exactly the point of \(\mathcal{D}_{/F(X)}\).
  To verify 2-naturality, let \(f {:} X \to Y\) be a morphism in \(\mathcal{C}\). The following square of categories and functors must strictly commute:
  \[
    \begin{tikzcd}
      \mathcal{C}_{/X} \ar[r, "F_{/X}"] \ar[d, "f_{*}"'] & \mathcal{D}_{/F(X)} \ar[d, "F(f)_{*}"] \\
      \mathcal{C}_{/Y} \ar[r, "F_{/Y}"'] & \mathcal{D}_{/F(Y)}
    \end{tikzcd}
  \]
  For any object \(a {:} A \to X\) in \(\mathcal{C}_{/X}\), tracing right-then-down yields \(F(a) ⨾ F(f) = F(a ⨾ f)\), while down-then-right yields \(F(a ⨾ f)\). Thus, the square strictly commutes.

  \emph{Action on 2-cells.}
  For a natural transformation \(\alpha {:} F \Rightarrow G {:} \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), we define \(D(\alpha) = (\alpha, \Phi)\).
  By \cref{def:diamond-over}, we must provide a modification \(\Phi {:} \varepsilon_F ; (\alpha ⨾ E_{\mathcal{D}}) \Rrightarrow \varepsilon_G\).
  For each \(X {:} \mathcal{C}\), the transformation \((\alpha ⨾ E_{\mathcal{D}})_X {:} \mathcal{D}_{/F(X)} \Rightarrow \mathcal{D}_{/G(X)}\) is postcomposition with \(\alpha_X {:} F(X) \to G(X)\). We require a natural transformation \(\Phi_X {:} F_{/X} ⨾ (\alpha_X)_{*} \Rightarrow G_{/X}\) in \(\mathbf{Cat}_{term}\).
  For an object \(a {:} A \to X\) in \(\mathcal{C}_{/X}\), the source is the object \(F(a) ⨾ \alpha_X\) in \(\mathcal{D}_{/G(X)}\), and the target is \(G(a)\). By the naturality of \(\alpha\) in \(\mathcal{D}\), we have a morphism \(\alpha_A {:} F(A) \to G(A)\) satisfying \(\alpha_A ⨾ G(a) = F(a) ⨾ \alpha_X\).
  This makes \(\alpha_A\) a morphism in \(\mathcal{D}_{/G(X)}\) from \(F(a) ⨾ \alpha_X\) to \(G(a)\). We define \((\Phi_X)_a := \alpha_A\).
  The naturality of \(\Phi_X\) with respect to morphisms in \(\mathcal{C}_{/X}\), as well as the modification axioms for \(\Phi\), follow directly from the naturality of \(\alpha\).

  \emph{Section and 2-functor axioms.}
  By construction, the underlying object, 1-cell, and 2-cell of \(D(\mathcal{C})\), \(D(F)\), and \(D(\alpha)\) are \(\mathcal{C}\), \(F\), and \(\alpha\) respectively. Thus, \(D\) is a section of the source 2-functor \(\mathbf{s}{:} (\mathbf{Cat}_{term})_{◆ \mathbf{Cat}_{term}} \to \mathbf{Cat}_{term}\).
  Identities and compositions are strictly preserved because the slice and postcomposition operations define a strict 2-functor \(\mathbf{Cat} \to \mathbf{Cat}\) componentwise.
  Therefore, \(D\) constitutes a \(\mathbf{Cat}_{term}\)-valued diamond.
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- remark-64: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:10}
  This restriction means that our aimed-for theorem will sadly not just be a direct generalization of \cref{thm:1}, and such a thing is probably impossible.
<!-- end remark-64 -->
<!-- definition-70: body_md -->
\label{defn_:5}
\index{diamonds!2-category of}
  Given a sub-2-category \(\mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}}\), the \emph{2-category of diamonds \(◆(\mathcal{A})\) over \(\mathcal{A}\)} is the 2-category:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:39} whose objects are pairs \((\mathcal{B}_{★}, D{:} \mathcal{A} ◆ \mathcal{B}_{★})\) with \(\mathcal{B}_{★}\) an oplaxly pointed 2-category:

\begin{figure}[H]
      \centering
      \begin{tikzcd}
      \mathcal{A} \ar[r, -{Triangle[length=9mm, width=3mm]}] & \mathcal{B},
    \end{tikzcd}
                               
    \end{figure}
  \item\label{item:47} whose morphisms \(Δ{:} (\mathcal{B}_{★}, D{:} \mathcal{A} ◆ \mathcal{B}_{★}) → (\mathcal{B}_{★}', D'{:} \mathcal{A} ◆ \mathcal{B}_{★}')\) are given by pairs of
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item \label{item:48} a point-preserving 2-functor \(\overline{Δ}{:} \mathcal{B}_{★} → \mathcal{B}_{★}'\) (i.e. \(★_{\mathcal{B}_{★}}⨾ \overline{Δ} = ★_{\mathcal{B}_{★}'}\)),

    \item\label{item:49} a cell \(\underline{Δ}{:} D' → D⨾ \overline{Δ}{:} \mathcal{A} ◆ \mathcal{B}_{★}'\)
    \end{enumerate}

    \begin{figure}[H]
      \centering
      \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
        & \mathcal{B} \ar[dd, "\overline{Δ}"] \\
        \mathcal{A} \ar[ur, -{Triangle[length=16mm, width=3mm]}, "D"{name=D}] \ar[dr, -{Triangle[length=15mm, width=3mm]}, "D'"'{name=E}] &\\
        & \mathcal{B}',
        \ar[Rightarrow, from=E, to=1-2, "\underline{Δ}", shorten <= 10pt]
    \end{tikzcd}
                               
    \end{figure}
        

  \item\label{item:50} whose 2-morphisms \(I{:} Δ \Rightarrow Δ°\) are given by pairs of

    \begin{enumerate}
    \item\label{item:51} a point-preserving 2-natural transformation \(\overline{I}{:} \overline{Δ} \Rightarrow \overline{Δ}°{:} \mathcal{B}_{★} → \mathcal{B}_{★}'\) and

    \item \label{item:52} a 2-cell \(\underline{I}{:} \underline{Δ}° \Rightarrow \underline{Δ}; (D⨾ \overline{I}){:} \mathcal{A} ◆ \mathcal{B}_{★}'\).
    \end{enumerate}

    So a filling of this diagram opposite to \(\overline{I}\):

    \begin{figure}[H]
      \centering
      \begin{tikzcd}[every matrix/.append style={name=m}, column sep=large]
        & \mathcal{B} \ar[dd, "\overline{Δ}"{yshift=-14pt}, "\hphantom{\overline{Δ}}"{name=T}, bend left]
        \ar[dd, "\hphantom{\overline{Δ}°}"'{name=U}, "\overline{Δ}°"'{yshift=-14pt, xshift=3pt}, bend right]; \\
        \mathcal{A} \ar[ur, -{Triangle[length=16mm, width=3mm]}, "D"{name=D}]
        \ar[dr, -{Triangle[length=15mm, width=3mm]}, "D'"'{name=E}] &\\
        & \mathcal{B}'
        \ar[Rightarrow, from=T, to=U, "\overline{I}", shorten >=3pt, shorten <=3pt, yshift=-5pt]
\ar[from=E, "\underline{Δ}"'{yshift=14pt, xshift=12pt}, Rightarrow, -{Implies}, shorten <=5pt, shorten >=-7pt,
    to path={ (\tikztostart) -- ($(m-1-2)!0.3!(m-3-2)$) \tikztonodes }]
\ar[from=E, "\underline{Δ}°"{yshift=-5pt}, Rightarrow, -{Implies}, shorten <=5pt, shorten >=3pt,
to path={ (\tikztostart) -- ($(m-1-2)!0.1!(m-2-1)$) \tikztonodes }, shorten >=10pt]
  \end{tikzcd}
                             
    \end{figure}
\end{enumerate}

  The \emph{2-category of diamonds \(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{◆}(\mathcal{A})\) over \(\mathcal{A}\) on monics} is the (on all levels) full sub-2-category of \(◆(\mathcal{A})\) on 2-pseudomonic 2-categories \(\mathcal{B}_{★}\) .
<!-- end definition-70 -->
<!-- proposition-44: body_md -->
\label{■pn_:9}
\index{subobject functor!contravariant terminality}
  For any subcategory \(\mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathbf{Cat}\) of monic categories and monomorphism-preserving functors,
  \(\mathbf{SOb}{:} \mathcal{A} → \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}\) is contravariantly terminal in \(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{◆}(\mathcal{A})\) (see \cref{defn_:9}).
<!-- end proposition-44 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
\label{prf_:7}
  The constructions of \cref{■pn_:6}, \cref{■pn_:7}, and \cref{le↘_:5} together furnish the morphism
  \((\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}, D_{*}){:} (\mathcal{B}_{★}, D) \to (\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}, \mathbf{SOb})\), as was discussed in the preceding paragraphs. It remains to show that
  this is an initial object in the hom-category \(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{◆}(\mathcal{A})\bigl((\mathcal{B}_{★}, D),\, (\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}, \mathbf{SOb})\bigr)\). We have also for each other morphism
  \((\overline{Δ}, \underline{Δ}){:} (\mathcal{B}_{★}, D) → (\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}, \mathbf{SOb})\) constructed a 2-morphism \((\overline{Δ}_{★}, \leq)\). For uniqueness, note that for any top-preserving natural transformation \(\mathcal{I}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}} \Rightarrow \overline{Δ}\) and \(ι{:} A \hookrightarrow X\) in \(\mathcal{B}_{★}\) it holds that the square

  \begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \begin{tikzcd}
    \overline{Δ}(A) \ar[r, "\overline{Δ}(ι)"] & \overline{Δ}(X) \\
    \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(A) \ar[u, "\mathcal{I}_{A}"]\ar[r, "ι_{*}"'] & \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}(X) \ar[u, "\mathcal{I}_{X}"']
\end{tikzcd}
                              
\end{figure}

commutes, so that \(\mathcal{I}_{X}(ι) = \overline{Δ}_{★, X}(ι)\), since \(\mathcal{I}_{A}\) preserves tops. Thus, \(\mathcal{I} = \overline{Δ}_{★}\), so that \(\mathcal{I}\) is unique since 2-cells in \(\mathbf{UBP}\) are unique.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{le↘_:6}
  \(ι_{\mathbf{UC}}\) is the terminal section of \(\mathbf{SOb}⨾ (-)_{*}{:} \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}} → \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}\).
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
\label{prf_:8}
  We just showed that \(ι_{\mathbf{UC}}\) is a section. Let \(S{:} \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}} → \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}\) be some other section. Then we can for each
  \(P{:} \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}\) define a functor \(μ_{S, P}{:} S(P) → ι_{\mathbf{UC}}(P)\) given by \(μ_{S, P}(X) := ι_{\mathbf{UC}}(μ_{X, *})(\top)\)
  for \(X{:} S(P)\), and for each \(f{:} X \hookrightarrow Y\) in \(S(P)\) by \(μ_{S, P}(f) {:} ι_{\mathbf{UC}}((\top_{f_{*}} \leq \top_{Y})⨾ μ_{Y, *})\). This is functorial in \(P\) since
  \(\mathbf{SOb}\) is functorial and \(ι_{\mathbf{UC}}\) a full embedding.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{le↘_:7}
  Assume that the image of \(\iota_{\mathbf{UC}}\) lies in \(\mathcal{A}\) and that \(\eta\) is a strict diamond 2-cell. For \(P {:} \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}\), identify
  \[
    \rho_P {:} P \cong \mathbf{SOb}_{P}(\top_P), \qquad a \mapsto (a \hookrightarrow \top_P),
  \]
  and let
  \[
    \theta_P {:} \overline{\mathbb I}(P) \longrightarrow G(P)
  \]
  be the component \(\eta_{\iota_{\mathbf{UC}}(P),\top_P}\), transported along \(\rho_P\). Define
  \[
    \Sigma_P := \theta_P^{-1}.
  \]
  Then \(\Sigma {:} G \Rightarrow \overline{\mathbb I}\) is a 2-natural isomorphism.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
The identification \(\rho_P\) is natural in \(P\): for a monotone map \(f {:} P → Q\), the induced comparison \(\mathbf{SOb}_{P}(\top_P) → \mathbf{SOb}_{Q}(\top_Q)\) sends the subobject \(a \hookrightarrow \top_P\) to \(f(a) \hookrightarrow \top_Q\), using the unique inequality \(f(\top_P) \leq \top_Q\). Hence evaluation at terminal objects, after restriction along \(\iota_{\mathbf{UC}}\), carries the diamond 2-cell \(\eta\) to a 2-natural transformation
  \[
    \theta {:} \overline{\mathbb I} \Rightarrow G.
  \]
  Since \(\eta\) is assumed invertible, each component \(\theta_P\) is invertible; thus \(\theta\) is a 2-natural isomorphism.

  It remains to check that the inverse components assemble into a 2-natural transformation. Let \(f {:} P → Q\). The 2-naturality of \(\theta\) gives the equality of 1-cells
  \[
    \theta_P ⨾ G(f) \;=\; \overline{\mathbb I}(f) ⨾ \theta_Q .
  \]
  Using invertibility of \(\theta_P\) and \(\theta_Q\), we compute
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
    \theta_P^{-1} ⨾ \overline{\mathbb I}(f)
    &= \theta_P^{-1} ⨾ \overline{\mathbb I}(f) ⨾ \theta_Q ⨾ \theta_Q^{-1} \\
    &= \theta_P^{-1} ⨾ \theta_P ⨾ G(f) ⨾ \theta_Q^{-1} \\
    &= G(f) ⨾ \theta_Q^{-1}.
  \end{aligned}
  \]
  Thus \(\Sigma = \theta^{-1}\) is natural on 1-cells.

  For a 2-cell \(\alpha {:} f \Rightarrow g {:} P → Q\), the 2-naturality of \(\theta\) gives
  \[
    \overline{\mathbb I}(\alpha) ⨾ \theta_Q \;=\; \theta_P ⨾ G(\alpha).
  \]
  Whiskering by the inverses of \(\theta_P\) and \(\theta_Q\) yields
  \[
    \theta_P^{-1} ⨾ \overline{\mathbb I}(\alpha)
    \;=\;
    G(\alpha) ⨾ \theta_Q^{-1},
  \]
  which is precisely the 2-naturality of \(\Sigma\). Since every component \(\Sigma_P = \theta_P^{-1}\) is invertible, \(\Sigma\) is a 2-isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:3}
\index{universal characterization of UBP}
  Given a sub-2-category \(\mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}}\), such that \(ι_{\mathbf{UC}}\) factors through \(\mathcal{A}\), let \(\mathbf{CT}(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{◆}(\mathcal{A}))\) be the sub-2-category of \(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{◆}(\mathcal{A})\) on the
  contravariantly terminal objects, whose morphisms \(Δ\) are the pairs from \cref{item:47} such that \(\underline{Δ}\) is a 2-isomorphism. Then
  \((\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}, \mathbf{SOb})\) is initial in \(\mathbf{CT}(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{◆}(\mathcal{A}))\).
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-65: body_md -->
\label{rmα_:24}
  It is surprisingly hard to tell which 2-functors out of \(\overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}}\) induce a contravariantly terminal diamond. Each point-preserving 2-functor
  \(F{:} \overset{→}{\mathbf{UBP}} → \mathcal{B}_{★}\) introduces a diamond \((\mathcal{B}_{★}, \mathbf{SOb}⨾ F)\) by \cref{■pn_:7} but to be contravariantly terminal, for each diamond
  \((\mathcal{D}, D)\) there has to exist an initial diamond-morphism from \((\mathcal{D}, D)\) to \((\mathcal{B}_{★}, \mathbf{SOb}⨾ F)\). Postcomposition with \(F\) induces a morphism given by
  \((\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}}⨾ F, D_{*}⨾ F)\), but the question is: when is this morphism initial? For this, each diamond-morphism
  \(Δ{:} (\mathcal{D}, D) → (\mathcal{B}_{★}, \mathbf{SOb}⨾ F)\) has to induce a unique 2-morphism \(\mathbb{I}{:} (\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}}⨾ F, D_{*}⨾ F) \Rightarrow Δ\). Unpacking the definitions we find that
  \(Δ\) consists of a 2-functor \(\overline{Δ}{:} \mathcal{D} → \mathcal{B}\) and a cell \(\underline{Δ}{:} (\mathcal{B}_{★}, \mathbf{SOb}⨾ F) → (\mathcal{B}_{★}, D⨾ \overline{Δ})\) in
  \(\mathcal{A} ◆ \mathcal{B}_{★}\). Unpacking further we find that \(\underline{Δ}\) consists for each \(\mathcal{C}{:} \mathcal{A}\) of a cell
  \(\underline{Δ}_{\mathcal{C}}{:} (\mathcal{C}, \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}⨾ F) → (\mathcal{C}, D(\mathcal{C})⨾ \overline{Δ})\) over \((\mathcal{C}, \mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}})\) and thus a 2-natural transformation
  \(\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{C}}⨾ F \Rightarrow \mathbf{id}_{\mathcal{C}}⨾ D(\mathcal{C})⨾ \overline{Δ} = D(\mathcal{C})⨾ \overline{Δ}\) in \(\mathcal{B}^{\mathcal{C}}\). So \(\underline{Δ}\) has to be a 2-cell making this diagram commute:

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \begin{tikzcd}
    \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{Cat}} \ar[dr, "\mathbf{SOb}"', ""{name=S}] \ar[r, "D"] & \mathcal{D} \ar[d, "\mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}}"{yshift=-6pt, xshift=1pt}] \ar[dr, "\overline{Δ}"] & \\
    & \overset{\hookrightarrow}{\mathbf{UBP}} \ar[r, "F"'] & \mathcal{B} \ar[Rightarrow, from=S, to=1-2, "D_{*}"']
  \end{tikzcd}
                               
\end{figure}

On the other hand, \(\mathbb{I}\) has to consist of a 2-natural transformation \(\overline{\mathbb{I}}{:} \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{D}}⨾ F \Rightarrow \overline{Δ}\) and a modification
\(\underline{\mathbb{I}}{:} \underline{Δ} \Rrightarrow (D_{*}⨾ F); (D⨾ \overline{\mathbb{I}})\). So for each \(X{:} \mathcal{C}{:} \mathcal{A}\) the horn

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \begin{tikzcd}
    (\mathbf{SOb}⨾ F)(X) \ar[d, "(D_{*}⨾ F)(X)"'] \ar[dr, "\underline{Δ}_{X}"] & \\
    (D⨾ \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}⨾ F)(X) & (D⨾ \overline{Δ})(X)
  \end{tikzcd}
                               
\end{figure}

has to have a unique filling:

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \begin{tikzcd}
    (\mathbf{SOb}⨾ F)(X) \ar[d, "(D_{*}⨾ F)(X)"'] \ar[dr, "\underline{Δ}_{X}", ""{name=E}] & \\
    (D⨾ \mathbf{SOb}_{\mathcal{B}}⨾ F)(X) \ar[r, "(D⨾ \overline{\mathbb{I}})(X)"'] & (D⨾ \overline{Δ})(X) \ar[Rightarrow, from=E, to=2-1, "\underline{\mathbb{I}}"'{xshift=-5pt, yshift=-1pt}, shorten <= 6pt]
  \end{tikzcd}
                               
\end{figure}
<!-- end remark-65 -->
